News.title: Panama earthquake live: Tsunami alerts across Central America as buildings crumble
News.content:
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama sparked tsunami warnings in several countries across Central America and lead to buildings crumbling

A massive earthquake in Panama sparked tsunami warnings in Central America and caused buildings to collapse.

The magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit Panama at around 1pm local time on Friday.

According to the USGS, the quake struck 12km west south west of Pitaloza Arriba. It was initially reported as magnitude 8, but this was later downgraded to 7.7. It remains unclear if there have been any fatalities at this point.

Footage showed the moment TV presenters ran for their lives as the quake struck.

It triggered tsunami warnings in nine countries - Panama, Mexico, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Peru and El Salvador - but they have since been lifted.

News.title: Hero firefighter honoured by the King reveal he's haunted by the faces of Grenfell Tower victims
News.content:
Hero firefighter honoured by the King reveal he's haunted by the faces of Grenfell Tower victims

Paul Courtney's astonishing 30-year career working as a firefighter saw him handed a Humanitarian Award by King Charles - but he told how he was secretly battling the trauma of attending the Grenfell Tower blaze

View 8 Images Paul Courtney was honoured by the King last year with his daughter, Delilah, while secretly battling PTSD

Beaming with pride as he's honoured by the King, it should have been the crowning moment of Paul Courtney’s astonishing career.

‌



‌



But the veteran firefighter was secretly battling crippling PTSD, haunted by the horrors of the Grenfell Tower blaze. Today he told how he spent 12 days scouring the charred tower block after the inferno left at least 72 dead in 2017.

‌



The father-of-two - a member of the elite UK International Search and Rescue - revealed how he discovered the bodies of a family huddled together among the blackened debris. In the days that followed, he learned their identities when their photos flashed up on TV screens as the true scale of the devastation emerged.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 8 Images Paul joined the LFB in 1997 before working with the elite UK International Search and Rescue outfit

Murdered Leah Croucher's parents demand fresh law that may have stopped killer sex predator READ MORE :

Sophie Lancaster killer to walk free despite denying he took part in attack on her READ MORE :

And Paul said their faces haunt him every night despite years of trying to come to terms with the trauma. Speaking just days after police handed files on 20 organisations and 54 people to the Crown Prosecution Service, Paul said he was sent to Grenfell just 24 hours after the fire to assess the structure.

‌



He said: "I would wake up screaming at 3am in the morning thinking somebody had broken into the house because there's people standing at the end of my bed looking at me. But there was nobody there. It started to affect me, I couldn't sleep and I was tired.

"I'd let my wife go to sleep, I'd come down downstairs and put the TV on or read a book. Then I'd fall asleep on the sofa and wake up with my neck all crooked and uncomfortable and then I have to go to work and do it all again.

View 8 Images At least 72 people died in the Grenfell fire in June 2017 and many more were left with the scars of what they witnessed (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I knew that that night I'd wake up and do exactly the same and it was just like Groundhog Day. It was just continuous and scary." Paul signed up to the London Fire Brigade in 1997 before he was seconded to the elite UKISAR, travelling to Malawi and Kenya to carry out life-saving work.

During his career he attended the 7/7 suicide bombing at Tavistock Square in 2005 to help forensic teams deconstruct the twisted wreckage of the number 30 bus where 13 people died and more than 100 were injured. And he was deployed to Morocco in 2023 to scour remote settlements across the Atlas Mountains when a 6.8-magnitude quake left 2,900 people dead.

Paul was awarded the Humanitarian Medal by King Charles at Buckingham Palace in 2025 for his work in north Africa. But despite being deployed at disaster zones in the UK and abroad, it was the haunting aftermath of the 2017 blaze in West London that left Paul traumatised.

‌



View 8 Images Paul went to Brazil in May for the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group global team leaders' meeting

And he is not alone. Fire brigade heroes traumatised by the Grenfell Tower tragedy have taken more than 8,000 days off work due to PTSD. Figures show that even nine years on from the blaze, firefighters took 445 sick days last year because of the psychological trauma they suffered.

A Freedom of Information request shows 8,218 working days have been lost due to firefighters suffering PTSD. Another 446 days were lost from 999 control room staff also affected by psychological trauma. London Fire Brigade says 30 staff – 27 firefighters and three control operators – have been diagnosed with PTSD since the disaster.

‌



So far, 16 staff – 15 firefighters and one member of the 999 control room staff – have been retired because of their psychological damage. Today Paul said: "Grenfell is constant, it's something I experience every evening, it's always a constant in the background. It's like the badge I bear for being there. It's a badge I don't want to have. I never want to do another Grenfell Tower ever again."

View 8 Images Paul said he found the strength to continue thanks to his wife, Rosalie, 46, and his two children, Harrison, 25, and Delilah, 17

Re-living his time spent at Grenfell, he said: "When I pulled up to it, it was pretty much like it looked like a scene from a movie set. It had a sort of ashen look, it almost looked like something out of a movie scene. It didn't look real. My first task was to inspect the structure so I walked every floor. Some of them were still smouldering away.

‌



"Nobody could have survived the fire inside the tower. When I arrived everybody that had been lost in the fire was still in the building. Okay. All around the base of the tower and the stairwell, you stepped through the debris on the floor, and it was just an indication of the chaos.

"On the stairs there were car keys, glasses, false teeth, clothes, pets, walking sticks, bodies, all of those are indications of how chaotic it must have been trying to get people out. There was no borrowed light, it was just complete darkness. It is a tube with a staircase in it inside the centre of the tower.

View 8 Images Paul spoke about the "chaotic" scenes which must have unfolded during the Grenfell Tower fire which claimed 72 lives (Image: PA)

‌



"So initially the search was all by torchlight, going up and down stairs with that circular beam of light. It would light up a pet or a body. I'm 5ft 10ins, quite broad shouldered, but two of us couldn't pass on the stairs together."

Paul, who lives in Watford, Herts., said it took nine months to finally realise how traumatised he was by the experience of attending Grenfell. He said: "I was at work and a senior officer said to me, 'Are you OK Paul?' Because I just wasn't myself I think. And I went, 'No, I'm not boss, really'. And he went, 'Come on let's go and grab a cup of tea'.

"And we went for a walk and then I explained what was going on, and he said, 'Right, let's get you some help'. And, you know, he's the man that made the difference, because it was a dark old place without him. I thank him every time I see him."

‌



View 8 Images Paul will bring the curtain down on an astonishing career next month when he retires

Paul - who became the training and assurance officer for the UKISAR team in 2021 - has spent years trying to come to terms with what he witnessed at Grenfell, sharing his experience with colleagues and undergoing Trauma Risk Management sessions. But he still wakes up each night to the faces of those who died in the blaze - but says he has learned to live with their presence.

It is only thanks to his wife, Rosalie, 46, a business relations manager in a care home, and his two children, Harrison, 25, and Delilah, 17, that he has found the strength to continue.

‌



Speaking on World Mental Health Day, Paul - who retires on November 29 - said: "I waited nine months to get help, which was stupid, I should have got help sooner." Paul told his story as he backed the Gratitude Games, designed to spark a national conversation about the mental health of emergency responders.

View 8 Images Paul told his devastating story to highlight the upcoming Gratitude Games, organised by ex-firefighter Ricky Nuttall (Image: Ricky Nuttall)

The event is designed to highlight the mental health challenges of those who protect us from harm. Paul took part last year in the clay pigeon shooting event, raising £600 for charities that help first responders.

‌



He said: "Money raised in the Gratitude Games can go a long way to help somebody, a fellow blue light responder." Sixty-six per cent of fire service personnel and 70 per cent of police officers have grappled with mental health issues, according to research from the charity, Mind.

For ambulance workers, this figure rises to 76%. Meanwhile, anxiety, stress, depression and other psychiatric illnesses were the most reported reasons for sickness in the NHS, accounting for more than 610,500 full-time equivalent days lost and 27.5% of all sickness absence in March 2025.

The Gratitude Games - supported by Grenfell Tower firefighter Ricky Nuttall - takes place next year but organisers are now asking participants to register to take part. The 2027 event will mark 10 years since the Grenfell blaze and a decade since the Manchester Arena bombing.

‌



The brainchild of Mike Downard, a serving firefighter with Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue. It was launched in 2018 when he saw a growing need for additional support for all the UK’s emergency service workers.

He realised that an annual sporting event could raise the funds required to help create a bespoke, tailored and most importantly unlimited mental health service for our nation's heroes. In June this year, the inaugural Gratitude Games saw athletes from all over the UK and across all our services, descend upon Manchester the host city, to take part and raise money, turning this dream into a reality.

Organisers are shortly about to open registration for next year's games, again hosted by Manchester and in partnership with E.J. Churchill, Forces Equine, Scimitar and Tour De Manc. Next year the games will be even bigger with the exciting addition of a huge 7-a-side football tournament alongside Clay Shooting, Equestrian, 10k road run, Cycling and more.

Article continues below

Participants are asked to raise funds with every penny going to our charity partners, Police Care UK, The Ambulance Staff Charity, The Firefighters Charity and The Blue Light Card Foundation.

More details can be found at www.gratitudegames.uk

News.title: Murder probe launched after pensioner found dead in UK town
News.content:
Murder probe launched after pensioner found dead in UK town

Avon and Somerset Police say their officers were called to a property on Friday afternoon when they made the tragic discovery - a man in his 70s has been arrested

View 2 Images Sherbourne Avenue in Bradley Stoke

A man has been arrested over the death of an elderly woman found dead in her home in a UK town.

Emergency services were called to a property in Sherbourne Avenue, Bradley Stoke in South Gloucestershire at around 2pm on Friday, October 9. The force have stated that the pensioner, in her 70s, was found with serious injuries and was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.

A man, also in his 70s, has been arrested on suspicion of murder and enquiries continue. Police say that the investigation is in its 'early stages' as the force attempt to establish an 'understanding of this tragic incident'.

Supt Karen Corrigan of Avon and Somerset Police said: “We would like to offer our sincere condolences to the woman’s grieving family at what will be a devastating time for them, and specially trained officers will provide them with ongoing support.

View 2 Images Police have released a statement [file image] (Image: DAILY RECORD)

Article continues below

“The investigation is in its early stages, but we have arrested a man, who remains in police custody, while we seek to gain an understanding of this tragic incident.

“This will come as a great shock to the community, but we do not consider there to be any ongoing risk to the public and if anybody has any concerns, they are welcome to approach officers in the area.

“We will have an increased police presence in the area over coming days in order to carry our vital enquiries as part of this investigation and to provide reassurance to members of the community.”

News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's pals 'urge him to take legal action against King Charles'
News.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's pals 'urge him to take legal action against King Charles'

King Charles stripped Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor of his titles and royal status last year after it emerged he continued to message Jeffrey Epstein despite claiming he cut off contact

View 3 Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's friends have reportedly urged him to consider legal action (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Friends of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor have reportedly urged him to mount a legal challenge against his brother King Charles over his decision to remove his titles and royal status.

Andrew's reputation was left in tatters after it emerged he had continued speaking with the paedophile Jeffrey Epstein, despite claiming to have cut off contact with him in December 2010. Andrew has consistently denied any wrongdoing regarding his association with the late billionaire.

Following the revelation, Charles stripped Andrew of his remaining royal titles in the autumn of last year.

But Andrew's confidence has reportedly grown in recent days after the High Court ruled warrants used to search his home were unlawful. Thames Valley had used the warrants to raid his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor as well as a property on the Sandringham estate.

View 3 Images Andrew's reputation has been left in tatters after details about his association with Epstein emerged (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Should King Charles stop giving money to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

"He remains the son, brother and uncle of future monarchs," a royal source told the Daily Mail. "Most people don’t realise that technically he is still the Duke of York – he still insists on being called 'Sir' and 'Duke' at home. Only an Act of Parliament can extinguish his title."

Disgraced Andrew has been buoyed by a reported stream of "fan mail" being delivered to his new Marsh Farm home on Sandringham Estate. Many of the letters are said to have been opened by his part-time secretary, who sends a formal acknowledgement to the well wishers.

The criminal investigation against Andrew is ongoing and the items seized in the raids in Norfolk and Berkshire remain with the police while his legal challenge continues. Andrew was arrested by Thames Valley Police last year on suspicion of misconduct in public and questioned for 12 hours.

View 3 Images Andrew was stripped of his titles last year (Image: AP)

Article continues below

Another court hearing will take place next year that will decide if police can keep items seized during the searches, which means the ex-prince could remain in limbo for several more months before learning if he will be charged with an offence.

Charles continues to provide his brother with cash, in the form of an annual stipend to help pay for his living costs at his Marsh Farm on the Sandringham estate.

A Buckingham Palace source said earlier this week it had been made clear that the money should not be used to fund the Judicial Review

News.title: Judge Navi Pillay beats Donald Trump to win Nobel Peace Prize 2026 - latest
News.content:
Judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize - dealing another blow to Donald Trump, who once again insisted he deserved the prestigious award

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to South African judge Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay for her "efforts to promote peace and international law".

The 85-year-old, a former United Nations human rights chief, is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar is accused by The Gambia of committing genocide against the Rohingya people.

Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said of Ms Pillay: "A common thread runs ⁠from her early work ⁠defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against ⁠apartheid to her service as a judge ⁠in some of ‌the key international court cases of our time."

Mr Frydnes said the committee had not yet been able to reach Ms Pillay to inform her of the award. Addressing her directly, he said that if she was watching and saw a call coming in from a Norwegian phone number, she should "please pick up".

Ms Pillay's win means US President Donald Trump has once again been snubbed for the prestigious award - despite insisting he deserved it. He told reporters on Wednesday that it would be a "great discredit" to the committee if he were not awarded the prize.

Pope Leo XIV and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney were among those tipped to receive the award.

News.title: Trump blasted as 'weak' by Zelensky after he takes 5million tonnes of diesel from Russia in Putin sweetheart deal
News.content:
Trump blasted as 'weak' by Zelensky after he takes 5million tonnes of diesel from Russia in Putin sweetheart deal

President Donald Trump says he has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of US pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine, in a bid to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.

View 3 Images Trump claims he's struck a deal with Putin for diesel (Image: Andrew Harnik, Getty Images)

Donald Trump claimed he's secured a deal to get diesel from R us sia, marking a remarkable U-turn from years of US pressure on Moscow regarding its conflict with Ukraine.

‌



‌



The deal would simultaneo us ly attempt to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. Trump revealed on social media on Friday that he reached the deal with R us sian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call that had been anticipated to address a s us pected outbreak of plague in R us sia.

‌



Instead, Trump declared that R us sia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes more in November and 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter".

‌



View 3 Images Trump claimed the deal would benefit Americans (Image: Aaron Schwartz-Pool via CNP/Shutterstock)

UK and allies stand up to Donald Trump and US over International Criminal Court sanctions READ MORE :

Trump orders firing squad execution days after Christa Pike's botched lethal injection READ MORE :

R us sia will deliver another three million tonnes "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote. The temporary license will allow Russian diesel into the US market.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

‌



Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

He said Russia would repay the deal "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged. "It plays into Russia's hands - allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

‌



This comes as petrol prices have spiked in the US amid the ongoing war against Iran. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev praised the deal in a social media post, adding: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

Trump's bombshell announcement follows his signing of a sweeping R us sia sanctions law last month, which sought to tighten the grip on R us sia's energy economy, amongst other sectors, that funds its war against Ukraine.

View 3 Images Trump has been scrambling to bring down petrol prices for Americans ahead of the midterm elections (Image: Aaron Schwartz-Pool via CNP/Shutterstock)

‌



The legislation sanctions R us sian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers, while prohibiting all new US investment in R us sia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also instructed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the top five importers of R us sian oil or natural gas, with an exemption for nations that import less than 15 per cent of R us sia's natural gas exports and have taken considerable steps to reduce those imports.

The UK will “maintain pressure on Russia” through tough sanctions, Downing Street has said as US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow.

Article continues below

The price of petrol and diesel have focused the minds of Americans ahead of the crunch midterm elections. The cost of living, particularly petrol, is a major concern among voters.

Polls have shown a clear majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the war.

News.title: UK weather maps show ‘4mm per hour’ snow and torrential rain within days
News.content:
UK weather maps show ‘4mm per hour’ snow and torrential rain within days

The Met Office has said snow could fall in some parts of the UK this weekend, and now forecasting models suggest even more may follow later this month

View 3 Images The outlook for 6am on October 22 (Image: WXCHARTS)

Forecasting models suggest a major weather front could be just days away from sweeping across the UK, bringing snow and torrential rain.

‌



‌



The GFS weather model shows the rain moving in from the Atlantic in the early hours of October 22, drenching most of Wales and England by 6am.

‌



By 9am, the maps show the precipitation falling as snow over Northumberland National Park, the Pennines and southern parts of Scotland. The data suggests snow could fall at a rate of around 4mm per hour, with some lighter flurries also hitting the Highlands.

‌



Most of the rain will have moved into the North Sea by midday, according to the maps, but some light snow could persist in western Scotland and around the Scotland-England border.

View 3 Images The outlook for 9am on October 22 (Image: WXCHARTS)

Met Office says snow could fall this weekend as UK braces for colder weather READ MORE :

Met Office snow forecast

This comes after the Met Office said snow could fall in some parts of the UK this weekend.

‌



The national weather agency said Saturday may “begin on a chilly note”, although “brighter conditions” are on the cards in southern areas.

“Showers will move through widely during the day, with northern parts of the UK likely to see the most frequent and intense downpours,” the forecast said.

The showers are expected to be heaviest in Scotland, where this is also a risk of hail and thunder. The Met Office added: “There could even be a temporary sprinkling of snow over the highest ground, adding a wintry flavour to the autumn weather.”

‌



View 3 Images The outlook for midday on October 22 (Image: WXCHARTS)

BBC Weather forecast

The BBC Weather forecast states: “[Saturday] is expected to remain windy, with showers in the north, especially the north-west, but southern regions should be generally dry with long sunny spells.

“Largely dry and settled on Sunday. There will be plenty of sunny spells, but in the southwest, cloud and patchy rain will move in by the end of the day.

Article continues below

“Monday will see some brightness in the east, but it will then turn cloudy and damp across the UK with spells of light rain.”

News.title: NI secretary to ban the Drumcree parade
News.content:
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said he will ban the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.

The dispute has led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.

Sir Chris said the chief constable advised him "it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland".

His decision has been welcomed by Sinn FÃ©in and the SDLP, but DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he now needs to "explain what his government intends to do to restore confidence in the rule of law".

The move comes on the 13th day of deadlock between residents and the local district lodge of the Orange Order.

The Parades Commission had ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place.

But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road.

Under legislation, a secretary of state can overturn a Parades Commission determination, especially following input from the police.

Sir Chris had been coming under increasing pressure from Sinn FÃ©in and the SDLP to stop the parade.

Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the parade.

On Friday night, Sir Chris said: "The Parades Commission have advised me that while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect.

"Consequently, and in the interests of wider public interest and safety, I've come to the conclusion that the circumstances under which that decision was made have now changed considerably.

"As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined."

Speaking about Sir Chris' decision, Boutcher said he had outlined to the secretary of state his "current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted".

"Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention," he said.

He added: "Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long-term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process."

In a statement, the Parades Commission said it "recognises the importance of resolving the issues arising from this dispute and hopes that a way forward can be found through constructive engagement between those concerned".

Earlier, First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute.

On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

News.title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Being a Traitor must be a nightmare.

While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.

Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.

And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).

When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.

"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."

Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."

Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."

On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised.

"I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.

"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.

"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."

I guess now we'll never know.

News.title: Polanski vows to stay on as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
News.content:
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.

The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Lichtenstein's comments come after two former Green leaders accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.

Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.

The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year.

Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

Following the by-election, Lichtenstein was asked whether it would be right for Polanski to continue as leader of the party. She told Times Radio: "No, I think he should resign."

Earlier in the week, Lichtenstein, who has been a member of the Green Party for nearly three decades, told Radio 4's Today programme it was "quite possible" she would leave the party after the Zionism row.

Speaking to the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire on Friday, she said she would not resign immediately because she is having conversations about how to "detoxify" the party.

When asked if she had confidence in Polanski's leadership, Lichtenstein said: "At the moment, no I don't." She added that she was "very disappointed" in him.

Calling on Polanski to apologise, she said: "I don't think that any Jew in the party is going to be in any danger...

"There just might be some unpleasant people who will direct some unpleasant comments, and some of us are going to have to deal with them robustly."

Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.

The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Adrian Ramsay, a Green MP and former co-leader, declined to back Polanski on Friday, and said he was now working to reverse the motion.

"A lot depends on what happens in the days and weeks to come," he told the BBC's Politics East, when asked if Polanski should still lead the party.

"[He] did not show leadership I would have been looking for."

News.title: Weekend showers and sunshine for UK ahead of warmer temperatures next week
News.content:
It will be a weekend of two halves weather-wise for most people with many seeing a cool start on Saturday.

A strengthening north-westerly wind will carry showers across the UK. But Sunday looks calmer with sunshine in the north and east and rain creeping into the south and west.

Looking further ahead, next week will see a return to above average temperatures.

Tuesday looks set to be the warmest day of the period and could reach 21C for some. However a deep area of low pressure is likely to bring some stormy weather across the north.

News.title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
News.content:
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.

The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.

Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.

Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-NiÃ±o fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.

Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.

In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"

Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.

Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El NiÃ±o conditions in the Pacific.

It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.

The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.

After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.

As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).

News.title: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend
News.content:
Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.

The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as JesÃºs Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison.

Debra Robinson, the brother's mother, told the courtroom in the northern Baja California state the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

During the trial the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area.

Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico.

Debra Robinson and her husband Martin Robinson have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict.

"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said Martin.

Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link.

Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".

During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.

At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

Amid the demands for action, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ãvila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state.

"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.

"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

News.title: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
News.content:
Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in February, in the middle of a storm of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The former Prince Andrew was moved to Sandringham, with his brother the King using his own money to provide his upkeep and accommodation.

Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested later that month on suspicion of misconduct in public office - and a court ruling on Thursday found fault with the search warrants used by the police.

But despite moving to Sandringham, Mountbatten-Windsor's lease on Royal Lodge had remained until October - and as that officially ends, the Crown Estate is revealing the terms on which it concluded.

When Andrew had taken on the 75 year lease in 2003, he had made considerable up-front payments, including about Â£7.5m for repairs, which meant that he did not have to pay a monthly rent.

It also meant that if he gave up the lease within the first 25 years he would be legally entitled to some compensation - with that amount reducing each year.

Leaving in October 2026 would have meant that the Crown Estate would have had to pay him back about Â£302,000.

However that amount has been overshadowed by what he owes to the landlord for the state of the building - and so the Crown Estate says it has now received a net amount of Â£1.5m.

It's understood that the payment of that money by the King is to avoid leaving the Crown Estate out of pocket.

Whether Mountbatten-Windsor will repay his brother is said to be a private matter - and there are no further details of what this might say about Andrew's personal finances.

There was also no comment on how the King feels about this arrangement - and there is said to be no connection between this payment and the King making clear this week that his financial support should not go to cover Andrew's legal costs in his battle over search warrants.

It has so far not been decided how the 30-room mansion in Windsor will be used in future, but it is expected to be used to deliver a commercial return - and at present there are no plans for another royal occupant.

"The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return," said a Crown Estate spokesperson.

A report by the National Audit Office had revealed earlier this year that Mountbatten-Windsor had been sub-letting buildings at Royal Lodge, although the amount was never revealed.

That report from the public spending watchdog also showed that Andrew's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Eugenie, had accommodation inside royal palaces which they did not pay for, with the cost being covered privately by the King.

News.title: Early release scheme prisoner jailed days after leaving
News.content:
A man has been jailed for a number of shoplifting offences days after being freed under the government's early release scheme.

Michael Bogle, 38, was released from HMP Wandsworth on 1 October as part of the first wave of prisoners to be let out under the plan.

Speaking to reporters outside the prison following his release, Bogle said the conditions inside were "awful" and said "people like me" should not be in prison "for a long time".

In the four days after his release, Bogle stole more than Â£100 worth of detergent from supermarkets in north London.

He was arrested on Tuesday and admitted the offences in court on Wednesday, resulting in an eight-month sentence.

The previous 32-week sentence he was released from early had been suspended but he was jailed for breaching its terms. He served 78 days.

Asked if he had a message for Prime Minister Andy Burnham after his early release, Bogle said: "Keep the early release going. It's good."

The scheme was brought in to relieve pressure on prisons across England and Wales which were dangerously close to reaching full capacity.

It is understood the force's highest ranking commander in north-west London referred to his case in a letter raising concerns about the early releases.

Det Ch Supt Luke Williams outlined the details of the "astonishing" case in correspondence to local politicians, which was later shared by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp.

Without naming Bogle, the letter, sent on Wednesday, said he had been identified as a high-risk offender by the probation service but was released on 1 October.

"Just one day after his release" he was recorded on CCTV stealing, Williams said.

News.title: Widdecombe suspect had 'particular hostility to Reform', court told
News.content:
The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe had a "particular hostility to Reform", prosecutors alleged on Friday.

They said Joshua Kerry, 28, "had an extreme left wing and/or anti-establishment mindset".

The prosecution also told the Old Bailey Widdecombe's murder had a "terrorist connection" as it was "politically and ideologically motivated".

Last week, Kerry, who had already been charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, was charged with a second offence of preparing terrorist acts.

He is accused of "online reconnaissance" of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Nigel Farage's home in South London on 19 April 2025, and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb agreed to the prosecution request to join the two charges into one case.

The prosecution argued they were "inextricably linked".

Kerry appeared in court by video link from Belmarsh prison wearing a prison-issue grey sweatshirt.

The judge set a date for a five-week trial on 8 June next year.

The next hearing will be on 29 January.

Nicholas Lumley KC, defending, told the court that Kerry was likely to contest all the charges against him.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform spokeswoman.

Widdecombe was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

The former Tory MP was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch, prosecutors said during a hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court in July.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

She became a member of Reform in 2019.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

News.title: Ofsted faces fresh calls to halt graded school inspections in England
News.content:
A second head teachers' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections in England, saying it is "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale" of its members.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) also raised the prospect of potential strike action, saying a new grading system had become an "overbearing mess".

On Friday, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said an independent survey of education providers showed it was "on the right track" with inspections.

The Department for Education (DfE) said ministers were "working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better".

ASCL's announcement comes after another union, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), said changes Ofsted made to inspections just under a year ago had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.

ASCL said it had passed a motion of no confidence in "the ability of Ofsted's leadership to address the damage being done by the new inspection system", adding that it was "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary, said the union did not take the step "lightly", but added Ofsted's "warm words about recognising wellbeing pressures... have not been matched by the action necessary" and that "negotiation [had] hit a brick wall".

"The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed," he said.

News.title: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership
News.content:
Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.

As first reported by the Financial Times, external, the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday.

Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one.

Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said: "The vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment.

Lib Dem MP and former leader Tim Farron also defended Sir Ed, saying under his leadership the party was in a position to match or even beat the "record numbers of MPs" the party won at the last election.

"To think we're helped by this kind of rubbish, you'd need to be smoking the kind of stuff even we aren't in favour of legalising," he quipped.

Several other Lib Dem MPs, including some frontbenchers, also gave Davey their backing in social media posts on Friday evening.

Julian Brazil, a Liberal Democrat council leader who has previously been critical of Sir Ed, said Maynard had "put his head above the parapet - we'll see if other people follow".

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live's Matt Chorley, he said: "I would have thought that in the next few days, we will see if there's a groundswell behind him."

Brazil added that Sir Ed had been a "fantastic leader" but added: "For whatever reasons people aren't listening to Ed, they don't take notice of him, so we need to have a fresh start and be able to articulate what our vision of the country is.

"I think that's best done by someone else."

Maynard was first elected to his Oxfordshire constituency in 2024, winning the traditionally Conservative seat, formerly held by David Cameron, with a majority of more than 4,000.

Before becoming an MP, he ran an international mergers and acquisitions advisory firm.

He is the second Lib Dem to leave the frontbench this week, following Alison Bennett's decision to resign her post of spokesperson for care and carers.

Bennett would not confirmed why she stepped down but it is understood it was not for personal reasons.

Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs.

To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties.

Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats.

However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels.

More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest.

Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty".

"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said.

One Lib Dem MP described Sir Ed's argument as "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

News.title: Autism, ADHD and mental health review: What you need to know
News.content:
No time should be wasted in tackling these challenges, the review says.

On long waits, it says everyone on a waiting list should be reassessed so that those most in need are prioritised for help. There should no longer be a first-come, first-served approach.

Some of those waiting may benefit from non-medical support, advice about sleeping better or getting more physical exercise, for example. That may even lead to some being removed from the waiting list.

There should also be better assessments before people are placed on waiting lists too. Not every problem needs a medical solution, the experts make clear.

Quality and consistency of autism and ADHD assessments must be improved, with the review highlighting concerns about those done by the private sector on behalf of the NHS. Half of ADHD and a third of autism assessments are done by non-NHS providers, such as charities and private firms.

But they are not subject to the same regulation as NHS providers â and this must change.

The experts also said it wanted to see a ban on direct-to-public advertising of assessments.

The review has said it wants to see action over the next 12 to 24 months. The government has promised to act â and is expected to set out more details in its forthcoming mental health strategy which is expected by the end of the year.

News.title: Woman found dead in burning van was pregnant, police say
News.content:
A woman found dead in a burning van was pregnant, police have confirmed.

The body of Samantha Natalie Phythian, 35, was discovered in the vehicle in Prestatyn, Denbighshire, on Sunday evening.

On Friday it was revealed in a court hearing that Samantha, from Rhyl, was alive when the fire started.

Thomas Bell, 38, from Wellington Road in Rhyl, appeared in Mold Crown Court charged with murder and was remanded in custody.

The court was told Phythian was known to Bell but he denies setting the vehicle alight.

After the hearing police said they had also arrested a 47-year-old "local man" on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson and possession with intent to supply drugs in connection with the death.

News.title: Teen's life transformed by gene editing
News.content:
A teenager has revealed how her life has been transformed thanks to pioneering gene editing, which reversed symptoms of a crippling blood disorder.

Vian, 16, was born with thalassemia, a condition that affects haemoglobin - used by red blood cells to transport oxygen around the body. It left her short of breath and with no appetite.

Her own stem cells were edited and she no longer needs the monthly blood transfusions she endured for most of her life.

"My whole life's different now. It's changed so much," she said.

The treatment, for patients with thalassaemia or sickle cell disease, is offered to young people at three children's hospitals in the country.

Vian, from Coventry, was one of the first to have it.

News.title: Abusive ex admits murdering woman after she began new relationship
News.content:
A man with a history of domestic abuse has admitted murdering his former partner a day after learning she had begun another relationship.

Lee Inglis pled guilty at the High Court in Edinburgh to stabbing Stacey Hogg to death in her home in Hawick earlier this year.

BBC Scotland News has learned that the 39-year-old had twice avoided prison for previous knife attacks on the mother of three.

He was still serving a home curfew and an unpaid work order when he killed the 35-year-old in June.

He waited until his curfew ended at 07:00 before making the three-minute journey from his parents' home to Stacey's house.

Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting

The court heard that he slipped in through the back door and attacked Stacey as she came down the stairs.

She suffered "catastrophic wounds" to her neck and head. Police found her in a pool of blood on a downstairs bathroom floor.

The court heard that when he was arrested by police he told them: "I intended to cut off her head."

"If I couldn't have her, nobody would," he added.

Inglis will be sentenced at the High Court in Edinburgh on 5 November.

News.title: New evidence gives family hope after death in Spain
News.content:
Four years after watching his brother die in his arms, Maximilian White believes new evidence could help him get answers.

Tobias White-Sansom, a father-of-two from Nottingham, died in a Spanish hospital in July 2022, five days after a night out in Magaluf, and his family believes the way security and police officers handled him that night led to his death.

A blood spatter report and a court order received by the family this month have reignited their hopes that criminal proceedings could commence in the Spanish courts.

White told the BBC: "I won't stop until we get justice for Toby."

The 46-year-old medical cannabis entrepreneur said he found it difficult to talk about the way he lost his younger sibling, who was on a family holiday at the time.

White-Sansom was pinned down at a nightclub following a row over him removing his T-shirt because he was too hot, his family said.

They told the BBC the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was called and he was handcuffed, Tasered and injected with tranquilisers before going into cardiac arrest.

News.title: Boosting US oil supplies with Russian diesel unlikely to have much impact on prices, experts say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S. more than 300,000 tons of diesel. That would be followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November, then 4 million more tons at some point after that.

The deal marks a stark reversal of policy by the U.S., which from the start of Russia’s war with Ukraine had banned imports of Russian oil, and comes at a time when the U.S. economy and consumers are being squeezed by a global rise in oil prices due to the eight-month-long U.S. war with Iran.

The price of diesel has shattered records in recent weeks, ratcheting up inflation for a broad swath of consumer goods.

The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22, according to motor club AAA. It averaged nearly $6.28 a gallon on Friday, up from almost $3.68 this time last year. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too.

Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That’s because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.

Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel.

That’s turned up the heat on Trump and the Republican Party to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The president’s approval ratings on the economy have hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll released last week, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.

A limited impact, at best

Energy policy experts on Friday expressed doubts that a boost in diesel supply from Russia will have a significant impact on oil prices, whether in the U.S. or globally.

“It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics.

“If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now,” Lynch said.

And while the White House may be counting on this move to give some relief at the pump for U.S. truckers, ranchers and farmers who have been hit hard by rising diesel prices, that’s not a given.

“The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe,” Lynch said. “It just means that the oil is just going to be shuffled around and it’s not really going to change the price globally or across the U.S.”

If Russia, which in July moved to ban diesel exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries, now believes it is able to resume exports of diesel, then that will help stabilize global diesel prices, said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy.

However, prices are likely to remain elevated overall because a lot of refining capacity in the Middle East isn’t available to the world market due to the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz from the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.

“Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels,” Sternoff said. “So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them.”

While the deal between Trump and Putin probably won’t have much of an impact on prices for diesel consumers in the U.S., it will benefit Russia, said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

That’s because Russia is trying to offload its summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months, Seigle noted.

“I don’t think it’ll be enough to materially lower prices in the United States or Europe, but it does certainly let Moscow off the hook in terms of revenue squeeze,” he said.

News.title: Doritos and other Pepsi Co snacks are about to get more expensive
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

PepsiCo will raise prices on Doritos and other popular snacks and drinks following a slump in North American sales, the company announced.

The price adjustments — driven by rising costs for fuel, aluminum and agricultural commodities — will be single-digit percentage increases. Despite the hikes, product prices will still be lower than at the start of the year.

Doritos, Ruffles, SunChips and some sodas are all expected to see increases, though the exact amount was not revealed.

Although PepsiCo previously offset higher expenses using a $178 million U.S. government tariff refund issued after the Supreme Court invalidated President Donald Trump’s far-reaching global tariffs, the company confirmed those funds would not carry over into later quarters.

open image in gallery PepsiCo announced that it is hiking prices on Doritos, Ruffles and select beverages after third-quarter sales stumbled across North America ( Getty Images )

To adjust for the softer domestic sales, the company reduced its full-year earnings expectations to between 2.5 percent and 3.5 percent adjusted growth per share, down from a prior estimate of 5 percent to 7 percent. Total revenue growth for the full year is now projected at 6 percent.

Raising prices poses serious risks for U.S. companies when so many American families are already financially strained. During 2022 and 2023, PepsiCo enacted eight consecutive quarters of double-digit percentage hikes to counter post-pandemic inflation.

In response to dropping sales volumes, activist firm Elliott Investment Management acquired a $4 billion stake in the company last fall and pushed for cost reductions. PepsiCo then lowered prices on Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos and Tostitos by up to 15 percent earlier this year.

Chief Executive Ramon Laguarta said lower pricing brought back some shoppers, but sales in Canada remained weak. Domestic Frito-Lay snack volumes were flat year-over-year for the July-September period, while North American beverage volumes dropped 2 percent.

“We don’t feel good about the beverage business,” Laguarta said on a conference call, adding, “We’re putting all the urgency of the business and the focus in improving our performance in soft drinks.”

open image in gallery Despite the hikes, product prices will still be lower than at the start of the year ( Getty Images )

Despite weaker North American sales, PepsiCo reported a 17 percent rise in third-quarter net income to $3.07 billion, while revenue grew 5.6 percent to $25.27 billion, beating Wall Street expectations of $24.95 billion.

Growth was driven by international markets, which account for 41 percent of total revenue. Global snack volumes rose 4 percent — the fastest pace since 2021 — led by strong demand in China, Brazil and the broader Asia-Pacific region.

Demand grew fastest for protein-enhanced items and simple-ingredient lines, including Gatorade Lower Sugar and Doritos free of artificial colors or flavors. Adjusted earnings reached $2.34 per share, topping the $2.29 predicted by analysts.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

News.title: New York prosecutors seek to sustain their case against Luigi Mangione, despite his federal plea
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

New York prosecutors sought Friday to keep their murder case going against Luigi Mangione, arguing that his federal guilty plea shouldn't end a separate, state-court case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

The state and federal prosecutions center on “different harms, different evils, different purposes, different crimes,” Manhattan Assistant District Attorney Joel Seidemann and colleagues wrote in a court filing.

Mangione's defense lawyers are trying to get the state murder and weapons charges thrown out, citing double jeopardy. It's the legal precept that broadly prevents a person from being repeatedly prosecuted for the same crime, though the particulars can be complicated and disputed when different courts are involved.

In response to prosecutors’ filing Friday, Mangione's attorneys pointed to their own previous court papers arguing that the state and federal governments are “prosecuting the same man twice for the same event.”

A ruling is expected in late autumn.

At stake is whether Mangione will continue to face a trial in a New York state court in Manhattan and, potentially, how much prison time he will serve if he's convicted. He's already looking at the likelihood of a lengthy federal sentence. A state conviction, if there is one, could add more time.

The Manhattan prosecutors argue that double jeopardy doesn't apply to Mangione's situation. Though their case and the federal prosecution both concern Thompson's December 2024 killing, the Manhattan prosecutors contend that the specific charges involve different legal elements and criminal conduct.

Mangione pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking and cyberstalking charges, admitting in court that he traveled across state lines to New York to kill Thompson and then shot him from behind on a Manhattan street. The 28-year-old said he gunned for the CEO after experiencing years of severe back pain and “navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”

In the state case, meanwhile, Mangione pleaded not guilty in 2024 to murder, weapons and fake-ID charges. If he goes to trial, his admission in federal court might be used against him.

Thompson, 50, led one of the United States’ largest health insurers. His killing — with ammunition that authorities said was marked “delay,” “deny” and “depose” — alarmed the healthcare industry while baring the anger that many Americans feel about it. Some people cast Mangione as a valiant figure, even as others, including public officials, said the killing was anything but heroic.

Mangione, a scion of a prominent Maryland real estate family, has undergraduate and master's degrees in computer science. He worked for a car-buying website for a time. He never had UnitedHealthcare's insurance, police said.

News.title: Kash Patel wants to bring in UFC trainers to teach FBI agents hand-to-hand combat: report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

FBI agents could soon get a new training course - from athletes in one of the president’s favorite sports.

Director Kash Patel has launched a bid to bring in Dana White’s UFC trainers to teach special agents mixed martial arts techniques, according to a report.

Patel, who attended President Donald Trump’s UFC birthday bash at the White House, is now seeking a one-year “sole source” contract with the UFC to provide a training program for agents in “defense tactical techniques,” according to an agency document released in September.

“The purpose of the training is to enhance physical combat abilities, mental toughness, and tactical awareness, which are crucial for special agents in high-risk situations,” the document, which was first reported by MS NOW, read. It’s unclear how much the contract is worth, as the estimated figure was redacted.

White is the president of the UFC and a longtime friend of Trump. The president has attended numerous UFC matches throughout the years, and even brought the Octagon to the White House South Lawn in June to celebrate America’s 250th birthday — and his 80th birthday. Patel is also a fan of the sport and has been seen at events.

open image in gallery FBI Director Kash Patel, who attended President Donald Trump’s UFC birthday bash at the White House, has launched a bid to bring in Dana White’s UFC trainers to teach special agents mixed martial arts techniques ( AFP via Getty Images )

The FBI said the UFC was “uniquely qualified” to conduct the training in its document, noting the trainers’ skills in “striking techniques, grappling/takedowns, weapon defense, ground control, as well as conditioning to the standard that the FBI expects and requires.”

The proposed deal would bypass the bidding process required for federal contracts, something the Trump administration has done in the past.

During the botched renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the National Park Service awarded Greenwater Services, an Ohio-based firm with ties to a Trump donor, a $1.7 million no-bid contract to install a water-purification system, The New York Times reported in June. Days after the project was complete, the basin turned green from algae blooms.

The FBI said in the newly revealed document that the proposed contract’s one-year term “will allow for more market research to be conducted and allow for vendors to become more equipped to handle this requirement.

“The long-term contract that will be created in the future will be done so on a competitive basis.”

The Independent has reached out to the FBI for comment on the proposed deal.

open image in gallery White and Trump have been close for years with the president attending numerous UFC events ( Getty Images )

This would not be the first time the FBI worked with the UFC.

The UFC announced in early March that its current and former athletes would visit Quantico that week to host a two-day training seminar for FBI Special Agent Academy students and senior FBI staff from around the world.

“This is a tremendous opportunity for our FBI agents to learn and train with some of the greatest athletes on earth - helping the world’s premier law enforcement agency be even better prepared to protect the American people,” Patel said in a statement at the time.

“Dana White has changed the game in the mixed martial arts industry and we’re extremely honored to be partnered with him, the professionals, and the UFC. We are grateful for their shared love of our nation, so that we can better defend her.”

News.title: Queen reveals King Charles favourite book genre and says he ‘roars with laughter while reading’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Queen has opened up on her love of reading and also offered an insight into the King’s literary habits.

Speaking on the BBC Arts programme The Book That Changed My Life, airing next week, Queen Camilla said reading is "like the best tonic in the world".

Camilla also revealed King Charles’ fondness for biographies, saying he will occasionally "roar" with laughter as they read before dinner.

She said: “My husband and I actually read before dinner, we just like sitting quietly and reading.”

The King loves biographies, the Queen says, adding: “I occasionally, when I’m deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something. It’s very off-putting. I can’t get back into my book.”

She added that it is “a lovely quiet time” and “I think it would be a complete and utter tragedy if books went forever”.

In the documentary, Camilla explored the transformative power of reading, bringing together four individuals whose lives have been altered by literature.

open image in gallery Camilla revealed Charles’ fondness for biographies ( PA )

She sat down with an HGV driver, a former prisoner, a roadside cafe owner, and a man who experienced depression following an incident at home.

Describing the gathering in a message delivered to a press preview, she called it "one of the most unusual book club meetings I have ever attended".

Camilla also spoke about where her passion for books originated, while discussing her own love of reading, alongside the King’s and her late father’s.

She said: “I left school quite young… so I think reading has been most of my education.

“We must’ve been very, very young when my father started reading to us. I think that’s where my love of reading came from.

“We were transported into all sorts of other worlds.

“I don’t think our childhood would’ve been the same if we hadn’t had books.

“We started off with Treasure Island and Peter Pan, all those lovely old classics.

“You learn so much about people, about life. I think people who don’t read miss out so much.

“That’s why I think it’s so important to get children reading early.”

Major Bruce Shand served in the Second World War as a 12th Lancer, fought alongside the Desert Rats, received the Military Cross twice and was wounded and taken prisoner while fighting in North Africa.

The Queen recounted memories of her father and his experience being held in a German prisoner of war camp when reading reinforced a lifelong enthusiasm for the written word.

“A sniper shot him through his face, he was incredibly lucky because the bullet went in one side, out the other, didn’t touch his tongue or his teeth,” she says.

open image in gallery Camilla spoke about where her passion for books originated ( PA )

“He was taken to a prisoner of war camp and incarcerated for two and a half years. Those places, there’s not much to do unless you’re plotting your escape.

“So he said he educated himself because he read every single book, from the bible to the encyclopaedia, whatever was there, he just sat all day long and read, read, read, and that’s, I think, how he survived it.

“Like all that generation, they never talked about the war. He buried it all because he’d seen such horrendous things.

“So we never heard him speaking about his wartime experiences, but he wrote it all down in this book, Previous Engagements.”

The Queen read an excerpt from the book, then said: “It was written from the heart. I mean, I cried through most of it. I found it so moving, because I didn’t know anything about it and reading managed to get him through it.”

In a message from the Queen delivered at a preview screening of the programme this week, she said books “have certainly enriched my own life beyond measure”.

She added: “While I find it impossible to point to a single title or author, or even to a single genre, that stands above others, reading for pleasure has helped entertain, comfort and inspire me in so many ways over the years.

“I have long believed that books are in fact the very best form of escapism, transporting us to other places and into other lives – other hearts and minds – in ways that greatly enhance our own.

“That is why, five years ago, I launched my Queen’s Reading Room, an online space I hoped would foster in adults and children alike a lifelong love of literature, and connect more people with that special magic that can only be found in the leaves of a book.”

Camilla said it is her “fondest hope that this film will build on that work, helping demonstrate to audiences around the world just what a difference reading has made to one particular group of people, each of whom has faced challenge or difficulty in their personal lives, and each of whom has been lifted up by the sheer joy and transformative power of reading”.

One of the documentary’s contributors, Ian Kirby, from Gateshead, fell into a deep depression after a traumatic incident at home.

He turned his life around after joining a local book club and picking up the autobiography of local boxing hero, Glenn McCrory, which offered a new perspective on his own experiences.

Now he describes himself as living a rich and fulfilled life, with reading at the heart of his recovery.

Speaking in the documentary, he says: “That is the beauty of a book. It can give you experiences you’ve never experienced, but they can also be an inspiration.”

The Queen ended the documentary by saying “books change people’s lives”.

The Book That Changed My Life will air on BBC Two and iPlayer on October 14.

News.title: ‘I’ve lost friends since my cancer diagnosis. People withdrew from me’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thousands of individuals living with cancer may be being "ghosted" by loved ones while navigating their diagnosis and treatment, a charity has warned.

Macmillan Cancer Support said this "cancer ghosting" leaves many patients feeling they are confronting the condition "alone".

Several patients have detailed losing decades-long friendships after being diagnosed.

One described how friends "disappeared from my life", while another felt "hurt" when close companions "withdrew" following her diagnosis of endometrial cancer – cancer of the lining of the womb.

Macmillan Cancer Support is encouraging people to take "small practical steps" to show up for relatives or friends. Simple actions can include sending a message, checking in regularly, or attending medical appointments with someone, according to the charity.

Among those affected is Lisa Walker, a retired social care worker from Edinburgh, who lost friends she had known for decades after receiving her diagnosis.

“I had people withdraw from me that I never thought would,” the 61-year-old said.

open image in gallery Lisa Walker, a retired social care worker from Edinburgh, described losing friends she has known for decades after she was diagnosed with cancer ( PA )

Ms Walker, who was diagnosed with kidney cancer when she was 50 and has since been diagnosed with four other types of cancer over the past decade, added: “Friends I’d known since school and others I had known for years, people I had spoken to two or three times a day.

“They just stopped talking to me and disappeared from my life, almost as though I meant nothing.

“It really affected me.”

Ms Walker went on: “I kept asking myself what I had done wrong and whether the friendship had ever been as genuine as I thought it was… and that was incredibly painful.

“But I’ve also learned that the people who truly matter are the ones who stay, even when they don’t know what to say, even when things are difficult, and even when you’re not the easiest person to be around.

“I would have much rather someone said, ‘I don’t know what to say, but I’m here for you’, than say nothing at all.”

Mev Ghazanfar, a HR business partner, was diagnosed with endometrial cancer in 2018.

The cancer has spread to other parts of her body and is now considered incurable.

“I’ve had quite a few people withdraw from me since my diagnosis, and I’ve lost some really close friendships because of it,” the 38-year-old from Hampshire said.
