World.title: The monetization of Discontent: Why happy marriages are unprofitable to big tech, by Stephany Shaakaa
World.content:
File image

To debate whether social media causes high divorce rates is to misunderstand the deeper problem. The more consequential question is what happens when the economic logic of the modern internet collides with the emotional logic of marriage.

We often describe the digital deterioration of relationships as an unfortunate side effect of modern connectivity. Online flirtation, secret direct messages, endless screen time, exposure to attractive strangers and the temptation to compare one’s marriage with the lives displayed on a screen. But that explanation misses something fundamental. Social media is not merely a technology that happens to sit inside our relationships. It is an economic system built to capture attention, and attention is easier to capture when people are restless than when they are content.

A happy marriage may be priceless to the people living it. To the attention economy, however, contentment is difficult to monetise.

Social media companies compete for the scarce resource of human attention. Their platforms are designed to keep people returning, scrolling, reacting, comparing, watching and sharing. The longer the engagement, the more opportunities exist for advertising and other forms of monetisation. The system therefore rewards novelty, emotional stimulation and material that makes people feel something strongly enough to keep looking.

That does not require a boardroom to declare war on marriage. It requires only an economic structure that benefits from sustained attention.

And marriage, at its healthiest, often asks for the opposite.

A person who feels secure in their home, anchored in their marriage and reasonably fulfilled by the ordinary work of partnership has less reason to spend hours searching for emotional stimulation elsewhere. Contentment can make the phone less interesting. A stable relationship can reduce the appetite for external validation. A life that feels sufficiently full does not constantly demand another screen to complete it.

Dissatisfaction is different

When we feel alone, we reach for any window into someone else’s world. When we feel behind, we look around to see who is keeping pace. When self-doubt creeps in, we search for a voice to steady us.And when the quiet becomes too quiet, we chase whatever promises to shake up the room.

Emotional frustration creates an appetite for recognition from somewhere else. None of these emotions was invented by social media, but digital platforms have built an extraordinarily efficient infrastructure for finding, measuring and rewarding them.

Every marriage eventually enters the unedited territory of ordinary life.Financial pressure, physical exhaustion, domestic chores, changing bodies, conflicting expectations, difficult conversations and seasons when romance gives way to responsibility. Long-term commitment is sustained not by permanent excitement but by the willingness to remain present when excitement temporarily disappears.

Social media operates according to a different logic.

It presents the extraordinary as ordinary. The feed is filled with expensive holidays, elaborate proposals, immaculate homes, beautiful bodies, romantic surprises, successful careers and apparently effortless happiness. What appears to be a picture of somebody else’s life is often only a carefully selected fragment of it, but repeated exposure can quietly distort the standard against which ordinary life is judged.

The tired spouse sitting beside you on the couch is not being compared with another tired human being. That spouse is being compared with thousands of carefully selected moments from thousands of other people’s lives.

It is an impossible contest

The argument before the photograph is invisible. So is the debt behind the holiday, the exhaustion behind the smile, the resentment behind the anniversary caption and the years of compromise behind the apparently effortless relationship. The internet gives us the polished outcome while marriage requires us to live through the unfinished process.

Over time, that asymmetry can impose a psychological tax on the home. Ordinary imperfections begin to look like evidence of failure. A difficult season begins to resemble a defective marriage. A spouse’s limitations, once understood as part of being human, can begin to feel like personal deprivation.

And then the smartphone introduces something older forms of marriage could not provide at this scale: an apparently infinite supply of alternatives.

A former lover can reappear with a single search. An old acquaintance can return through a suggested connection. A stranger can become an admirer through a comment, a reaction or a private message. Thousands of people who would once have remained completely outside one’s social world are now permanently available through a device in one’s hand.

The psychological consequence is profound. The question inside a difficult marriage can quietly change from “How do we work through this?” to “Is this really the best I could have done?”

That is the danger of permanent option value.

When alternatives appear abundant and accessible, the normal friction of a long-term relationship can stop being treated as something to work through and start being interpreted as evidence that a better option is waiting elsewhere. Patience begins to look like settling. Compromise begins to look like deprivation. Commitment itself can begin to feel irrational when the digital world is constantly displaying other possibilities.

The small currencies of digital validation deepen the problem. A like, a compliment, a saved photograph, a flattering comment or a private message may appear insignificant in isolation. But repeated micro-validations can become an alternative emotional economy, providing recognition precisely when a person feels unseen, frustrated or dissatisfied at home.

A person does not necessarily have to leave a marriage to begin withdrawing from it.

They can remain physically present while gradually moving their emotional attention elsewhere.

This is why the modern relationship crisis cannot be reduced either to individual morality or to technology alone. Marriages fail for countless reasons, many of them having nothing to do with social media. Platforms can also strengthen relationships, reconnect families, sustain long-distance intimacy and create communities that would otherwise be inaccessible

But those benefits do not change the underlying economic incentive.

The attention economy does not need human beings to be unhappy. It merely benefits when they are sufficiently dissatisfied, curious, insecure or stimulated to keep looking.

That distinction matters because marriage depends upon a quality the attention economy has little financial reason to cultivate,enough contentment to stop looking.

Marriage asks two people to invest deeply in one imperfect human being. The platform asks the user to keep exploring what else is available. Marriage rewards patience, the feed rewards novelty. Marriage requires tolerating repetition; the algorithm is built around preventing boredom. Marriage asks us to repair what is difficult; the digital marketplace makes replacement perpetually visible.

These are not merely competing technologies. They are competing ideas about how human attention should be used.

We have allowed the private sanctuary of the home to exist inside an economic system that has learned how to monetise restlessness. The danger is not that Big Tech has secretly decided that marriages must fail. The deeper danger is that an industry whose revenues depend upon sustained attention has incentives that can amplify precisely the comparison, dissatisfaction, novelty and validation-seeking that make contentment harder to sustain.

The question, therefore, is not whether social media single-handedly causes divorce. It does not.

The harder question is whether we are willing to recognise that the digital environment surrounding modern marriage is not neutral.

We have built an economy in which attention is currency, dissatisfaction can be engagement, comparison can be traffic, and emotional restlessness can be profitable.

And then we wonder why people find it increasingly difficult to be content with what they already have.

A marriage does not become fragile merely because temptation exists. It becomes more vulnerable when every frustration is accompanied by a thousand visible alternatives, when ordinary life is constantly measured against manufactured perfection, and when the patience required to build something lasting is interrupted by an economy that profits from the next click.

Protecting marriage in the digital age therefore requires more than love. It requires an awareness of what is competing for that love’s attention.

Because marriage survives through the quiet accumulation of ordinary acts: staying, listening, forgiving, adjusting, sacrificing, repairing and beginning again.

None of that is particularly profitable to Big Tech.

Two people sitting quietly together, satisfied with one another and uninterested in what the algorithm wants to show them, may be one of the least monetisable things on the internet.

Perhaps that is precisely why, in an age built to keep us looking, learning how to be content with one another has become an act of resistance.

World.title: Asaba Massacre at 59: Wounds, apologies and a day of forgiveness
World.content:
Asagba Azinge, SAN (L) exchanging pleasantries with Obi of Onitsha during the Asaba Massacre memorial on Wednesday.

•Asagba recalls Odi massacre, punctures OBJ’s ‘never again’ narrative; Col Taiwo’s son, a rtd Maj Gen, atones for father’s role in massacre

By Egufe Yafugborhi

59 years after the pogrom that wiped out an estimated 1,000 Asaba men, memories remain raw as apologies, forgiveness and the quest for national closure turn front burners.

The sun was going down in Asaba 59 years ago when a generation of families lost fathers, husbands, brothers and sons.

The killings of October 7, 1967, during the Nigerian Civil War left an estimated 1,000 Asaba men dead and a community carrying a wound that time has failed to erase.

On Wednesday, October 7, 2026, Asaba remembered again.

But the 59th memorial was not only about mourning. It became a remarkable encounter between the pain of the past and gestures towards reconciliation.

Former President Olusegun Obasanjo expressed regret, Major General Ahmed Ibrahim Taiwo (retd.), son of Col Ibrahim Taiwo, apologised over late father’s role, and the Asagba of Asaba, HRM Prof. Epiphany Azinge, SAN, publicly declared forgiveness for the Taiwo family.

Yet, beneath the forgiveness was a condition.

For the Asagba, Asaba can forgive without forgetting. But the community’s long search for closure, he insisted, requires a formal apology from a sitting President of Nigeria.

Former President Obasanjo, who participated virtually as Chairman of the occasion, described the massacre as “one of the most painful, one of the most terrible aspects” of the Civil War.

He said, “When Chief Nduka-Eze (Memorial Convener), some two months ago, came to see me about this unfortunate event and gave me written documents of what I had only heard by word of mouth, I wept.

“I wept that such an event—which is not fiction—happened in my own country, in my lifetime; a country that I fought to keep united, not divided.”

For him, the remembrance should be accompanied by a national resolve that such tragedy must never recur.

According to Obasanjo, “Whatever may have been the cause of such a brutal act, this is the time to remember and pray for souls that were lost.

“We must vow and pledge that never again will such a dark, black, and unpleasant day occur in Nigeria.”

Then he made his emotional appeal: “To all of you assembled: let us keep one thing in mind—forgiveness, forgiveness, and forgiveness again,” he urged.

But the Asagba’s response showed that forgiveness, for Asaba, is a journey rather than an eraser of memory.

“From the going down of the sun till the morning, we will always remember them. We have remembered them in the past 57 years, and we are still ready to continue remembering them.

“57 years ago, the annihilation and extermination witnessed on our soil is not something that can’t be glossed over.”

Then came a historic moment.

“On behalf of the Asaba community, and as the prescribed authority -the Asagba of Asaba – I hereby publicly proclaim that we have forgiven the Taiwo Family,” he declared.

The declaration followed the appearance of Major General Ahmed Ibrahim Taiwo, son of the late Colonel Ibrahim Taiwo.

The retired general recalled he first encountered the story of the massacre in 1995 while serving in Enugu and travelling to Lagos through Onitsha.

“I cannot describe how I felt reading it. I felt terrible. And I do not want to imagine how the successors, or the victims and those that were left behind, must have felt”, he said.

Taiwo said he subsequently sought information from three of his father’s friends and colleagues but found them evasive.

His later encounters with online discussions about the massacre, he said, confronted him with two disturbing realities: denial of the killings and attempts to reduce the number of victims.

“I used to come online and start telling people that it happened. I would tell them, ‘My father is the one mentioned. I have all to gain by denying it, but you cannot deny what happened. It is what it is.”

Eventually, he said, he felt compelled to come to Asaba personally.

“I have come, in private capacity as Taiwo to render our deepest regrets and apologize on behalf of our father and family for any act of omission or commission on his part that led to this heinous massacre.

“I know it will not right the wrong, but I believe and pray it is a start towards reconciliation”, he said.

For the Asagba, the apology represented an opportunity to demonstrate the forgiving spirit of Asaba.

“In Asaba, we say that Asaba bu anyi’m (Asaba is compassionate/welcoming).

“With a lot of conviction and courage, he open-mindedly admitted the fault of his father and apologized to us. His father allegedly commanded the troops that massacred the people during the war.

“I believe that as a people, we should also have the strength of conviction and character to accept that apology”, Nna Agu told his people.

But accepting the apology did not end the community’s national demand.

The Asagba recalled taking the matter to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in May 2025, saying the President addressed other matters but remained silent on the massacre.

“But it will never deter us, and we have made this abundantly clear: there will be no closure, no healing until a sitting President—not an ex-President, but a sitting President—publicly apologizes to us.

“Yes, General Gowon did, but out of office. We need a sitting President to apologize to the Asaba people, and that will bring closure”, he said.

He also questioned Obasanjo’s call for “never again”, recalling that the Odi killings occurred during Obasanjo’s presidency.

“We listened attentively to General Obasanjo, and I note with a little bit of regret: it is easier said than done for us to say ‘never again.

“How long do we say ‘never again’? But it happened at Odi. Odi came years after Asaba, and he (Obasanjo) was sitting there as President when that happened.”

For Chief Chuck Nduka-Eze, Convener of the Asaba Massacre Memorial, the tragedy continues to raise a fundamental question about citizenship and the value of Nigerian lives.

“The message we’ve been sending about the Asaba Massacre is that Nigerian lives matter. And the fact that Nigerian lives have continued not to matter speaks to what happened in Asaba on October 7, 1967.”

Nduka-Eze said Asaba residents had believed the Federal troops approaching their town were coming as fellow Nigerians, not as enemies.

“They felt safe; Asaba was part of Federal territory, not part of Biafra. So, they felt if these troops came here, they would welcome them because ‘they are part of us.’ So, it was actually those believers in ‘One Nigeria’ who are no more today”, he explained.

Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, represented by Secretary to the State Government, Dr Kingsley Emu, said the State would continue to support efforts to preserve the memory.

“For many families, the pain was compounded by the denial of traditional burial rights to their loved ones. Yet, despite the passage of time, the people remember. Let us speak clearly: the killing of unarmed civilians can never be justified”, Oborevwori said.

He described the Memorial Center as significant because it would give the history “a permanent home”, preserving “names, personal objects, and records” for future generations.

The Governor also urged Nigerians to learn the history without inheriting its bitterness, adding, “Do not inherit its bitterness; inherit its lessons.”

Enotie Ogbebor, son of late Colonel Paul Ogbebor, also spoke of the tragedy as a reminder beyond Nigeria. “The massacre in Asaba is not any less than any of such unfortunate incident in other part of the world. It ranks at the same level,” he said.

At 59, therefore, Asaba’s story is no longer simply one of bloodshed. It is a story of widows who raised children alone, of survivors who rebuilt a city, of descendants who refused to allow the dead to disappear into history, and of a community now attempting to turn memory into reconciliation.

The Asagba captured that delicate balance in a few words: “We may not forget, but certainly, we have to forgive.”

That may be Asaba’s long road forward — carrying the wounds, accepting sincere apologies, forgiving where it can, remembering those it lost, and continuing to ask the nation for the closure it believes is still due.

On October 7, 1967, Asaba was plunged into one of the darkest episodes of the Nigerian Civil War. As Federal troops entered the town, residents came out to welcome them, believing they were fellow Nigerians and not enemies.

According to survivor accounts and historical records, men and boys were subsequently separated from their families, taken to gathering points and executed, over 1000 person estimated to have been exterminated.

The killings shattered families and left generations of widows, orphans and survivors carrying the scars. With traditional burial rites denied to many victims and no immediate accountability, the horror remained an open wound in Asaba’s collective memory -59 years later, a wound that demands remembrance, recognition and closure.

World.title: Billboard war, internal crises mar campaigns in North
World.content:
By Soni Daniel, Northern Region Editor

The 2027 general elections may be over 100 days away, but political campaigns across Northern Nigeria are yet to gather full momentum, with billboard disputes, high signage fees, internal party crises and government restrictions threatening to shape the early phase of electioneering.

Read Also: 2027: Three months to polls, campaigns, rallies yet to begin

Although the INEC has approved the commencement of campaigns, findings by Saturday Vanguard show that political activities vary sharply across the region.

While Kaduna, Nasarawa, Sokoto, Taraba, Katsina and parts of Adamawa and Bauchi are witnessing growing mobilisation, campaigns remain relatively subdued in states such as Kebbi, Benue, Kano and Borno, where parties are still grappling with internal issues or yet to formally launch their campaigns.

In some states, the contest has already shifted to billboards, posters and public spaces, producing allegations of discrimination against opposition parties.

The sharpest confrontation is in Niger State, where opposition parties have accused the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, of using its incumbency to frustrate their campaigns.

The African Democratic Congress, ADC, raised the alarm shortly after nominating its governorship candidate, Dr Mohammed Kpautagi, alleging that the ruling party was blocking opposition parties from mounting billboards in strategic locations while erecting its own campaign structures.

Niger ADC chairman, Alhaji Hassan Musa, described the situation as a threat to multiparty democracy.

“From all indications, the APC does not want opposition political parties to exist. This is not democracy. It is unfortunate that opposition parties have become targets of the ruling party at all levels of political engagement. This is not a good omen for Nigeria’s democracy,” he said.

Musa alleged that his party had secured the necessary approvals to erect a billboard in Paiko, headquarters of Paikoro Local Government Area, but was prevented from doing so.

“What we are witnessing in this state suggests possible connivance with regulatory authorities to restrict the activities of opposition parties, while granting the APC unfettered access. This directly undermines Nigeria’s democratic process,” he added.

The PDP governorship candidate, Mohammed Mamman Nami, a former Chairman of the Federal Inland Revenue Service, FIRS, has also complained about the removal of his campaign materials.

Nami alleged that Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago ordered the removal of his posters and banners following his criticism of the administration’s policies.

“I know I am determined to do right for the state. This is a state that is richly endowed with resources but mismanagement by successive administrations has not allowed the citizens to benefit from the dividends. That is what I’m coming to do. I have the discipline and I know I will do it,” Nami said.

The Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, governorship candidate, Yahaya Mohammed Adam, also alleged intimidation and destruction of his campaign materials.

The party’s senatorial candidate, Muhammed Rabiu Sadiq, complained after his billboard was marked for removal in Bida Local Government Area. The council chairman, Hon. Usman Mohammed Manko, was said to have ordered opposition parties to pull down their billboards.

But the APC in Niger State has also complained about billboard destruction, blaming some aggrieved members and supporters for vandalising its campaign materials.

Plateau, Kwara impose restrictions

In Plateau State, the Jos Metropolitan Development Board, JMDB, has warned parties and candidates against pasting posters or mounting campaign materials on public infrastructure.

The board said the restriction was in line with Executive Order No. 003 of 2024 and covers public buildings, bridges, roads, utility poles, traffic structures, street furniture and trees.

“The posting or pasting of posters on public infrastructure is prohibited,” the board said.

It added that political s must receive prior approval, with only designated locations available for campaign materials. Violators risk enforcement action and a ₦500,000 penalty.

Despite the restrictions, the PDP governorship candidate, Kefas Wungak Ropshik, has begun consultations and meetings with party supporters, including in Quanpan Local Government Area.

In Kwara State, controversy has also erupted over campaign billboards belonging to PDP governorship candidate, Engr Suleiman Bolakale Kawu.

The Kwara State Signage and  Agency, KWASAA, removed some of his billboards, saying they violated advertising regulations and environmental and public infrastructure rules.

KWASAA General Manager, Toba Adeyeye, denied targeting the opposition.

“We are not really partisan, but we will do our job, no matter the party involved, no matter the candidate involved. The most important thing for us at KWASAA is Kwara. Kwara comes first, no matter the party, no matter the candidate,” he said.

Kawu’s camp, however, described the action as a “disturbing display of intolerance” and an abuse of administrative power designed to suppress opposition visibility.

Campaigns take different forms

In Zamfara State, the APC has flagged off its campaign, while the PDP senatorial candidate for Zamfara Central and candidates of other parties have commenced various forms of mobilisation.

However, campaign posters and billboards remain largely absent from Gusau streets.

Kebbi State presents an even quieter picture. No serious campaign has started, although parties are preparing to launch their activities. Posters of candidates are largely absent from the streets, apart from billboards of the governor erected before the campaign period.

In Adamawa, however, candidates have commenced serious mobilisation. Campaigners have remained largely peaceful, apparently conscious of the violence and destruction that characterised the previous election.

The parties and candidates recently signed a peace accord, pledging to conduct their campaigns peacefully before, during and after the election.

An executive order banning the pasting of election posters and banners has, however, drastically reduced campaign materials in the state, apart from posters and billboards of President Bola Tinubu and some APC candidates.

Nasarawa is among the states where campaign activities have taken off strongly. APC, PDP and SDP candidates have launched programmes and engaged supporters.

APC candidate, Senator Wadada, unveiled his HEART agenda and said he was the candidate to beat, while PDP’s David Emmanuel Ombugadu, contesting for the third time, has aligned with the FCT Minister’s Rainbow Coalition.

Former Inspector-General of Police, Muhammed Abubakar Adamu, is the SDP candidate and has attracted former APC supporters.

An interesting feature of the Nasarawa campaign is that the major parties have adopted President Bola Tinubu as their presidential candidate.

In Benue, however, political activities are yet to gain significant momentum. While some National Assembly candidates have begun consultations with political leaders, stakeholders and constituents, most parties are yet to officially flag off campaigns.

Yobe, Kogi, Bauchi gather momentum

Yobe State is witnessing increasing political visibility, with colourful posters and billboards appearing in Damaturu.

Candidates are also meeting traditional rulers, community leaders and other stakeholders. However, large rallies remain limited.

In Kogi, campaigns are gradually picking up, with support groups holding town hall meetings and unveiling posters and banners, particularly for APC figures.

High signage charges may, however, discourage a full-blown billboard contest. Approved fees reportedly include ₦150 million for presidential candidates, ₦50 million for senators, ₦30 million for House of Representatives candidates and ₦5 million for State House of Assembly candidates.

Bauchi is also witnessing increasing mobilisation, with the APC and APM holding rallies, ward visits, stakeholder meetings and door-to-door campaigns.

Security agencies have urged parties and supporters to avoid violence, hate speech and other electoral offences.

Sokoto, Taraba and Katsina heat up

Sokoto is becoming one of the more visible political battlegrounds, with APC, ADC and NDC posters and billboards appearing across major streets.

APC has the strongest physical presence, with images of President Tinubu and Governor Ahmed Aliyu prominent at strategic locations, government buildings and flyovers.

The ADC is also strengthening its grassroots machinery behind former Deputy Governor Manir Muhammad Dan’iya, while the NDC has begun political engagements around its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and running mate, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso.

There is, however, no indication that opposition posters are being systematically removed in Sokoto.

Taraba is also recording increasing political activity. Billboards and posters are appearing across Jalingo, while candidates are conducting ward-to-ward tours and consultations. Governorship aspirants are attracting endorsements from community, youth and socio-political groups.

In Katsina, parties and support groups are concentrating heavily on grassroots mobilisation.

Governor Dikko Umar Radda has pledged a door-to-door campaign in support of President Tinubu and other APC candidates. The PBAT Door to Door Movement has deployed campaign vehicles to coordinators across the state’s 34 local government areas.

Support organisations have also opened offices in Katsina, while former PDP members from the 34 local government areas have joined the APC and begun integration into its campaign structure.

Kaduna full-blown campaign

Kaduna stands out among the states where campaigns are already in full swing.

Campaigns for the presidential and National Assembly elections commenced following INEC’s August 19 declaration, while governorship campaigns started September 19.

Eighteen parties are contesting, including incumbent Governor Uba Sani of APC, Isah Ashiru of ADC and Usman Bawa of PDP.

The state is witnessing intense poster competition, with the APC dominating major locations with large billboards while ADC, PDP and NDC candidates rely heavily on walls, bridges and party offices.

PDP candidate Shehu Bawa has alleged that some billboard owners in Kaduna North rejected opposition posters after collecting payment, asking prospective advertisers to disclose their party affiliation.

Kano held back by crises

In Kano, the campaign atmosphere remains subdued despite the proximity of the elections.

The APC has commenced mobilisation, but full-scale campaigns have yet to begin, largely because major parties are dealing with internal disputes, candidate replacements and court cases.

The NDC is facing a leadership dispute involving former Governor Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso and members of the party’s North-West leadership over candidate changes and the emergence of Kwankwaso’s son as deputy governorship candidate.

The ADC is also facing a legal battle over its governorship ticket between Sheikh Ibrahim Khalil and Ibrahim Ali-Amin, popularly known as Ibrahim Little.

Although INEC recognises Ibrahim Little as the candidate, Khalil’s camp has challenged the process in court.

The PDP has also replaced its governorship candidate, Muhammad Dalha, with Muhammad Sani Abacha.

The APC, meanwhile, has begun grassroots mobilisation, vehicle donations and the inauguration of campaign councils under the slogan, “APC SAK.”

Yet, the poster and billboard war usually associated with Kano elections is still missing.

Borno starts late

In Borno, most opposition parties, including ADC, Accord, PDP and NDC, are yet to officially commence their campaigns.

The APC flagged off its 2027 campaign on September 27 at the Government House, Maiduguri, with Governor Babagana Umara Zulum mobilising support for President Tinubu and APC candidates.

Some opposition candidates in Southern Borno, including Biu, Bayo, Kwaya Kusar, Shani and Askira-Uba, have nevertheless started “Thank You Visits” to religious leaders, traditional rulers and stakeholders.

Across the North, therefore, the 2027 campaign is unfolding unevenly. In some states, billboards and posters have become the first battleground; in others, parties are still resolving internal disputes, consulting stakeholders or building grassroots structures.

With the January 2027 elections drawing closer, the subdued campaign environment is expected to give way to a more intense contest, raising fresh questions about equal access to public space, campaign regulation, internal party cohesion and the ability of opposition parties to compete on a level playing field.

Demola Akinyemi, Peter Duru, Femi Bolaji, Boluwaji Obahope, Ndahi Marama, Golok Nanmwa, Maryam Abdulaziz Usman, Christopher Ameh, Fauziyya Lawal, Idris Salisu, Edwin Phillip, Usman Aliyu, Musa Ubandawaki, Hadiza Usman, Ben Ngwakwe, Clare Nnabuike & Mohammed Yusuf contributed to this report.

World.title: 2027: Three months to polls, campaigns, rallies yet to begin
World.content:
By Clifford Ndujihe

THREE months to the 2027 general elections, political parties and their candidates are yet to fully hit the streets for campaigns, despite the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, opening the campaign window nearly two months ago.

According to the commission’s timetable, the Presidential and National Assembly polls will be held on January 16, 2027 while those of the governorship and state houses of assembly will take place, three weeks later, on February 6, 2027.

INEC cleared the way for Presidential and National Assembly elections campaigns last August 19 and that of the governorship and state assemblies, September 9.

Since then, no serious campaigns have commenced. A couple of the leading parties have raised their Presidential Campaign Councils, PCCs, most are yet to do so.

As it is, exactly 97 days to the Presidential and NASS polls, and 118 days to the governorship and state assembly balloting, no party or candidate has unveiled his/her or its campaign plan and itinerary.

Unlike previous election cycles, when streets would, at this stage, be awash with posters and billboards and candidates would be criss-crossing their constituencies, in an unmistakable poster war, the current political atmosphere is relatively subdued.

Now, the scenario is different as Saturday Vanguard’s checks across the country show. Only a handful of leading parties have constituted campaign councils, while many candidates are concentrating on consultations, grassroots mobilisation, party structures and legal battles.

But where campaigns have begun, another battle is emerging — the struggle for billboards and other public advertising spaces, with allegations of removal, destruction, intimidation and partisan use of regulatory powers.

APC crisis stalls poster war in Ondo

Political activities remain low in Ondo State, with only a few APC candidates displaying posters at strategic locations.

Unlike previous election seasons, there is no poster war, as candidates of opposition parties are largely absent from the streets.

Investigations showed that only a handful of opposition candidates have pasted posters, while many are yet to print theirs.

The development has been linked largely to the crisis within the APC, where several aspirants who lost the party’s primaries have gone to court to challenge the outcome.

Even among incumbent National Assembly members who secured return tickets, only a few have printed and displayed campaign posters.

The uncertainty surrounding candidacies has therefore slowed political activities.

The APC National Working Committee had dropped some aspirants after the primaries, triggering fresh crisis and litigation, which have combined to prevent the usual billboard and poster war.

Meanwhile, billboards bearing the image of APC presidential candidate, Senator Bola Tinubu, are prominent across major towns and roads, while only a few posters of ADC presidential candidate, Alhaji Abubakar Atiku, are visible.

Another factor is that there will be no governorship election in Ondo in 2027. The state will vote in the presidential, National Assembly and State Assembly elections.

Tinubu dominates Ekiti

The situation is similar in Ekiti, where the campaign landscape remains markedly different from the intense poster and billboard competition normally associated with elections.

Tinubu’s posters and billboards are prominent across several locations, while the presence of opposition parties, particularly ADC and NDC, remains subdued.

A major political development is the decision of Dr Wole Oluyede, who contested the June 20, 2026 governorship election on the PDP platform, to support Tinubu’s re-election.

Oluyede has established the Oluyede Progressive Alliance for Renewed Hope Agenda, OPARHA, to mobilise support for Tinubu across the state’s 16 local government areas and 177 wards.

At a mobilisation rally in Ado-Ekiti, Oluyede and Governor Biodun Oyebanji jointly canvassed support for Tinubu and pledged to work for at least 90 per cent of the President’s votes in Ekiti.

For now, the physical campaign landscape is heavily tilted towards Tinubu and the APC.

Osun: No defacing of posters

Osun presents a different picture.

Campaign posters and banners are being displayed competitively without the widespread defacing that characterised the August governorship election.

Different parties have mounted campaign materials at public places without reports of widespread destruction.

The development contrasts sharply with the recent governorship election, which witnessed extensive destruction of posters and billboards belonging to major political parties.

Billboard war, opposition cries foul in Lagos

In Lagos, political activities are taking place amid heightened tension, early mobilisation and strict regulation of public advertising space.

The governorship contest involving the APC, ADC and PDP is attracting more attention than the Senate, House of Representatives and State Assembly contests, which remain relatively subdued.

APC governorship candidate, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, and his running mate, Princess Damilola Sonayon-James, have established a strong presence, alongside President Tinubu.

Billboards bearing the images of Tinubu, Vice President Kashim Shettima and Hamzat are prominent in Ikeja, Alausa, the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, Obalende and around the Third Mainland Bridge. The posters, which began appearing in August, are also visible around Agege, Alimosho and other areas.

By contrast, billboards of ADC presidential candidate and his running mate, Rotimi Amaechi, as well as NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi and his running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, are yet to achieve comparable visibility.

The opposition has alleged harassment and removal of its campaign materials.

NDC supporters accused the Lagos State Signage and  Agency, LASAA, of removing more than 50 banners belonging to Peter Obi and House of Representatives candidate, Dr Adefolaseye Adebomi, in Surulere while leaving APC materials intact.

NDC chieftain, Aisha Yesufu, condemned the alleged action, describing it as the behaviour of a party that is “scared, desperate, and crumbling rather than one in control.”

She also criticised the high cost of billboard advertising, alleging that fees running into hundreds of millions of naira were being imposed in some areas.

The Lagos State Government had yet to respond to the allegation at the time of filing this report.

Campaign materials under attack in Ogun

Political activities are gathering momentum in Ogun, with the PDP formally commencing its governorship campaign and the ruling APC intensifying mobilisation across the three senatorial districts.

But posters, banners and billboards mounted in public spaces are increasingly being vandalised.

Some campaign materials have been torn down, defaced or damaged, with different parties and candidates reportedly affected.

The development has raised concerns as the parties intensify grassroots engagement and public messaging ahead of the elections.

The growing appearance of campaign materials on major roads and in communities has already transformed parts of the state into political battlegrounds, even though the full campaign season is yet to peak.

Battle for visibility moves to billboards in Oyo

In Oyo State, the struggle for political visibility is gradually moving to the streets, particularly billboards and posters.

Across Ibadan and other areas, campaign materials of prominent contenders have begun appearing at strategic locations, although the state is yet to witness a full-scale poster war.

Controversy erupted in July when the ADC alleged that a billboard belonging to its governorship candidate, Olooye Taofeek Adegboyega Adegoke, at Idi-Ape Junction, Ibadan, was removed and replaced with materials bearing the images of Governor Seyi Makinde and APM governorship candidate, Bimbo Adekanmbi.

Adegoke said: “My money is still running on that billboard till 20th August 2026.”

The APM denied responsibility, attributing billboard disputes to advertising agencies and regulatory authorities.

The APC later raised similar allegations, claiming that some of its billboards for governorship candidate, Senator Sharafadeen Alli, were being removed or destroyed.

APM again denied involvement, saying: “We do not destroy opponents’ materials, we do not sponsor thuggery, and we do not engage in violence.”

For now, Oyo’s contest is still at the early stage of the battle for public attention, with candidates also relying on radio, television, social media, rallies and consultations.

Campaign activities in Delta are yet to fully take off, but the political atmosphere is warming up as aspirants intensify consultations with party leaders, traditional rulers, community leaders and supporters.

Posters and billboards belonging to candidates are becoming increasingly visible in Asaba and other major towns, but the development has not translated into a full-blown poster war.

Political actors are adopting a cautious approach, seeking to establish visibility while strengthening party structures and grassroots networks.

For many candidates, consultations and mobilisation are currently more important than committing huge resources to full-scale advertising.

The gradual appearance of posters and billboards, however, indicates that the 2027 contest is entering the public consciousness.

Complaints of billboard destruction rein in Edo

Political activities are picking up across Edo’s three senatorial districts, with junctions and public spaces increasingly competing for campaign posters and banners.

The APC has inaugurated its campaign council, while Governor Monday Okpebholo, his deputy, Dennis Idahosa, and party leaders have commenced mobilisation visits to the state’s 18 local government areas.

The NDC is also campaigning but has complained about attacks on its posters.

The party’s candidate for Akoko-Edo II State Constituency, Paul Alaba Lawani, said the NDC was prepared to defeat the incumbent through its grassroots strength.

Other active campaign groups include the Chief Thomas Attah Movement, backing Dr Thomas Attah’s House of Representatives ambition in Akoko-Edo Federal Constituency, and the Abbaas Naasamu campaign team of the ADC.

However, the campaign has already recorded an allegation of political violence.

Suspected political thugs allegedly attacked the campaign office of NDC candidate for Oredo Federal Constituency, Hon Frank Uyi Omosigho, in Benin City.

Several campaign materials at the Stadium Road office were pulled down and damaged.

Omosigho said youths alerted him to the attack and urged young people not to allow politicians to use them to perpetrate violence.

“My appeal to youths is not to allow politicians to use them to perpetrate violence or other illegal acts. Anyone caught violating the law would face the consequences,” he said. He added: “The campaign materials were meant to introduce candidates and political parties to the electorate. The voters had the right to make their choices independently.”The incident was reported to the police, while the Commissioner of Police and Department of State Services, DSS, were also informed.

Another NDC candidate, St Moses Eromosele, has similarly complained that his billboards were being pulled down and accused the APC.

With the elections drawing closer, the subdued campaign atmosphere across the eight states may soon give way to the familiar frenzy of rallies, posters, billboards and political mobilisation.

For now, however, the battle is being fought largely behind the scenes — in party meetings, courtrooms, consultations and the increasingly contested public spaces where candidates seek to make their first impressions on voters.

Dayo Johnson, Olasunkanmi Akoni, Egufe Yafugborhi, Rotimi Ojomoyela, Ozioruva Aliu, Shina Abubakar, James Ogunnnaike & Adeola Badru contributed to this report

World.title: Asaba massacre: Remember all Biafra war victims, veterans — ‘Corporal Nwafor’
World.content:
By Steve Oko

UMUAHIA — A 75-year-old Biafran war veteran, Mr Sasa Ugwumba Kalu Nwoke, popularly known as “Corporal Nwafor” for his exploits during the Nigerian Civil War, has called for the establishment of a Biafra Remembrance Day to honour victims and veterans of the 30-month conflict.

Nwoke, who spoke exclusively with Vanguard in Umuahia, said the commemoration of the 1967 Asaba massacre was a welcome development but should mark the beginning of a broader national effort to confront the painful history of the civil war.

He spoke against the backdrop of the 59th memorial of the Asaba massacre, chaired by former President Olusegun Obasanjo on Wednesday.

The veteran said remembering the victims of Asaba was important, but insisted that other victims of the war, including those killed in different parts of the former Biafran territory, should also be remembered.

He queried:“Who is afraid of remembering Biafra? If you can remember a massacre and some other genocides committed in different parts of the world, what is actually wrong with having Biafran Day remembrance?

“Since they have started remembering Asaba genocide, that’s okay. One by one they will remember other genocides, including the one in Aba and other parts of Biafra.

“We should not be suppressed from talking about it. It’s our history that cannot be buried. We should start talking about them until we tell ourselves the truth and accommodate every area where people were wronged.”

According to him, the Asaba commemoration could provide an opportunity for Nigerians to begin a painful but necessary national conversation about the civil war.

“They’ve been hiding this thing; they’ve been trying to cover it up. They’ve been attempting to cover up that it was a massacre. Now they’ve realised that it’s something that they need to talk about.

“Let’s go along with them. After now, we will go in a second step, a third step, until we reconcile all the patches involved in this Biafran experience.

“All this while, they’ve not taken this Biafran thing seriously, this massacre, this genocide. But now, I think somebody is telling them that they should bring it up and make things better.”

‘Civil war was needless’

The war veteran blamed the Nigerian government for the civil war, describing the conflict as needless and questioning the justification for the enormous loss of lives.

“Nigerians don’t want to mention it because they know that it was a futile war they fought,” he said.

“They wasted lives of Igbos and other Biafrans for nothing, saying they want to keep Nigeria one. Look at the country now. Is there any justification for the war?”

Nwoke said the country could not genuinely reconcile without confronting the circumstances, atrocities and consequences of the conflict.

“We need to reach out to the war veterans. This is our history. Whether it was right or wrong, we have a history.“Let us build on this history and ask ourselves where we went wrong so that we can do it right the next time. But when we don’t talk about it, nobody gets to know.”

‘Nigeria denying its children their history’

The veteran also accused successive governments of deliberately failing to teach younger Nigerians about the civil war and the country’s historical figures.

According to him, suppressing history only ensures that younger generations grow up without understanding the events that shaped the country.

He urged Nigerians to confront the country’s difficult past rather than bury it, arguing that honest remembrance could become a pathway to reconciliation

“If you’re proud of your history, if you go to America now, one of the first places you meet is American history. And so, you get to know

the people you’re dealing with.

“You come to Nigeria, our children have no idea about Nigeria. I talked to them, None of them can tell you anything about Nnamdi AZikwe. None of them can tell you about Nigerian patriots. It’s like hiding behind a finger and you can’t do it. We ought to start opening up. Even if you made a mistake, you own up. Our children will learn from it.”

‘We’ve forgotten our war veterans’

Nwoke lamented what he described as the neglect of Biafran war veterans, saying many who survived the conflict had died in poverty without recognition.

“We’ve not done anything for our veterans. So, we don’t expect more from Nigeria,” he said.

“The war veterans have been totally forgotten. Nobody else remembers us. ‘Pampas’ died, wretched. And they’re waiting for me to die too, so that they’ll come and say, ‘Corporal Nwafor has died.’

“I wanted to buy you a jeep. Bring it now. They won’t bring it.”

He said the Igbo community should also look inward and honour its own historical figures and veterans instead of waiting for the Federal Government.

“You don’t remember Ojukwu. You don’t remember Akanu Ibiam. You don’t remember Mbakwe. You don’t remember anybody.”

‘I defended Umuahia 50% during war’

Recounting his experience on the Biafran front, Nwoke singled out the Uzuakoli sector as one of the fiercest theatres of the war.

“The Uzuakoli sector was the hottest of the battles we fought,” he said, recalling that the fighting lasted about seven weeks, with two battles fought daily.

He made the striking claim that only three Biafran officers effectively defended Umuahia during the war.

“Colonel Emeka Ananaba (who later became Abia Deputy Governor) defended Umuahia 30 per cent. Colonel Joe Achuzie defended Umuahia 20 per cent. And myself, Corporal Nwafor, defended Umuahia 50 per cent,” he said.

Nwoke also referred to the book Tragedy of Victory, saying its title aptly captured what he considered the paradox of the Federal Government’s victory.

“I’ve never seen a victory that turned into a tragedy. I’ve never seen. Only the Nigerian victory turned into a tragedy,” he said.

‘War must have a reason’

Explaining his earlier assertion that he would have committed suicide if he had fought on the Nigerian side, Nwoke said war should only be fought for a clearly defined and morally defensible purpose.

“You go to war with genuine reasons. War is serious business because you are going to kill somebody as well. You must have a good reason to go to war.

“Why did Nigerians go to war? To kill people, or to wipe people out, or did they go to build a nation? Maybe they didn’t tell us why they went to war. But they should come and tell us why they went to war.”

He argued that nation-building, rather than military victory, should have been the ultimate objective.

“You want to build a nation. You’re not going to rig an election. You’re not going to wipe out people’s race. It doesn’t make sense.

“And after wiping out people’s race, what’s next? Look at the country today.”

The veteran said the lessons of the civil war should therefore be used to build a more just and inclusive Nigeria.

World.title: 2027: What insecurity may do to APC’s bid
World.content:
AI-generated image from illustration.

By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – The road to an NYSC orientation camp became a kidnapping route on October 1 when gunmen attacked buses near Umunoha in Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State and abducted prospective corps members. Six days later, 20 of them were rescued.

Read Also: 2027: 30 days can’t erase over three years of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu

They were young Nigerians travelling for a national service programme. Their ordeal carried a political question far bigger than the incident itself: how safe are Nigerians on the roads they must use?

That question is beginning to sit alongside the economy, cost of living and governance in calculations for 2027. For President Bola Tinubu, insecurity is not yet an electoral verdict, but it is becoming a vulnerability the administration cannot afford to ignore.

The road to 2027 runs through security

Nigerians do not experience insecurity through statistics. They experience it when children leave for school, farmers head to their fields, traders travel, worshippers return home or families wait for abducted relatives.

The Imo incident carried significance beyond another kidnapping. It involved young Nigerians on a journey meant to symbolise national integration, yet their route became a site of fear and criminal control.

The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) says mass kidnappings averaged at least 100 incidents per quarter in 2025, compared with fewer than 70 per quarter in 2026 so far. The level is lower than last year’s peak, but still elevated.

ACLED also says armed bandits accounted for more than 80 per cent of recorded mass abductions since early 2025, with ransom increasingly important to financing such violence.

That leaves Tinubu facing a political test: can increased security spending and operations translate into a visible improvement in the everyday sense of safety?

Rescue is not the same as prevention

The administration has a substantial record of security interventions. It declared a nationwide security emergency in 2025, expanded recruitment, redeployed some police officers from VIP protection, backed forest guards and surveillance, and pushed intelligence-led operations and military modernisation. The 2026 budget proposed N5.41 trillion for defence and security.

Finding a kidnappers’ camp is not the same as preventing an abduction. Rescuing hostages is not the same as arresting abductors. Arresting suspects is not the same as dismantling the networks, financiers, informants and routes that make another attack possible.

The Imo episode raises operational questions. How did the attackers identify and stop the buses? Was the route regarded as vulnerable? Were intelligence agencies sharing information before the attack? How quickly could security forces move after the camp was located?

Human rights lawyer and activist, Deji Adeyanju, told Saturday Vanguard in Abuja that insecurity could become a serious political challenge for Tinubu because its consequences are deeply personal for Nigerians.

“Insecurity is not simply a question of statistics or the number of attacks recorded,” Adeyanju

Opposition sees an opening

Mark Adebayo, Head of the Directorate of Media and Communications of the Adewole Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign, said the crisis had serious implications for Tinubu’s re-election prospects and the legitimacy of the state.

“The political implications of Nigeria’s worsening security situation ahead of the 2027 general elections are profound, primarily threatening President Bola Tinubu’s reelection bid and undermining state legitimacy,” Adebayo told Saturday Vanguard.

He attributed the administration’s difficulties to what he described as uncoordinated counter-terrorism strategies, alleged military corruption and a perceived disconnect from grassroots realities.

Those are opposition arguments, and some wider performance and casualty claims require verification. Politically, however, the opposition needs to persuade voters that the government has not made them safer.

The voters will have the final say

Insecurity will not automatically deliver votes to the opposition. Its political effect could be subtler: punishment of the incumbent, declining confidence, or reduced turnout where voters fear violence.

A Yiaga Africa survey found that 84 per cent of respondents were willing or likely to vote, but 61 per cent said fear of violence could prevent them from doing so. In the North-East, the figure rose to 78 per cent. Security also ranked among the leading issues respondents wanted addressed.

Voters may punish a government they believe has failed to protect them. But insecurity may also suppress turnout without transferring those votes to an opponent.

The regional picture matters. In the North-East, insurgency and election-related violence remain major concerns. In the North-West, banditry and mass kidnapping dominate the security conversation. The North-Central faces attacks on farming communities and displacement, while parts of the South-East and South-South contend with road kidnapping, separatist violence and criminal networks.

For insecurity to become a decisive electoral liability, several developments may have to converge: continued high-profile abductions despite increased spending; attacks spreading into previously safer areas; slow or contradictory official responses; repeated rescues without arrests or prosecutions; continuing ransom payments; and a growing connection between insecurity, food prices and economic hardship.

Anger is not an electoral strategy. The opposition must convince voters that it can do better, finance security, improve intelligence coordination, protect highways and bring perpetrators to justice.

Tinubu still has time to change the argument. A sustained decline in attacks, safer highways, disruption of kidnapping finances, prosecutions and faster responses would give the administration something more powerful than another security announcement: evidence.

The political verdict will not be determined by budgets or troop numbers alone. It will depend on whether Nigerians see measurable improvements in their security before they cast their ballots.

For Tinubu, the challenge is therefore clear: turn security operations into safer roads, fewer abductions and greater confidence that the state can protect its citizens. If that happens, insecurity may remain a difficult issue without becoming a decisive electoral liability. If it does not, the opposition will have a ready-made case against the administration in 2027.

World.title: Vanguard summit: Experts demand action on Mental Health Act, school counselling, affordable care
World.content:
File image

•Say Nigeria can’t afford to fail its youth

By Sola Ogundipe & Chioma Obinna

Nigeria cannot afford to fail its young people as experts at the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit called for urgent, coordinated action to address the country’s youth mental health challenges, insisting that government policies, school-based interventions, affordable treatment and stronger accountability must translate into measurable results.

Read Also: 2027: 30 days can’t erase over three years of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu

They warned that awareness campaigns alone would not protect young people from depression, anxiety, substance abuse, suicide risk and the growing psychological pressures associated with social media, insecurity, and other social challenges.

The experts, who spoke at the 4th Vanguard mental health summit on Friday in Lagos, stressed that government, health professionals, schools, families, religious institutions, the media and technology platforms must share responsibility for protecting young people’s mental well-being.

They urged the Federal Government and state governments to move beyond policy declarations to full implementation of the Mental Health Act, adequate funding of mental health services, integration of care into primary healthcare and the establishment of accessible counselling and referral systems in schools.

In his presentation titled: “Making Youth Mental Health Everyone’s Business: From Policy to Practice”, President of the Nigerian Medical Association, (NMA) Prof. Ernest Omoti, represented by the association’s Financial Secretary, and also a professor of psychiatry, Prof. Olayinka Atilola, said youth mental health must become everyone’s business, with practical action replacing isolated interventions.

Atilola called for the implementation and funding of the Mental Health Act, the National Mental Health Policy and the National Suicide Prevention Strategic Framework, alongside the integration of mental health services into primary healthcare.

Omoti also stressed the need to train a multidisciplinary mental health workforce and establish counselling and referral systems in schools and universities.

Families, religious leaders, community organisations and the media, he said, had important roles to play in reducing stigma, identifying distress early and ensuring that young people receive appropriate support.

He urged people to listen to young people without rushing to judge them, stressing: “Listen before you label.”

The NMA president also called for responsible media reporting of suicide and greater participation of young people in decisions affecting their mental health.

Mental Health Act: Experts demand implementation

A major concern raised at the summit was the gap between Nigeria’s mental health policies and their implementation.

A Professor of Psychiatry, Prof. Taiwo Lateef Sheikh, argued that mental health should be treated as an essential component of national development rather than a marginal health issue.

He called for the effective implementation of the Mental Health Act, including measures to decriminalise attempted suicide, expand community-based services and improve access to treatment.

Sheikh said the country must recognise the wider social consequences of untreated mental health conditions, particularly the effects of conflict, insecurity, displacement and trauma on individuals, families and communities.

He also advocated investment in what he described as “psychological infrastructure”, arguing that the country’s development priorities should extend beyond physical infrastructure to include the emotional and psychological well-being of its people.

According to him, restoring mental well-being, trust and social cohesion is important to national progress, while mental health has value beyond its contribution to economic productivity.

Speaking, President of the Association of Psychiatric Association of Nigeria, (APN), Dr. Nyamali Veronica Oluyemisi, also called for urgent implementation of the Mental Health Act.

She urged the government to establish the department and Mental Health Fund provided for under the law and ensure that mental health services receive dedicated, sustained funding.

Nyamali further called on state governments to domesticate and implement relevant provisions of the Act, while integrating mental health services into primary healthcare and community-based care.

She advocated the training and deployment of mental health focal persons in secondary and tertiary schools to identify students experiencing psychological distress and link them with appropriate services.

The APN president also called for wider access to affordable treatment, the use of telehealth where appropriate, stronger public education and measurable targets against which progress could be assessed before the next summit.

Social media, new pressure on young minds

The experts also warned that the digital environment had created additional challenges for young people, requiring coordinated action from parents, schools, health professionals, technology platforms and policymakers.

Speaking, a professor of Psychiatry, Professor Mashudat Abiola Bello-Mojeed, who spoke on protecting young minds in the age of social media, highlighted concerns around cyberbullying, online exploitation, misinformation, unhealthy social comparison and pressures linked to body image and sleep disruption.

She called for stronger national coordination to address online harms and urged schools to establish clear safeguarding policies, reporting channels and counselling support for students affected by cyberbullying.

Bello-Mojeed cautioned against relying solely on blanket restrictions, stressing the importance of building trust between parents and young people while equipping children with digital literacy and the ability to recognise harmful online experiences.

She also called for greater accountability in the digital environment and urged clinicians to consider young people’s online experiences when assessing their mental health.

Her recommendations included the SAFE-MIND framework as part of a broader approach to protecting young people in an increasingly digital world.

Drug abuse, mental health-linked

Also, the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA, Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (retd.), warned that substance abuse and mental health problems frequently reinforce each other, making prevention, treatment and rehabilitation as important as enforcement.

Represented by the Assistant Comptroller General, Archie- Abia Ibinabo, said the human distress behind drug abuse must not be ignored in efforts to address the problem.

“Behind almost every case of drug abuse is a story of pain: anxiety nobody noticed, depression nobody named, trauma nobody treated,” Marwa said.

He urged stakeholders to reach young people with appropriate information, support and treatment before substance use develops into more serious problems.

“We must meet young people where they are,” he said.

Marwa disclosed that the NDLEA had counselled, treated and rehabilitated 53,843 people through its 31 rehabilitation centres, while its War Against Drug Abuse, WADA, initiative had conducted 17,213 outreach activities in five years.

He called for stronger community-based prevention, early intervention in schools, affordable treatment outside major cities and the integration of mental health support into primary healthcare.

Marwa also urged stakeholders to challenge the online glamorisation of drugs and reduce the stigma that often prevents people with substance-use and mental health problems from seeking help.

He stressed that a comprehensive response must combine law enforcement with prevention, counselling, treatment and rehabilitation.

Affordable care, confidentiality essential

Also speaking on behalf of the Lagos State Controller of Corrections, Mr. Daramola George, represented by Mr. Ajayi Francis Akinlou, also called for accessible, quality and confidential mental health services.

He emphasised the need to strengthen community and primary healthcare services, provide young people with reliable, age-appropriate digital information and protect their privacy when they seek help.

It also urged the media to report suicide and self-harm responsibly, while encouraging young people to participate in developing policies and programmes intended to address their needs.

He stressed that discussions about mental health must lead to concrete interventions rather than end with expressions of concern.

Treatment options and early intervention

Also, a UK-based consultant psychiatrist, Dr. Olufemi Oluwatayo highlighted the importance of recognising mental health conditions early and ensuring that young people receive appropriate, evidence-based care.

He identified depression, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder among conditions that may affect young people, noting that treatment should be tailored to the individual and may include psychotherapy, medication or a combination of interventions.

Oluwatayo also discussed transcranial magnetic stimulation, TMS, as a possible treatment option for selected patients with depression who have not responded adequately to established treatments.

Citing the BRIGhTMIND trial involving 255 patients with treatment-resistant depression, he said the treatment involved 20 sessions over four to six weeks.

However, he stressed that TMS should not be presented as a universal solution for mental health conditions. Potential side effects and suitability must be assessed by qualified professionals, and the treatment does not replace established care for every patient.

The presentation reinforced calls for improved access to mental health professionals, early assessment and treatment options suited to patients’ needs.

From summit declarations to accountability

In his welcome remarks, Vanguard Editor, Mr Eze Anaba, challenged participating organisations to ensure that the summit produced practical commitments rather than another round of discussions.

He urged each organisation to identify specific actions, assign responsibility to named individuals and set deadlines for delivery, with progress assessed over the following year.

The approach, he stressed, would help determine whether the commitments made at the summit translated into tangible improvements.

Expert urges treatment over punishment

A US based specialist, Dr Daniel Ikpechukwu, said Nigeria must rethink how its justice system handles young people whose involvement with drugs leads to offending, with greater emphasis on addiction treatment, rehabilitation and recovery rather than punishment alone.

In his presentation, titled: “Youth Drug Addiction and the Justice System: Advancing Treatment, Rehabilitation and Recovery in Nigeria”, Ikpechukwu, a substance abuse and behavioural health counsellor and adjunct professor of psychology at Georgia Gwinnett College, United States, highlighted the need to balance accountability with appropriate care for young people affected by substance dependence.

Nigeria’s national drug use survey estimated that 14.4 per cent of people aged 15 to 64, representing about 14.3 million people, had used psychoactive substances. The scale of the problem calls for coordinated action involving healthcare providers, families, communities, and the justice system.

For young people whose substance use is linked to offending, the consequences can extend beyond legal penalties to their health, education, family relationships and employment prospects. Untreated dependence may compound these difficulties and make rehabilitation more challenging.

A key priority is early identification and professional assessment to determine the appropriate intervention. Not every young person who uses drugs is dependent, making individual assessment essential.

Police officers, prosecutors, judges and correctional personnel also need training to recognise possible substance use disorders and facilitate referrals for treatment. Where legally appropriate, treatment based alternatives may complement conventional justice measures without compromising accountability or public safety.

Rehabilitation must continue beyond formal treatment. Follow up care, counselling, family support and opportunities to return to education or employment can help young people sustain recovery and rebuild their lives.

Government agencies responsible for health, justice, education and drug control need to coordinate their efforts, expand access to qualified treatment providers and ensure continuity of care.

Schools, families and youth organisations also have a role in identifying warning signs and directing young people to professional help early.

Sustained funding, trained personnel and accessible treatment facilities are essential. Relevant agencies should also track treatment access, rehabilitation outcomes and continuity of care to determine whether interventions are producing lasting results.

However, the call for accountability ran through the discussions, with experts emphasising that government agencies must fund and implement policies, schools must establish support and referral systems, health institutions must expand access to care, families must listen without stigma, and digital platforms must take online harms seriously.

For young Nigerians confronting psychological distress, the experts said, the central challenge is not simply whether the country recognises the importance of mental health, but whether help is available when and where it is needed.

They insisted that Nigeria must move from awareness to implementation, from policy to funded services, and from promises to measurable action if it is to protect the mental well-being and future of its young people.
