World.title: 2027: INEC Vows Crackdown on Vote Buying, Campaign Spending
World.content:
.Wike Berates INEC over Amaechi’s campaign incitement

.Issues no work, no pay warning to labour

Olawale Ajimotokan in Abuja and David-Chyddy Eleke in Awka

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has said it would pay attention to spending by candidates in the 2027 general elections, insisting that those who engage in vote buying would be prosecuted.

This was as the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has faulted INEC for failing to sanction or call to order the Vice Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Rotimi Amaechi, for inciting the public on matters that were not issue -base in his campaign.

Wike delivered the disapproval yesterday in Abuja after a brief meeting with FCT Area Council chairmen.

The INEC Resident Electoral Commission (REC) in charge of Anambra State, Dr. Queen Elizabeth Agwu, stated this yesterday during a stakeholders’ meeting attended by leaders and representatives of political parties, candidates, community leaders and media representatives.

She said, “We don’t want a repeat of what happened during the 2025 governorship election in Anambra State where people were talking about families and other matters away from the election. INEC will not accept it.

“We will not tolerate campaign of calumny. Campaigns have been lifted and we expect candidates to go into the field and tell the people what they can do. It is immaterial if a candidate is impotent or if a candidate’s wife’s last child is not the candidate’s, it is immaterial. Just tell the people what you will do for them.”

Speaking on vote buying, the REC said, “We will monitor vote buying and we are urging people to report vote buyers. I have never witnessed one, but we call on those who notice it to report to us.

“The money you will use to buy votes, why not give it to the people during election campaigns and tell them what you will do for them. This is the time to campaign. It is not INEC that engages in vote buying, and it is not done by the police or other organisations, but by political parties. All parties are engaged in vote buying and at the end you blame INEC and want us to stop it when you are the ones doing it.”

She also insisted that the commission is very prepared for the 2027 elections, adding that those planning to use thugs to carry ballot boxes during the election will be disappointed because such stolen boxes would be useless to those who took them.

“We beg you not to engage thugs, if you don’t get to power today you will get tomorrow. Election is about planning. You must plan, you must engage the people, you don’t just jump out hoping to win because you have paid young boys to disrupt the process for you. We want to assure you that plans are in place and very soon, election malpractice would be a thing if the past

“INEC is ready for the coming elections and we have made adequate preparation and I want to assure you there will be no glitches in the 2027 elections. I told you people so during the Anambra governorship election and it came to pass, so I’m promising you again that there would be no glitches in the coming election.

“It’s 97 days to elections and we are ready. We want the political parties and their candidates to prepare early enough too.

“We have warned our staff not to take money from politician and if we catch politicians who are luring our staff for result sheets or to rig elections, we will prosecute you. Some people get scammed by people who are not even our staff because of desperation, but they come and say it is our staff. We will not let that happen in 2027.

“Snatching ballot boxes is now obsolete and if you do it, we have enough technology to make it useless to you,” the REC said.

Meanwhile, FCT Minister, Wike, said INEC inadvertently turned a deaf ear after Amaechi reportedly told voters in Edo State that “only thieves and mad people” would vote for President Bola Tinubu.

He said, “Many Nigerians have called INEC to sanction political parties, candidates, or some politicians who, in their campaigns, incite the public or raise matters that are not issue-based.

“We have been told to go on campaign based on issues: what are you going to do for the people? Not on attacking personality, not on insulting individuals.

“And up till now, I have not heard that INEC has been able to call or draw attention of the vice presidential candidate of the ADC, one Chibuike Amaechi, who has shown he’s more of a… All of us watched on television yesterday, and the media, where he said it’s only thieves that can vote for Bola Ahmed Tinubu. And this was said in Edo, that only mad people can go and vote for Ahmed Tinubu, and that if Edo people vote for him, it means Edo people are mad.

“This is supposedly a vice presidential candidate of a political party and not an ordinary politician, seeking to take over power and preside over the affairs of this country.”

Wike then proceeded to launch a blistering verbal rant at Amaechi and questioned his mental stability, saying men like him would not be allowed to attain the presidency of the country.

“He cannot preside over the affairs of this country! He said those who want to vote for Tinubu are thieves. So, I’m a thief? That’s what he’s saying,” Wike said.

He vowed that Amaechi would face severe resistance in his home turf if he continued to insult supporters of the President.

“You can’t continue with that kind of way and think that we will allow you. We will not allow it! I will not!

“I’m not the Governor of Rivers State, but I do know that our supporters will not allow him in Rivers State to do that, and it will be difficult—we’ll make it difficult for him not to campaign in Rivers. He cannot do that.”

Wike also decried the indefinite strike declared by the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) as action that was politically motivated insisting the FCT Administration had no dispute with teachers.

He urged area councils to call their teachers and civil servants back to work, warning that “no work, no pay” would be implemented.

“This so-called strike declaration is political and we will not accept it. There’s no basis for anybody to call for a strike. All the things they are talking about have been agreed and are being implemented,” he said.

He said the Trade Union Congress (TUC) and the Academic Staff Union of Secondary School (ASUSS), the body of senior primary school teachers, had disowned the strike.

World.title: APC Writes INEC, Demands Enforcement of Supreme Court Judgement On Party Membership Register
World.content:
Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

The All Progressives Congress (APC) has called on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to immediately enforce the Supreme Court judgement on party membership register and compliance with Sections 77 of the Electoral Act 2026.

It would be recalled that the Supreme Court delivered a judgement on 24 September, 2026 in INEC v Zenith Labour Party with Suit No. SC/CV/495/2026 regarding compliance with the statutory requirements governing the submission and use of political parties’ membership registers for party primaries, congresses and conventions.

In a letter dated 9th October, 2026, which was addressed to the INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, and signed by National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda and National Secretary, Sen. Ajibola Basiru, the party said INEC, as appellant in the suit, is constitutionally bound to give effect to the judgement under Section 287(1) of the 1999 Constitution.

The Supreme Court in Suit No. SC/CV/495/2026 set aside the Court of Appeal order that had nullified Section 77(5) to (7) and Section 84(2) of the Electoral Act 2026 and Activity Serial No. 2 of INEC’s Revised Timetable for the 2027 general election.

The APC said the judgement affirmed the mandatory nature of Section 77.

Section 77(4) provides that each political party shall make its membership register available to the Commission not later than 21 days before its primaries, congresses or conventions.

Also, Section 77(5) provides that only members whose names are in the register shall be eligible to vote and be voted for, while Section 77(6) prohibits use of any other register.

The governing party cited the Supreme Court’s pronouncement at page 24 that the practical effect of Section 77(7) is that a party that fails to submit its digital membership register within the prescribed period may be precluded from fielding candidates.

The ruling party noted that the objective of Section 77 is to ensure that political parties adhere to the principles of internal democracy, particularly through the fair, transparent and verifiable conduct of party primaries, congresses and conventions.

The party maintained that the court anchored its decision on Section 228(a) of the Constitution which empowers the National Assembly to make laws to ensure internal democracy, citing Ardo v Nyako (2014).

The party noted, “In the circumstances, the All Progressives Congress respectfully requests the Commission to: (i) Immediately enforce the judgment of the Supreme Court in INEC v Zenith Labour Party, Suit No. SC/CV/495/2026, delivered on 24 September 2026, in accordance with its terms and legal effect.

“Verify compliance with section 77(4) of the Electoral Act 2026 by determining whether each political party submitted its digital membership register within the statutory period of not later than 21 days before the relevant primary election, congress or convention.

“Apply the statutory consequences of non-compliance in accordance with Section 77(7) of the Act and the Supreme Court’s decision, including the exclusion of any party from fielding candidates where the statutory conditions for that consequence have been established.

“Ensure strict adherence to Sections 77(5) and 77(6) by requiring that only candidates whose names appear in the register duly submitted to the Commission are recognised as eligible to vote and be voted for in the relevant internal party election, and that no alternative register is used in place of the register submitted to INEC.

“As a political party, we insist that compliance with section 77 of the Electoral Act 2026 is not a matter of discretion but a statutory obligation whose interpretation has been authoritatively addressed by the Supreme Court.

“Allowing political parties to disregard the prescribed statutory requirements without the application of the consequences stipulated by law would undermine the objectives of internal party democracy, electoral transparency and the rule of law.

“We, therefore, urge the Commission to act expeditiously and decisively, in strict conformity with the provisions of the Electoral Act 2026, the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended), and the judgment of the Supreme Court, which must be enforced in any part of the Federation by all authorities and persons, to ensure that the statutory regime governing party membership registers is effectively implemented.”

World.title: Go Get Your PVCs, ADC-PCC Urges Nigerians
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has called on all eligible Nigerians to turn out en masse to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) as the nationwide collection exercise organised by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) commenced yesterday

The Council assured Nigerians that their votes must count in the 2027 general elections, declaring that no individual or political party should be allowed to manipulate the electoral process or subvert the will of the people.

In a statement issued yesterday by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the ADC-PCC dismissed the notion that votes would not count and that the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) would simply write results in favour of its candidates, describing such claims as false, deceptive and designed to discourage voter participation.

“Go and collect your PVC. Your voter’s card is your power and your guarantee that you will vote on January 16, 2027.

“The notion that votes will not count and that the APC will write results is deceitful and unattainable. Nobody will be allowed to manipulate the 2027 general election,” Ologbondiyan said.

He alleged that the narrative was being promoted by agents of the ruling APC to instil fear, encourage voter apathy and discourage Nigerians from participating in the electoral process.

According to him, the strategy reflects the ruling party’s fear of rejection by Nigerians at the polls following its poor performance in government.

“The APC knows it cannot win a free, fair and credible election after plunging Nigerians into hunger, hardship and insecurity. That is why it wants Nigerians to believe that results will be written. It is a lie. The era of writing results in hotel rooms is gone forever,” he stated.

Ologbondiyan noted that the Electoral Act, as amended, the deployment of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS), the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) and the heightened political consciousness of Nigerians have strengthened safeguards against electoral manipulation.

“Every polling unit will be protected. Every vote will be counted, and every vote will count. Nigerians are more determined than ever to take back their country through the ballot,” he added.

The ADC-PCC called on traditional rulers, religious leaders, youth groups, women’s organisations and civil society organisations to mobilise eligible Nigerians to collect their PVCs and disregard attempts to discourage them from exercising their democratic rights.

“We urge all Nigerians not to be deterred. Go and collect your PVC today and keep it safe. In 2027, you will vote, and your vote will count. No one can stop the will of the people,” Ologbondiyan said.

The Council further assured Nigerians that the ADC, under its presidential candidate, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, would deploy polling agents to every polling unit across the country to monitor the electoral process, protect votes and prevent any attempt to steal the people’s mandate.

World.title: Solomon Adeola:Ogun Should Not Be State Where You Make Money and Spend It in Lagos
World.content:
Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, is the All Progressives Congress candidate for the 2027 Ogun State governorship election. Having served as senator representing Lagos West from 2015 to 2023 and Ogun West since 2023, Adeola brings more than two decades of legislative experience to the race. He outlines his vision for industrialisation, infrastructure, job creation and inclusive growth, arguing that Ogun must retain more economic value from businesses operating within its borders. He also responds to the controversy over his indigeneship and change of name. Wale Igbintade brings the excerpts:

Amid the controversy over your indigeneship and the allegations surrounding your change of name, what verifiable documents or official records are you prepared to make available to establish your claim that you are an indigene of Ogun State?”

Let me say this, I can’t be running for such an exalted office and I will not be confronted with these challenges. People who are doing this know they are doing it to discredit and destroy my person. There’s what is called investigative journalism. Where my father was buried is 30 minutes away from here (Ikeja), go and investigate. It is in Almosho, number 3, Ogunsola street, Alagutan, bus stop, in his house, that’s where he was buried. My mother was buried at Vaults and Gardens, Ikoyi, there. My grandmother, the mother of my mother, was buried at Ikeja, the burial ground is there. My great-grandfather was buried at Ishaga. So, how can I be running for a governor’s office, and I’ll be having such a big skeleton in my cupboard, and I’ll be comfortable? Having served The Guardian, and I resigned, I left, and somebody said, “He did change his name.” Yes, I did change of name, and I did it in The Guardian newspaper. I advertised it in The Guardian; I notified The Guardian newspaper of my change of name. They don’t understand, because they have nothing to fight with. So, they have to say something to discredit me, and I’m the candidate to beat. They can’t match me. I don’t want to join issues with them. They have nothing to offer. The know Yayi is from Ogun State. What they can do is to destroy Yayi, and those who are from Ogun State have responded, “Let him come from Afghanistan”. We will vote for him.

Now, how did your political journey begin?

My sojourn into politics has not been an easy road, but at least I managed to find my level. Because that was dated back to the June 12, 1993 struggle. Along the line, I lost my immediate younger brother to that riot, and that got me discouraged. I had to look for a way to step aside and make sure that I don’t get involved in politics again. I became very disheartened and decided to step aside and concentrate on my work. But God has a way of directing one’s path. It is something He destined you to do. In 2002, I found my way back into politics and contested for the position of member representing Alimosho Constituency in the Lagos State House of Assembly. I was there for eight years.

Judging by my performance, I was encouraged to go to the Federal House of Representatives to represent Alimosho Federal Constituency, where I served for four years. Within those four years, I was able to convince my constituents and, by extension, the leadership of the state and the current President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, my father, my leader and my mentor, that I was ripe enough to represent the Lagos West Senatorial District in the Senate. By God’s grace and with the support of my constituents, I represented Lagos West for eight years. Before then, I knew that originally I was not from Lagos; I am from Ogun State. That was evident in all my documents and forms that I filled. There was no cause for doubt. I attempted to return home for the first time, but I met some resistance. Since things were working for me in Lagos, it was easy to return and contest the Senate seat there, which I did successfully. For the second time, I attempted to return home to contest for the governorship of Ogun State. That was also met with some resistance, and again I returned to the Senate from Lagos West. I am giving you this history so that you will understand how I eventually found myself in Ogun State.

What eventually brought you back to Ogun politics?

For the third time, that was when God answered our prayer. When God opened the way and the political opportunity came, I was encouraged to return home. At a point, I was asked whether I would be interested in contesting for a Senate seat in Ogun State. I said yes. Initially, I did not want to run for the Senate again. My intention was to complete my two terms as a senator of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and then prepare myself for the governorship. But some people insisted that it was not possible to wait outside the political structure. They said I had to be in a position where I could remain politically relevant and then migrate from there to the governorship. It took me some time to deliberate on it. I never knew that it was the platform God wanted to use to elevate me to become governor of Ogun State. When I eventually decided to run for the Senate, I noticed that there was a lot of confusion and that several people were also showing interest. I did not realise initially that everybody was galvanising themselves around that platform as a possible route to the governorship in the future. I decided to throw my hat into the ring and, graciously, by the special grace of God, I got the ticket and won the election. By the end of that period, I had spent 12 years in the Senate of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and 24 years as an elected legislator, serving in both Lagos and Ogun states.

What experience from your legislative career do you believe prepares you for the governorship?

I have had the opportunity of getting to the zenith of the legislative body, which is the Senate. I also served in various capacities. In the Lagos State House of Assembly, I was Chairman of the Committee on Finance. In the House of Representatives, I was Chairman of the Committee on Public Accounts. That was while I was in the opposition party because, under the rules of the National Assembly, the opposition traditionally chairs the Public Accounts Committee. In the Senate, I was the pioneer Chairman of the Local Content Committee in the Ninth Senate. In the 10th Senate, I served as Chairman of the Finance Committee. With that experience, I believe I have what it takes to govern Ogun State and take it to the next level. Another important point is that my senatorial district has never produced a governor of Ogun State after 50 years of our existence. I believe that I have the experience and capacity required to provide leadership at this point in the state’s history. Today, I stand before you as the gubernatorial candidate of the APC in the February 6, 2027 governorship election.

You have said your ambition is driven by a passion to serve. Why should Ogun people believe that?

My quest to become governor of the state is not based on personal interest. It is not about enriching myself or occupying an exalted office simply to be called governor. It is driven by passion to serve. I want to serve the people for good. That is why I have chosen to engage the fourth estate of the realm and other opinion holders. There are a lot of issues in the political space. You read something about YAYI today, something about the opposition tomorrow, something about the governor the next day, and so on. But today, this gives you a first-hand, one-on-one interaction with the man called YAYI. I want you to hear directly from me what I intend to do for Ogun State.

Your development agenda places considerable emphasis on continuity. What exactly do you mean by continuity?

I want to work with someone whose experience has brought about some level of advancement to Ogun State. I strongly feel that the next person in line should come to consolidate on the gains we have made in the last seven and a half years as a state.

I make bold to say that, under the administration of Governor Dapo Abiodun, Ogun State has done exceedingly well. I can testify to that. Of course, people will ask: if the government has done well, why are there complaints about certain things? I understand that. No government can completely address all the challenges confronting a state within a limited period in office. Governance is about the seen and the unseen. The seen are the physical structures we see—the roads, hospitals, rail transport and other infrastructure. The unseen are the policies, economic foundations and other things that, when put together and properly implemented, eventually give birth to the visible development. Under Governor Abiodun, we have been able to establish a strong economic foundation. For example, we have the proposed $7 billion deep seaport project in Ogun State, with groundbreaking expected in November. If that project becomes fully operational in the next few years, you can imagine the multiplier effect it will have on the state’s economy. There is also the dry port at Kajola and the proposed rail connection from Apapa to Kajola. The biggest dairy farm in Nigeria is also coming up in my local government area, starting with about 5,000 cattle and eventually increasing to a minimum of 15,000 cattle to produce dairy products from Ogun State. A major furniture manufacturing company is also coming up. As we speak, Ogun State is the most industrialised state in Nigeria. When Governor Abiodun came on board, our internally generated revenue was less than N100 billion annually. Today, we are talking about around N300 billion a year. There has also been oil exploration activity. We may, in the near future, be referred to as an oil-producing state. All these things are part of the foundation that has been laid. My responsibility, if elected, will be to consolidate on these gains and ensure that the multiplier effects are properly harnessed for the benefit of the people.

Does continuity mean you intend to continue everything the present administration is doing?

No. I don’t want anybody to misconstrue what I mean by continuity. Continuity does not mean that I want to take everything this administration has planned or implemented and say that I must continue with it. There are areas I need to continue; I will continue them. There are areas I need to improve upon; I will improve them. There are areas I need to change; I will change them. I will introduce new ideas and new initiatives that will put Ogun State on the path of growth. The essence of continuity is that whatever this administration has achieved and needs to be taken forward will not be abandoned simply because there is a change of government. Many of the projects are still works in progress. A responsible government coming on board will consolidate and ensure that these projects come to fruition. That is what “ITESIWAJU” is about.

What does ITESIWAJU mean in practical terms?

ITESIWAJU is the framework for the kind of government I want to run. The “I” stands for Infrastructure. The “T” stands for Tourism and Culture. The “E” stands for Education and Environment. The “S” stands for Security and Law Enforcement. The second “I” stands for Inclusive Growth and Well-being. The “W” stands for Women and Youth Development. The “A” stands for Agriculture. The “J” stands for Job Creation and Industrialisation. The “U” stands for Urban Physical Planning and Environment. All these nine pillars are critical to Ogun State. None of them can be treated in isolation.

When you talk about tourism and culture, for instance, you cannot compare Ogun with Lagos because we are more of a rural setting and our culture is well appreciated. There are many activities and festivals that take place in Ogun every year.

The question is: Are we deriving the maximum economic benefit from them for the state and its people? That is an area we want to focus on. We want to turn our cultural and tourism assets into economic opportunities.

Let us take infrastructure, which is the first pillar. What would be your priority?

Infrastructure includes roads, rail, housing and transportation. On transport connectivity, we want to deal first and foremost with interstate connectivity, and subsequently intra-state connectivity. I want a situation where I can conveniently stay in a corner of my house in Ilaro, get to the bus terminal and take a vehicle straight to Abeokuta. From Abeokuta, I should be able to take another vehicle to Sagamu, from Sagamu to Ijebu and then back to other parts of the state. When you look at the geographical location of Ogun State, you will understand the challenge. Lagos is different. In Lagos, you can move from one part of the state to another within a relatively short period. In Ogun, you can spend two hours travelling to the next town. You can travel for one hour and 40 minutes to get to certain parts of the state. If you are coming from Ilaro, you can spend several hours getting to another part of Ogun. That is how dispersed Ogun State is geographically. So, we need to have an effective transport system that connects all these areas within the shortest possible time. The road network is one area in which a lot of people residing in Ogun are challenged. I don’t want to embark on any road project that will not lead us anywhere. Yes, there are roads that need to be fixed along the way, but we want to focus on roads that will unlock economic opportunities. For instance, from Ijoko in Ota, we can put in place a road that will lead straight to the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, with three bridges and about one kilometre of road. You can imagine what that means to us as a state. Not only will we open up that corridor, but economic activities will spring up around it. You will not believe the impact that a single intervention of that nature can have. There are many other examples like that.

What is your plan for Ogun’s border towns, particularly those adjoining Lagos?

The border towns are another area of interest. Presently, Lagos has an upper hand in many of the border town areas. When you look at the Ojodu axis and some of the surrounding areas, you will see that there is a lot of development on the Lagos side. But on our own side of the divide, we are not competing effectively. If I intend to increase the value of the state and work on the economy of the state, I must work on the border towns. That is why I refer to urban development, physical planning and the environment. I can create a new Magodo in those border towns that belong to Ogun. The land is there. What is required is the development. It is possible. I intend to give attention to the border towns and ensure that Ogun gives Lagos a run for its money in terms of development. You can imagine travelling from the Lagos side towards Ogun. Once you approach the border and get to certain points, the standard of infrastructure changes. That has to change, and it has to change immediately.

You have used the condition of the Lagos-Ogun border to illustrate your environmental concerns. What would you do differently?

If you are coming from the mainland in Lagos and travelling towards Ogun, you see a certain level of environmental cleanliness and organisation. You get to the Ogun side and, in some places, the picture changes. You see trailers parked along the road, people trading where they should not, and activities taking place that affect the environment and traffic. Under my watch, that will change. If there are businesses that need to operate there, they must do so in an organised manner. You cannot have trailers simply taking over the road. If there is a designated facility where a trailer can park and the operator is required to pay, then that is where the trailer should go. We must bring order to the environment. When the environment is clean, you are happy and more relaxed. When I was serving in Lagos, I could go to a hotel and relax. You could move around and feel comfortable. That is what we need to achieve in Ogun. If Lagos can maintain that level of cleanliness on its side of the same road, why can’t Ogun do the same? Some of us are committed to making sure that our state is clean, organised and better. I will declare a state of emergency on waste management and collection. I will also declare a state of emergency on environmental protection. The relevant agencies will have to sit up. For instance, as far as I know, we do not have an incinerator in Ogun State. We need to look at waste management comprehensively. Every government comes with its own area of focus. Governor Abiodun has done excellently well in laying a solid economic foundation for the state. My responsibility will be to consolidate on that foundation while focusing on other sectors that need attention. I want to reposition Ogun State not merely as a dumping ground for industries, but as a place where people want to invest and live.

You describe Ogun as the most industrialised state, but you have also raised concerns about how much revenue the state derives from that industrial base. What is the problem?

Ogun is the most industrialised state, no doubt about it. But does that automatically translate into revenue for Ogun? The answer is no. The industries are here, but many of the companies have their headquarters or regional offices in Lagos. That means the executives and other workers are based in Lagos. Their salaries are paid in Lagos, and the taxes associated with those salaries are paid in Lagos. So, what is the benefit to Ogun? How do I intend to address it? Very simple: I am not asking for more. Bring the regional offices to Ogun State. If you want to operate a major industry in Ogun, bring your regional office here. By that singular action, you bring middle-level and senior workers to the state. They live here, spend money here and pay taxes here. I intend to create a central business district for industries that are willing to invest in Ogun, where the government can facilitate land for regional offices. If somebody approaches me and says he wants to invest in Ogun State, I will embrace that investment. But if the investment is substantial and the company is going to make its money in Ogun, I will encourage it to establish its headquarters or significant regional operations in the state. Ogun should not simply be a place where you make money and then spend it in Lagos. I believe a portion of that economic value belongs in Ogun, and we should devise legitimate ways of retaining it. The intention is to ensure that when you come and invest in Ogun, you also work here and live here. That is why I have put forward strategies to address the environment and housing.

You have made a bold projection about Ogun’s economic potential. What is the basis for your optimism?

In terms of GDP, Ogun State is already running an economy comparable to that of some countries. Our GDP is about $12 billion. We are ranked among the leading state economies in Nigeria, ahead of countries such as Togo and Sierra Leone in terms of the size of their economies. With the right kind of leadership, a focused government and determination, Ogun can move from about $12 billion to $20 billion and beyond. Imagine what that means for the people. All these things—industrialisation, the seaport, agriculture, mining, oil and gas exploration and other investments—can contribute to the expansion of the economy. That is why I believe that, with the right leadership, you can imagine what Ogun State will look like in the next eight years.

Let us turn to job creation. How do you intend to ensure that Ogun’s expanding economy creates jobs for its people?

A lot of graduates are coming out of Ogun State without jobs. We must address that. I am not promising that government will employ everybody. But government can create an environment where jobs are created and can also recruit qualified people where there are genuine needs. If, for example, we recruit 50,000 people through a transparent and merit-based process, that alone would make a significant difference. Those who qualify should go through tests and the necessary processes. We also have to look at the number of industries coming into the state every day. People complain that Chinese and other foreign investors are taking over Ogun. I ask: what is the logic? The logic is that we need to ensure that our people participate in the opportunities created by those investments.

Agriculture is another major component of your agenda. What is your vision for Ogun’s agricultural sector?

Ogun is an agricultural state. We feed other states. What I want to do is transform agriculture from basic production into agricultural transformation and food security. You will begin to see high-level mechanised farming. We have already seen tractors, planters and other agricultural equipment being provided to farmers. As governor, I will not call myself a farmer, but I will make sure that I run an all-round government that addresses every sector of the Ogun economy. We need to work with the private sector and create commodity exchanges. We need to become the off-taker from farmers. We need to establish processing zones. Let me give you an example from my town in Ilaro. There is a farmer who buys cocoa from many cocoa farmers. He has acquired a significant portion of the produce in the area. If one individual can identify the opportunity, imagine what the government can do with the right policy. We can connect with other cocoa-producing states and establish processing facilities. There can be what I would call a cocoa mall or processing centre where cocoa can be processed, preserved and prepared for the market. Once you preserve and process the product, you find a customer for it. We need to move beyond producing raw materials and selling them cheaply. We need to produce, process and market. We need to encourage our youths and people generally to go into agriculture. Government will not be the farmer. Government’s responsibility is to create the enabling environment. We need to encourage young farmers, provide quality loans and empower them. If somebody is encouraged to become a farmer and knows that, at harvest, government or an organised market is ready to buy the produce and pay promptly, that person will be willing to farm. It is not enough to tell people to go into agriculture. They need access to land, finance, equipment, processing and markets. That is the complete value chain.

Security is another pillar of your agenda. What is your approach?

I believe security is everybody’s responsibility. We need to bring industries and captains of industry into the security conversation. When I was serving as a member of the Lagos State House of Assembly, there was a move to establish a security trust fund. How do we fund it? You bring together the industries and captains of industry and say: come, this is a security trust fund. You are going to be represented in its management because we want you to see exactly what we are doing. We are not necessarily asking you for cash. We can ask industries what equipment they can provide to support security—communication gadgets, security equipment, vehicles and other necessary items. There should be transparency and accountability in the process.

You also mentioned using revenue from gaming and lottery. How would that work?

There is a gaming and lottery industry that generates significant economic activity. In Lagos, for instance, the state established a framework for regulating the industry. Everybody involved in gaming and betting should register with the state. Once you regulate the sector properly, part of the revenue can be directed into the security trust fund. If thousands of people participate in betting, the industry generates significant revenue. The state can legitimately collect the appropriate taxes and levies and channel part of the proceeds towards public safety. That is one of the ways I intend to support security.

You have also expressed support for state police. Why?

I am in support of state police. Nobody understands the environment better than the people who live there. Local security management requires knowledge of the terrain, the communities and the people. That is why I support state police. I am also happy that the President is in full support of state police and that the constitutional process for establishing it is being considered. Once state police is established, it will give the state greater control over security management. For me, that is part of true federalism.

What about the welfare and motivation of security personnel?

We must encourage our law enforcement personnel. It is not easy. They work under difficult circumstances and put their lives at risk. We must ensure that they have the equipment, communication systems, welfare and support required to perform their duties.

Security is not just about giving orders. It is about giving personnel the tools and motivation to do the job.

Your ITESIWAJU framework also speaks about inclusive growth and well-being. What does that mean to you?

Development must ultimately improve the lives of the people. It is not enough to say that Ogun is industrialised or that GDP is growing. The question is: what is the benefit to the ordinary citizen? If the economy grows, people should have jobs. If industries come, local businesses should benefit. If infrastructure is developed, people should have better access to markets and services. That is what inclusive growth means to me. We must ensure that economic development reaches ordinary citizens and is not concentrated in the hands of a few.

How do women and young people fit into your development agenda?

Women and youths are critical to the development of Ogun State. We need to create opportunities for them to acquire skills, start businesses, enter agriculture, participate in industry and benefit from the digital and creative economy. The government should create vocational training centres and other platforms where young people can acquire practical skills.

We should not have a situation where a young person finishes school without any employable skill. If someone is trained in catering, machine operations, technology, agriculture or another vocational area, the government should create opportunities for that person to practice and earn a living.

Government programmes and events should also patronise people who have been trained through such programmes. That is how empowerment becomes sustainable.

Finally, what kind of government should Ogun people expect if you are elected?

They should expect a government that is focused, inclusive and determined to move the state forward. I have said repeatedly that I will continue what needs to be continued, improve what needs to be improved, change what needs to be changed and introduce new ideas where necessary. I do not want a government that sits in an office and is surrounded by sycophants. I want to remain connected to the people. I want to be on the road and understand what is happening in the communities.

At the end of every day, there must be an opportunity to review what has happened, what has been achieved and what needs attention. Leadership is about constant assessment. Ogun has enormous potential. We have the land, the industrial base, the agricultural capacity, the human resources and the strategic location. What we need is focused leadership that can bring all these advantages together.

My ambition is not simply to become governor. It is to use the opportunity to build on what is working, correct what is not working and create new opportunities for the people. That is the meaning of ITESIWAJU. Ogun must move forward.

World.title: PINL: No Pipeline Fracture Recorded in Two Months
World.content:
.Provides employment, livelihood support for over 35,000 youths

Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL) has reported zero pipeline fractures across its operational areas in the past two months, attributing the development to improved collaboration among host communities, surveillance personnel, contractors and security agencies.

The company also disclosed that its surveillance operations provide employment and livelihood opportunities for more than 35,000 youths, while its scholarship programme has awarded over N2 billion to more than 1,500 undergraduate and postgraduate students.

PINL’s General Manager, Community and Government Relations, Dr. Akpos Mezeh, disclosed this yesterday at the company’s Stakeholders’ Engagement Forum, in Port Harcourt, where he called for sustained cooperation to protect critical oil and gas infrastructure and support economic growth in the Niger Delta.

Mezeh said the absence of pipeline fractures in the past two months demonstrated the value of collective action but warned stakeholders against complacency.

“This is a positive development and demonstrates what can be achieved when communities, surveillance personnel, contractors, security agencies and operators work together,” he said.

He added, “Pipeline protection is a shared responsibility. Our objective is not simply to respond to incidents after they occur, but to prevent them through vigilance, intelligence sharing, effective surveillance and strong community relationships.”

PINL, which operates across Bayelsa, Rivers, Imo and Abia states, maintains relationships with 215 host communities along the Trans Niger Pipeline and Eastern Gas Network corridors.

Mezeh said the company had also extended its community development interventions to women’s empowerment, education and environmental management.

According to him, more than 2,000 women have benefited from empowerment initiatives along the Trans Niger Pipeline corridor, while PINL’s annual Christmas palliative programme provides relief materials and medical outreach to its 215 host communities.

He announced that the company’s scholarship programme had been approved as an annual intervention for eligible students from host communities for the duration of its contract with the federal government.

The PINL executive said protecting oil and gas infrastructure had become increasingly important as Nigeria’s energy industry pursued higher production targets and attracted new investments.

He urged host communities to promptly report suspicious activities, including suspected pipeline vandalism, illegal connections and crude oil theft, through appropriate channels.

“Early information allows early intervention. A small issue identified and addressed early can prevent a much larger problem later,” he said.

On environmental responsibility, Mezeh disclosed that PINL had evacuated refuse from identified dumpsites at Okoloma-Afam, Obeama, Miriwanyi, Izuoma and Kom-Kom in Zone 3.

He appealed to residents to discourage indiscriminate waste disposal and activities that could obstruct pipeline rights of way.

Addressing questions of transparency and accountability, Mezeh said PINL welcomed legitimate scrutiny of its operations and remained prepared to cooperate with lawful reviews by competent government institutions.

The company reiterated its commitment to strengthening community relations, promoting environmental responsibility and protecting infrastructure vital to Nigeria’s oil and gas industry.

The Paramount Ruler of Eberi-Omuma Kingdom in Rivers State, King Onyekachi Amaonwu, urged community leaders and residents to sustain their cooperation with PINL.

“Once we unite, traditional rulers and the host community, more results will come,” he said, emphasising the importance of peace and collaboration in achieving development.

Former Bayelsa State lawmaker Ingo Iwowari also urged community members to communicate their experiences with PINL’s education, employment and women’s empowerment programmes.

She encouraged residents to engage constructively in public discussions about the company’s activities while ensuring that community concerns were addressed.

World.title: NHRC Seeks Death Penalty Moratorium as 3,000 Inmates Languish On Death Row
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has called on the federal government to declare an official moratorium on executions and state governors to commute eligible death sentences to life imprisonment, amid concerns that more than 3,000 inmates remain on death row across Nigeria.

The commission said Nigeria was approaching 10 consecutive years without a state execution, a development it described as meeting the international standard for a de facto moratorium, despite the continued imposition of death sentences and the prolonged detention of condemned inmates.

The Executive Secretary of the NHRC, Chief Tony Ojukwu, made the call yesterday in Abuja during the commemoration of the 2026 World Day Against the Death Penalty at the commission’s headquarters.

Ojukwu urged the federal government to formalise the suspension of executions, while calling on state governors to exercise their constitutional prerogative of mercy to commute death sentences, particularly in cases where inmates had exhausted their appeals but remained on death row.

He also advocated a review of laws prescribing mandatory death sentences, arguing that judges should have the discretion to consider mitigating circumstances and systemic vulnerabilities before determining appropriate punishment.

Although capital punishment remains constitutionally valid in Nigeria, the NHRC chief stressed that its administration must be consistent with the country’s human rights obligations and the fundamental principles of fair trial and due process.

He expressed concern that inadequate access to pro bono legal representation, forced confessions and delays in bringing suspects to trial continued to undermine procedural justice, raising questions about the fairness of proceedings in capital cases.

According to him, the protection of human rights requires more than the existence of legal provisions, insisting that the justice system must guarantee fair hearings and ensure that the death penalty is restricted to the most serious crimes in line with applicable international standards.

The commission outlined three immediate policy measures: an official moratorium on executions, the commutation of eligible death sentences to life imprisonment, and a comprehensive review of laws prescribing mandatory capital punishment.

Ojukwu’s appeal places renewed focus on the position of condemned inmates who have exhausted their legal options but remain in custody, as well as the wider implications of prolonged confinement on the administration of criminal justice.

A formal moratorium, the commission argued, would provide an immediate policy framework for suspending executions while the country considers broader reforms to its capital punishment regime.

The proposed review of mandatory death penalty provisions would also allow courts to take individual circumstances into account when sentencing offenders, rather than being compelled by law to impose the same punishment regardless of relevant mitigating factors.

The commemoration was organised by the NHRC in partnership with Avocats Sans Frontières (ASF) France, the Australian High Commission and the Embassy of Germany, with support from the Royal Norwegian Embassy.

Ojukwu expressed hope that deliberations at the event would produce a joint call-to-action communiqué to advance sustainable reforms in Nigeria’s justice sector.

The commission’s position comes amid continuing debates over capital punishment, the protection of the rights of accused persons and the need to strengthen safeguards against miscarriages of justice.

World.title: Imo West Senatorial: Court Orders Okorocha, Araraume, Others’ Arrest over Alleged Criminal Conspiracy, Forgery
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja

A senior Magistrate Court in Abuja has issued a bench warrant for the arrest of former Imo State Governor, Senator Rochas Okorocha and a former Senator, Ifeanyi Araraume, and two others over alleged criminal conspiracy, forgery and tendering of false documents.

The two others are Timothy Ama Chuks and Amen Okorocha.

They are accused of forging and tendering false results of the All Progressives Congress (APC) primary election for Imo West Senatorial, which presented Okorocha as winner of the May 18 primary election.

According to the court documents sighted by THISDAY, all police officers across Nigeria are, by the bench warrant authorised to seize Okorocha, Araraume, Timothy Chuks and Amen Okorocha and produce them before the Senior Magistrate Court 3 at Jiwa ,Abuja.

In the bench warrant dated September 9,2026 and issued by Ebiwari E Damini, the four defendants are charged with criminal conspiracy, forgery, perjury and uttering false documents.

In the case numbers CR/M/JW/084/2026, and CR/M/JW/085/2026, the matter is between the Inspector General of Police and the four wanted persons.

Meanwhile, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has asked both the Police and DSS to investigate Okorocha for allegedly parading fake APC primary results.

Besides, the electoral umpire has also disowned a document allegedly being circulated by Okorocha claiming that he won the primaries.

The commission in the separate letters to the DSS and Police stated that the authentic document by APC before it showed that Governor Hope Uzodimma won the primaries upon which his name was duly forwarded to it by the APC as the candidate for Imo West Senatorial Zone (Orlu Zone).

In the letter to the Commissioner of Police, Imo State Command, and his DSS counterpart, INEC declared the document allegedly being paraded by Okorocha as fake and urged the security agencies to investigate the former governor.

In the letter dated October 8, 2026 and signed by the Resident Electoral Commissioner, Imo State, Chukwuemeka C Ibeziako, INEC declared that it was reporting a case of “fraudulent and fictitious All Progressive Congress senatorial party primary report for Imo State dated May 18,2026.”

It raised the alarm that contrary to the document duly signed by APC and forwarded to its headquarters with Uzodimma as the clear winner of the primary election, the one circulating in the social media purported Okorocha as the winner, hence the petition.

“The fictitious document wrongly presented Senator Ethelbert Rochas Okorocha as the elected candidate for the party,” INEC stated.

While enclosing the original results it claimed declared Uzodimma as the rightful winner of the primary and the alleged fake one being paraded by Okorocha, INEC urged the police and the DSS to thoroughly investigate the forgery.

“In these circumstances, I urge you to graciously use your good offices to investigate and neutralise this spurious conduct that has serious likelihood of causing the breakdown of law and order in Imo State,” INEC charged the police and the DSS.

World.title: World Bank: Only Lagos, Enugu Generate Enough Revenue to Cover Recurrent Costs
World.content:
Nume Ekeghe

The World Bank has said that only Lagos and Enugu states generated enough internally generated revenue (IGR) to cover their recurrent expenditure in 2025, underscoring the continued dependence of most state governments on federal allocations to meet their day-to-day obligations.

The Bank, in its October 2026 Nigeria Development Update (NDU), titled ‘Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Shaped State Priorities’, noted that although states had recorded significant improvements in revenue collection, their internally generated revenue remained insufficient to finance recurrent spending in most parts of the country.

According to the report, state governments’ IGR covered an average of about 40 per cent of recurrent expenditure between 2021 and 2023, before improving to approximately 50 per cent in 2024 and 2025.

However, Lagos and Enugu were the only states whose internally generated revenue exceeded their recurrent expenditure. In 2025, Lagos generated revenue equivalent to 160 per cent of its recurrent spending, while Enugu recorded a significantly higher ratio of 377 per cent.

The World Bank warned that the inability of most states to finance recurrent expenditure through their own revenue sources remained a significant fiscal risk, particularly if federally collected revenues were to decline.

It states, “Tax administration improvements in many states have also boosted IGRs, contributing to a bigger resource envelope for state governments. In real terms, aggregate state IGR grew by 55 per cent between 2023 and 2025, supported in part by the growing adoption of automation and other digital technology initiatives in revenue administration. Enugu state saw by far the highest growth in its IGR during this period. Its total IGR grew from N25 billion to N209 billion, 732 percent growth in real terms.”

It added that all components of the state’s IGR grew and that the Direct Assessment Tax personal income tax paid by business owners, contractors, landlords and other self-employed individuals grew the most from N280 million to N14.5 billion, almost 4,000 per cent growth in real terms over the two-year period. The state achieved this by aggressively expanding its tax net capturing thousands of previously unregistered self-employed informal businesses, landlords, and contractors into the formal tax structure and implementing deep systemic and digital technology reforms. By automating its revenue collection processes and enforcing cashless payments made directly into the state treasury, the government enhanced collection efficiency, blocked leakages, and phased out unauthorised roadside collectors.

The report noted that several state Internal Revenue Services have increasingly embraced digital technology and data integration to automate revenue collection, improve tax compliance and minimise revenue leakages. It added that the integration of revenue systems with geographic information systems and other government databases had helped states expand their tax base and enhance collection efficiency. Meanwhile, inflation-driven salary increases also contributed to higher Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) tax receipts, which remain the largest source of internally generated revenue for most states.

It further stated, “Despite strong IGR growth in 2023–2024, states’ IGRs are insufficient to cover their recurrent expenditure, leaving them fiscally vulnerable. On an aggregate basis, state governments’ IGR covered only about 40 per cent of recurrent costs on average over 2021-2023, although this improved slightly to 50 percent in 2024 to 2025. On an individual basis, the only exceptions were Lagos state and, more recently, Enugu state, for which IGR exceeded recurrent spending.

“In 2025, Lagos State’s IGR was 160 percent of its recurrent expenditure, while Enugu’s was a much higher 377 per cent. The inability of most states to finance recurrent expenditure through own-source revenues remains a key risk for states, as they would be unable to sustain essential service delivery should federally collected revenues suffer a setback, reinforcing the need to strengthen IGRs to improve budget sustainability and resilience.”

World.title: Power outage to affect parts of Johannesburg
World.content:
A power outage is scheduled to affect 14 suburbs in Johannesburg, according to City Power Johannesburg.

It will occur on Sunday, 11 October 2026.

The power outage is due to City Power’s essential maintenance of their electricity network to ensure that customers receive better service.



OUTAGE AFFECTS SEVEN SUBURBS

The power utility urged customers to keep their electricity supply points as live to prevent damage to material when the power returns. Here is a list of the suburbs that will be affected at Sebenza Substation from 9:00 to 17:00:

Alexandra

Belleview

Orchard

Gressworld

Observatory

Westield

Cydna

ELECTRICITY RESTORED IN JOHANNESBURG AREA

Following a community outcry at an Imbizo in Pennyville, City Power Johannesburg cracked down on illegal connections in the area. This comes after community members from Pennyville complained of ongoing electricity challenges in the area during an Imbizo, the power utility took the step forward.

Upon investigating the cause of the challenges, the team established that the transformer had been overloaded. According to the statement by the power utility, illegal electricity connections were one of the contributing factors.

“These illegal connections place significant additional pressure on the electricity network because electricity is consumed outside the designed capacity of the infrastructure. This can result in transformers becoming overloaded and eventually burning out, causing extended outages that affect the broader community,” read the statement.

World.title: How to cook a hearty meal for under R20 [video]
World.content:
Cooking a budget meal for under R20. Image via Canva

Frugal food blogger Olivia Viglatzis has posted a video on how to create a low-cost meal with ingredients that cost under R20.

The social media star is known for sharing her tips for cooking hearty, nutritious meals on a budget.

FOODIE CREATES BUDGET MEAL FOR UNDER R20

In one of her most-viewed videos to date, food blogger Olivia Viglatzis revealed how she prepared a meal for R20 that could easily feed more than one person.



The meal – boerewors, rice and butternut – contained protein, carbs and a side of veggies too. She paid R8.39 for the sausage, R4.51 for the butternut, and R3.25 for a quarter packet of rice.

Olivia purchased the ingredients at her local Shoprite supermarket, where she often finds food items at a fraction of the price.

Olivia cooked all the ingredients, using her own oils and spices, to reveal a hearty spread.

“This worked out to R16,50 – it’s delicious!”, she shared.

Olivia added that for many South Africans living below the poverty line, this could be their only meal of the day.

MORE LOW-COST CUISINE

Olivia Viglatzis has shared other viral budget meals on her social media accounts.



They include the following spreads;

Meal for two: Chicken, noodles and mixed vegetables – Total cost = R28.48

Instant noodles: R7.99

Mixed vegetables: R9.99

Chicken fillet: R10.50]

Meal for two: Rice, Polony, Tomato, and Potato Meal – Total cost = Under R20

Polony – R4,40

Potato- R2,96

Onion – R3,48

Rice -R12,99

HELPING THOSE IN NEED

Olivia Viglatzis has spoken about using her platform to normalise cooking affordable, healthy meals on a budget. She is often seen hunting for a good deal in the vegetable or meat section.

She and her spouse cook and distribute budget-friendly meals to underprivileged communities in Cape Town

She shared: “I love cooking, but Covid made a big difference because that is when we really started helping people in our community and saw the struggle. As time went on, I realised there is a very big need out there”.

She added: “I want to try and support people who are trying to support themselves”.

WHAT DOES SOUTH AFRICA’S MONTHLY FOOD BASKET COST?

According to recent statistics, a household food basket – made up of commonly purchased food items intended to reflect the needs of low-income households – can cost approximately R5,488.

The basket includes staples like and other everyday foods such as:

Maize meal, rice, flour and bread

Cooking oil, sugar and salt

Milk and eggs

Meat, chicken and fish

Beans and other legumes

Potatoes, onions and other vegetables

Fruit and other basic food items

According to figures from Stat SA, South Africans earn an average of R30,611 a month as formal, non-agricultural workers.

However, it is important to note that this is an average salary, not the salary earned by the typical South African.

The salary bracket is not an accurate representation of what ordinary South Africans earn, given factors like the gap between mean vs median earnings, gender and racial wage gaps, and the exclusion of unemployed individuals, to name a few.

World.title: Reality TV royalty: RHOP star shows off daughter’s Matric Dance
World.content:
Real Housewives of Pretoria star Kiki La Coco – real name Karlien Wentzel – beamed with pride as she posed for pictures with her stepdaughter, Chante, at the latter’s Matric Dance this week.

The reality TV star is married to businessman and TikToker Malcolm Wentzel, who has three daughters from his marriage to his late wife, Lizane.

REAL HOUSEWIVES OF PRETORIA STAR SHOWS OFF STEPDAUGHTERS’ MATRIC DANCE PICS

On her social media account, Kiki La Coco posted pictures of her stepdaughter Chante’s Matric Dance look.



Chante wore a stylish, embroidered strapless gown in duck blue. She posed for pics with Kiki, dad Malcolm and her date.

She captioned the post: “Since you were little, you couldn’t wait for the day! Now you are exactly where you always wanted to be. May it be very special and, going forward, even more beautiful”.

Under the post, Kiki’s followers praised her for doing a stellar job in raising the teen and her sisters. Others commented that the girls’ mother, Lizane, who died in 2017, would have been “proud” of her daughters.

SORISHA SETS THE TONE

Fellow Real Housewives star Sorisha Naidoo also had her Matric Dance mom moment with son Saihil, who celebrated both his 18th birthday and his recent Matric Dance.



The son of Sorisha and businessman Vivian Reddy kicked off the milestone occasion with a party at the family’s Umhlanga mansion.

Take a look…

World.title: Free State primary school mourns three children killed in minibus crash
World.content:
Three JCS Independent primary school learners died in a minibus crash this week. Images via Canva/X

JCS Independent, a private Christian school in the Free State, is mourning the deaths of three primary school learners who died in a minibus collision with a truck in Sasolburg on Thursday,8 October.

The driver of the scholar transport, the school’s director, was also killed in the crash.

FREE STATE SCHOOL MOURNS LEARNERS WHO DIED IN MINIBUS CRASH

In a statement on their Facebook page, JCS Independent confirmed the tragic news of the fatal car crash that claimed the lives of three primary school learners, aged between 6 and 9.



The minibus driver, a 60-year-old man, has been referred to as the school director.

Other learners in the vehicle were transported to nearby medical facilities, where they were treated.

The crash happened on the R57 and R59 bridge in Sasolburg on Thursday afternoon. The driver of the truck survived the collision.

Circumstances surrounding the collision are under investigation. A case of culpable homicide has been opened at Sasolburg Police Station.

The school – which closed for the day – appealed to the public not to share any pictures or videos taken at the crash scene. It also pledged to provide counselling support to learners and staff.

PRAYERS UP FOR ANOTHER STUDENT RECOVERING FROM CAR ACCIDENT

Meanwhile, St Patrick’s College in KwaZulu-Natal has urged its community to pray for one of its learners, Ethan Ingram and his father, Richard, who were injured in a serious crash this week.



Richard is an athlete who has represented South Africa abroad.

No other details of the crash have been publicly revealed.

World.title: Aimee Barrett-Theron opens up about breast cancer fight
World.content:
Aimee Barrett-Theron has opened up about her breast cancer fight. Images via IG

International female rugby referee Aimee Barrett Theron has opened up about her battle with breast cancer and how she was “lucky” to detect it in its early stages.

The 39-year-old went public with her diagnosis in July, sharing that she would step away from the pitch to undergo treatment.

She is now using her platform to encourage women to take early prevention steps.



AIMEE BARRETT THERON OPENS UP ABOUT HEALTH BATTLE

Speaking in light of October being recognised as breast cancer awareness month, Aimee Barrett-Jones spoke about her experience of diagnosis and treatment.

The 39-year Old Girl of Northlands Girls High School shared in a video post: “I was very lucky that I found mine in the early stages. It literally saved my ver active career and potentially my life”

Aimee – who is currently undergoing chemo treatment – revealed that she was fit and healthy, and did not have a family history of breast cancer. Her concerns were heightened when she performed a self check and discoveree an irregularity.

The international female refere chose to share her health battle publicly in the hopes of inspirig others to get screenings and do self-checks.

She shared: “We know our bodies best, and if something doesnt feel right, please go and get it checked.

“It could have a massive impact on your treatment plan and your future”



In July, Aimee revealed that she was stepping away from the pitch to focus on treatment.

She shared: “I’m approaching this the same way I would approach any high-performance environment: with the right team around me, a clear plan, honest conversations, and full commitment to the process.”

I was determined to make it through the ranks as a referee. Now, I’m even more determined to get through this and return to the field stronger”.

OCTOBER IS BREAST CANCER AWARENESS MONTH

October is National Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a month dedicated to bringing awareness about breast health and the importance of early detection.

Women are encouraged to practise self-awareness, have clinical breast exams, and have regular mammograms.

World.title: Calls for Roosevelt High School to REFUND Matric Dance tickets
World.content:
Roosevelt High School has come under fire again relating to allegations from its Matric Dance last week. Image via Facebook

Roosevelt High School continues to face social media backlash amid calls for a refund of Matric Dance ticket sales after principal Cristèl Venter shut down the event early last week.

This was reportedly due to reckless behaviour by Grade 12 learners, including underage drinking, drug use, and a firearm incident.

In a lengthy open letter published on the school’s Facebook page, Venter apologised to students who were not involved in the alleged misconduct. She also vowed to thoroughly investigate the incident and launch disciplinary proceedings against any perpetrators.



Earlier this week, podcaster Penuel Mlotshwa addressed the school learners, urging them to exercise responsibility and accountability.

CALLS FOR ROOSEVELT HIGH SCHOOL TO REFUND MATRIC DANCE TICKETS

On Facebook, preacher and influencer Curt van Heerden called for Roosevelt High School to refund the Matric Dance ticket sales or fund another event out of their own pocket.

This is related to principal Cristèl Venter shutting down the event over alleged misconduct by several Grade 12 learners. Following the event, Venter posted a 10-page open letter condemning students and some parents for their reckless behaviour.

Van Heerden accused the principal of failing to establish the facts and of “misusing her authority” in admonishing the students.

He said: “It’s completely unfair that 95% of the matric students should suffer for what 5% have done.

“You closed down one of the best nights every high school student looks forward to. It’s wrong, it’s unfair, and it should not have happened.



He continued: “The way you spoke to them was unfair. You, as the SGB and principal, need to do one of two things: refund all the students, or come together and plan a proper Matric Dance”.

“This must be investigated. I won’t let it go”.

AVIANTO RESPONSE, AND DEMANDS FOR ‘PROOF’

In another video, Chris van Heerden shared “receipts” that Roosevelt High School’s principal had acted prematurely in shutting down the Matric Dance.

This included screenshots, email correspondence by the events venue, Avianto Hotel, which disputed claims that it had called for the event to end early.

Avianto disputed that alcohol was served to Matric learners or that intoxicated learners had damaged or vomited on their property, as was alleged. The venue also claimed that the firearm incident involved adults, and not Grade 12 learners.

Several parents also expressed their disappointment and frustration, particularly at the principal admonishing the students at the venue and posting an open letter on Facebook.

One mother told TimesLive that she had saved money to give her daughter the best Matric Dance experience, only for it to be cut short.

Another father, Mohamed Kader, went on record to state that the sequence of events described by the principal was incorrect.

Other parents are requesting “proof” of the principal’s claims of underage drinking, drug use and claims that students had become violently ill at the venue.

When approached for comment, principal Cristèl Venter stated that she was not authorised to speak to the media.

World.title: Cardoso playing mind games? Mokoena weighs in on Sundowns injury concerns
World.content:
Former Orlando Pirates winger Lebohang Mokoena believes Mamelodi Sundowns coach Miguel Cardoso could be playing mind games ahead of Saturday’s MTN8 final.

Masandawana will face the Buccaneers at the Moses Mabhida Stadium in Durban, with both sides looking to get their hands on the first major trophy of the season.

Cardoso revealed this week that Teboho Mokoena, Bathusi Aubaas and Aubrey Modiba could miss the highly anticipated clash due to injuries sustained while on international duty with Bafana Bafana.



However, the Sundowns coach indicated that late fitness tests would determine whether the trio would be available for selection.

Cardoso looking to win first domestic cup with Sundowns

Despite the injury concerns, Lebohang Mokoena believes Cardoso could be attempting to keep Pirates guessing about his starting line-up.

“It might be an advantage in the midfield if they don’t have Mokoena and Aubaas, but they also have an Allende and Mkhulise. I think the battle is going to be in that midfield,” he told Soccerbeat.

Mokoena suggested that coaches often use uncertainty surrounding player availability to gain a psychological advantage over their opponents before major matches.

He also pointed to reports that Monnapule Saleng had returned to training, although the Sundowns winger has yet to feature for the club this season.

“There’s always those mind games played by coaches before big games. I also heard Saleng is training, he might be available, but he’s never there.



“Psychologically, the game has those things where the coaches are throwing in those ducks, saying certain players might be available so as not to give away the line-up.”

Mokoena believes the uncertainty surrounding Sundowns’ team selection could be part of Cardoso’s strategy, with Pirates left waiting to discover which players will be available for the final.

He suggested that Teboho Mokoena and Modiba could be fit enough to feature against the Buccaneers, despite the concerns raised earlier in the week.

The final promises to be another intriguing encounter between the two South African giants, with Pirates looking to extend their dominance in the MTN8 while Sundowns aim to reclaim the trophy.

Do you think Cardoso is playing mind games?

World.title: Heading to the beach? Saturday’s tides could surprise you
World.content:
If you’re heading to the coast on Saturday, check the tide times before planning your activities, as spring tides bring changes to water levels along South Africa’s coastline.

However, tides are only part of the picture. Wind, waves and swell can also affect conditions along the shore and at sea.

Spring tides are here

Spring tides coincide with the new moon on Saturday, 10 October, bringing higher high tides and lower low tides than usual.



These changes can affect swimming, surfing, fishing and other coastal activities. Conditions will vary from beach to beach depending on the seabed, wind and swell.

Higher tides can cover rocks and reefs that are normally visible at low tide, while lower tides can expose more of the shoreline.

Time to watch along the coast on Saturday

Checking the high and low tide times can help beachgoers, anglers and boat users plan their activities around changing coastal conditions.



Check the tide times and the latest weather and marine warnings before you head to the coast.

⁠Home Affairs⁠ has withdrawn its ⁠asylum-seeker directive⁠ following the Constitutional Court’s Scalabrini Centre judgment. It denies political interference. Protests have left Durban and Soweto tense; Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi seeks dialogue as police remain deployed in KwaZulu-Natal.

⁠Navi Pillay⁠ has won the ⁠2026 Nobel Peace Prize⁠ for advancing peace and international law. The former UN human rights chief dedicated it to survivors of international crimes. The Nobel Committee warned of pressure on legal institutions.

A ⁠pastor’s wife ⁠accused in connection with the ⁠death of a four-month-old baby⁠ remains in custody after her ⁠Atteridgeville⁠ court case was postponed to Monday. Police seek her husband over alleged rape and murder.

⁠Randburg residents⁠ fear health risks after nearly two weeks without refuse collection. ⁠Pikitup⁠ blames reduced capacity and says it is working to restore services.

The ⁠MK Party⁠ says ⁠Jacob Zuma⁠ is in good spirits after a reported routine medical check-up. His hospitalisation raises questions about election preparations.

The Johannesburg High Court has ordered the ANC to reinstate ⁠Andile Lungisa⁠ to its Nelson Mandela Bay candidate list, ruling his removal unlawful.

⁠Manchester City⁠ face Liverpool after a commission found more than 100 ⁠Premier League financial-rule breaches⁠. City denies wrongdoing and has appealed. Manager Enzo Maresca backs the club.

⁠Orlando Pirates⁠ meet ⁠Mamelodi Sundowns⁠ in Saturday’s ⁠MTN8 final⁠ in Durban. In cricket, Australia ended day one of the Durban Test on 187 for six after bad light stopped play.

Watch ⁠News Bite⁠ for these stories and more on ⁠eNCA.com ⁠and DStv channel 403.

The three suspects were certified dead at the scene, while two AK-47 rifles, multiple rounds of ammunition and magazines were found inside their vehicle.

“The injured victims were transported to hospital for medical attention,” she said.

According to Nevhuhulwi, the shootout followed a crime intelligence operation in which law enforcement officers received information about a group using two vehicles allegedly planning to commit a robbery in Roodepoort.

She said the white vehicle involved in a high-speed chase with police was spotted on Kliprivier Road.
