World.title: Tax cut to bring ¥36,000 benefit per citizen, Takaichi says
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Friday that the planned consumption tax cut for food is expected to reduce household financial burdens by about ¥36,000 per citizen.

“The tax rate cut will basically be reflected in prices,” Takaichi said at a plenary meeting of the Senate, the upper chamber of parliament.

She explained that the ¥36,000 figure was calculated by dividing the total tax revenue loss to the central and local governments from the tax cut by the country’s population.

During the Upper House meeting, Yasue Funayama of the Democratic Party for the People asked the prime minister how her administration will make up for local government revenue losses.

Takaichi vowed to fully cover these revenue losses with state funds, saying, “We’ll properly secure necessary local tax grants.”

The prime minister also said the government is considering measures to support agricultural and fishery businesses, as well as food companies and restaurants whose operations could be affected by the tax cut. “It is necessary to assess circumstances on the ground and respond according to the impact on each sector,” she said.

Meanwhile, Komeito Secretary-General Makoto Nishida called on the government to clarify who would be eligible for a financial aid program for workers that will be introduced alongside the consumption tax cut.

Takaichi indicated that the government will explain the matter during parliamentary deliberations, based on discussions by the suprapartisan National Council on Social Security.

Sanseito leader Sohei Kamiya argued that the consumption tax reduction should apply across the board, not only to food.

Takaichi countered that such a move could affect public services, including pensions, medical care, nursing care and measures to address the declining birthrate.

World.title: Beer maker leaders may have been aware of price cartel
World.content:
Top management officials of some of the four major beer makers suspected of a price cartel are believed to have been informed of details of shipping price hikes negotiated among the companies, informed sources have said.

The Japan Fair Trade Commission is investigating whether these top officials recognized that the information was a result of negotiations, the sources said Friday.

According to the sources, some officials of the companies — Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Holdings — have admitted to the cartel during the commission’s investigation.

Officials from the companies are believed to have held unofficial talks after industry group meetings to exchange information on the timing and scale of shipping price increases and compile price tables.

On Wednesday, the commission conducted compulsory inspections of the headquarters of the four companies on suspicion of violating the Antimonopoly Act.

Under the act, companies found to have engaged in illegal price fixing can face penalties, including financial surcharges and orders to prevent further violations. Unlike routine administrative inspections, compulsory investigations allow authorities to search premises and seize evidence under court warrants, typically in cases considered particularly serious or damaging to consumers.

The four companies, which collectively control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market, are suspected of coordinating the timing and scale of price increases for beer, low-malt beer and other beer-like beverages over several years.

World.title: China militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan’s east coast, patrol finds
World.content:
A Chinese militia boat was spotted along with two other vessels off Taiwan’s Pacific coast in August, according to a surveillance report reviewed by reporters, the first known sighting of such a craft in the sensitive area.

The report by Taiwan’s Apex Aviation identifies the Minfudingyu 07902 as a fishing boat that doubles as a Chinese militia vessel, which was seen operating with a Chinese coast guard cutter and a research vessel one day in mid-August.

China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.

World.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport
World.content:
The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv’s international airport, the United Arab Emirates’ top prosecutor said on Friday.

In the aftermath of the incident, people on board — the majority of whom were Israeli — described a sudden plunge in altitude and a fight for control of the aircraft, which was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were repatriated on a second flydubai flight hours later.

The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s Sept. 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life,” according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media.

World.title: U.S. lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
World.content:
The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, according to the U.S. Treasury Department’s website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist.

The move comes a after report this week that said the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump had opened talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government, reversing U.S. policy that sought to isolate the generals who overthrew elected leaders in 2021.

It was unclear if the decision to remove Myanmar national Theint Win Htet from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) was a result of the talks.

World.title: China and EU strike deal to halve Chinese hybrid exports
World.content:
China and the European Union have reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said Friday after talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU’s ballooning trade deficit with China.

The “shared understanding” would “moderate” China’s export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU, and would cut the imports of several million cars over four years, Sefcovic said after the two-day talks, without offering details on how the agreement will be implemented.

Shares of European carmakers, which have slid steadily over the past two years due to U.S. tariffs and soaring Chinese exports, broadly gained on the news.

World.title: Iran guards ability to build missiles as Trump eases attacks
World.content:
Iran has managed to preserve its missile and drone factories despite months of U.S. and Israeli bombing, officials familiar with the matter said, allowing it to replenish its arsenals while President Donald Trump holds off on strikes ahead of the midterm elections.

Tehran still has the capacity to manufacture weapons to rebuild its arsenal, according to the Western officials, who asked not to be identified discussing private assessments. One official said Iran remains well-stocked with ballistic missiles and some anti-ship weapons, and can quickly add more.

The Western official said Russia was providing missiles as well, echoing a separate assessment in June. Russia’s Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Republican opposition widens to livestreamed execution; Trump still weighing it
World.content:
Republican U.S. lawmakers joined religious leaders and international observers on Friday in opposing a Pentagon plan to livestream an execution by firing squad, while President Donald Trump said he has not yet decided whether to allow the live feed.

Vice President JD Vance expressed skepticism over whether the Pentagon will proceed with livestreaming the scheduled Dec. 3 execution of former U.S. Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan, who was found guilty in a U.S. military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

“I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to the livestream plan championed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

World.title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: Blind musician with rare birth disease plays her heart out
World.content:
A year after a seven-hour surgery in Hong Kong in 2025, Cassie Li Pui-ying was on stage at Queen Elizabeth Stadium, playing the drums before an audience of more than 2,500 people. She heard the applause but could not see who it came from.

That March night was organised by Live Theatre, which her mother Marine Mak also helps run. Li sang, spoke and played the drums. The group gives visually impaired students a stage to perform on.

Despite having been through several serious health scares, what comes across is Li’s faith, optimism and cheer. She moves people.

World.title: Lack of heat action plan leaves Hong Kong’s vulnerable residents at risk, experts warn
World.content:
Environmentalists and academics have criticised the omission of a systemic heat-health action plan in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and latest policy address, warning that relying on “common sense” is failing to protect vulnerable residents from rising temperatures.

Their comments came as new research from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) found that extreme heat may have contributed to as many as 3,238 excess deaths in the city over the past decade.

In response to the South China Morning Post’s queries about the lack of a cross-departmental heat action plan for vulnerable groups, a government spokesman said there were ongoing efforts to “elevate the response capabilities of the government and the community”.

World.title: Hong Kong lawmakers back 5-year plan as firms urged to align with blueprint
World.content:
At the close of a three-day Legislative Council debate on Friday, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki thanked lawmakers for their suggestions, saying they would help improve governance.

“The process of formulating the city’s five-year plan and the in-depth discussion at the Legislative Council have demonstrated a positive interaction between the administration and the legislature, with both striving for the best for Hong Kong,” he said.

World.title: Developer of One Stanley pledges 6-year warranty and checks amid steel bar probe
World.content:
The developer of One Stanley has offered flat owners a six-year structural warranty and free independent property inspections amid an investigation into suspected steel reinforcement deficiencies at the seaside luxury residential development in southern Hong Kong.

K Wise, a subsidiary of One Stanley developer K&K Property, addressed the brewing scandal on Friday, a week after allegations of substandard work were reported by a local property media outlet, issuing a statement outlining remedial measures for homeowners and buyers completing transactions.

“The company understands that the incident has caused concern among property owners, buyers and the public, and will make building safety and safeguarding the interests of owners its top priority,” K Wise said.

World.title: Travel agencies tout Huanggang Port tours, but security chief urges later visits
World.content:
Hong Kong travel agencies are offering tours featuring “five-minute clearance” at the revamped Huanggang Port when it opens on Monday, but the security chief has urged those who do not need to use the crossing immediately to delay their visits.

Three days before the port’s official opening, the South China Morning Post on Friday found a number of tour packages advertised on social media that promoted the redeveloped border checkpoint as a new attraction for trips to mainland China.

An  posted by Sino Step Travel Services on its Facebook page said: “Early access to the Huanggang Port for a brand new clearance experience!”

World.title: US lawmakers push green card bill for Hongkongers, but observers doubt success
World.content:
Two US lawmakers are pushing for a bill that would allow Hongkongers in the country to apply for permanent residency, but authorities and observers have dismissed it as a political move unlikely to succeed.

Senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, and Representative James McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, announced the Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act, seeking to provide a pathway to green cards and ultimately citizenship for Hong Kong residents in the US currently protected under the Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) programme.

Introducing the bill, Merkley accused Beijing and Hong Kong authorities of continuing to “undermine the fundamental rights and freedoms of Hongkongers”.

“The United States must protect Hong Kong residents who have sought refuge in America,” he said. “Congress must take action and enact our legislation to ensure Hongkongers residing in the US do not have to fear deportation.”

World.title: Girl filmed carrying beer bags to be placed in temporary care with siblings
World.content:
A 10-year-old Hong Kong girl filmed carrying heavy bags of beer will be placed in temporary care with her two siblings after welfare assessments found it would “not be suitable” for them to return home following the arrest of their parents on suspicion of ill-treating a child.

Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that the three children were still in hospital for health checks and were expected to be discharged later that day or on Saturday.

“Even after the three siblings are discharged from hospital, the Social Welfare Department’s assessment is that it will not be suitable for them to return home immediately,” he said.

“We have therefore arranged suitable temporary accommodation for them after their discharge.”

World.title: News commentator denies unlawfully revealing police meeting details online
World.content:
A Hong Kong news commentator accused of violating the national security law has denied exposing police intelligence operations, telling a court that details of his meeting with officers were already public knowledge before he posted them online.

Wong Kwok-ngon, 72, who ran a YouTube commentary channel under the pen name Wong On-yin, stood trial at the District Court on Friday. He is the first person in Hong Kong to be prosecuted for allegedly prejudicing an investigation into national security offences by unlawfully disclosing details of a police interview.

He was also charged with knowingly publishing seditious publications in connection with videos covering local and international news.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.title: Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.content:
Two books translated into English from Chinese have been shortlisted for the 2026 U.S. National Translation Awards, which recognize excellence in both original and translated literary works.

The shortlist, announced Tuesday by the American Literary Translators Association, includes two originally written in Chinese: Chinese author Shuang Xuetao’s short story collection “Hunter,” translated by Jeremy Tiang, and Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu’s “Mending Bodies,” translated by Jacqueline Leung, among a total of 11 poetry and prose works translated from nine languages.

“The Ruins,” an anthology by Chinese poet Ye Hui and translated by Li Dong, was longlisted among 23 works across prose and poetry on Sept. 3 but did not make the shortlist. Ye is known for his spare, understated poems that draw on everyday life and nature and explore questions of time, memory, and existence.

Established in 1998, the awards rank among the world’s top professional accolades for literary translation. Winning translators in both categories — poetry and prose — each receive a $4,000 prize. Translations of Chinese works have previously been listed for the prize, including works by contemporary writers Xu Zechen and Yan Lianke, as well as Qing dynasty (1644–1911) novelist and playwright Li Yu.

Shuang Xuetao, author of “Hunter,” one of the two shortlisted Chinese works, was born in 1983 in Shenyang, capital of the northeastern Liaoning province. He is widely considered a leading figure in the “Dongbei Renaissance,” a cultural movement emerging from northeast China, or Dongbei. Known for his use of local dialect, Shuang often portrays the lives of ordinary people in the region, long dismissed as a cultural backwater and rust belt. Several of his works have been adapted into films.

“Hunter” features 11 standalone stories, some of which were originally written in Dongbei dialect: from provincial ambulance drivers searching for a hospital in the middle of the night, to a legendary knife fighter working in a factory. In a note about their selection published alongside the announcement, the competition’s judges wrote that Shuang’s stories “paint a portrait of a region marked by gritty pragmatism, dark humor, and magical realism.”

The work was translated by Shuang’s long-term collaborator Jeremy Tiang — a novelist in his own right. The judges wrote that Tiang “expertly translated Shuang’s often inventive, utterly unique description; his English texts are layered and witty.”

The second book nominated for the prize, “Mending Bodies” by Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu, is a work of speculative fiction and follows a young woman adjusting to life after surgically binding her body to a partner, in a future where people are encouraged to do so. Hon has previously drawn praise for her surreal, introspective fiction, which often explores the fragility of the body, memory, and human relationships.

According to the judges, Jacqueline Leung, the book’s Hong Kong-based translator, “flawlessly translates the between-the-lines subtleties of the languages.”

“The shortlisting of these works carries substantial significance for the overseas circulation of Sinophone literature and its greater visibility within global professional literary circuits, representing, in a sense, a multifaceted retelling of Chinese stories across fiction and poetry,” Shao Dong, an assistant professor of creative writing at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, told Sixth Tone.

The overall award winners will be announced on Oct. 23 as part of the American Literary Translators Association’s annual conference.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Covers of “Hunter,” “Mending Bodies,” and “The Ruins,” by Shuang Xuetao, Hon Lai Chu, and Ye Hui, respectively. Reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.title: ‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.content:
The thieves came in the dead of night in late August — seven ghostly figures illuminated only by the glow of their flashlights and burning cigarettes. When they left, tucked under their arms were 10 chickens and two geese.

The next day, watching footage of the theft recorded by a security camera, Xu Lingni’s heart sank. It was the end of a dream.

The poultry had been kept overnight in a hilltop coop at the bucolic Huxi campus of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (SCFAI), in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing, and belonged to the Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative, a student-led club aimed at rebuilding the bonds between humans and nature.

The group had intended to use the project to promote interest across campus and beyond in food-waste conversion, community-supported agriculture, plastics consumption, and other sustainability issues.

For Xu, the club’s leader, those plans vanished along with those 12 birds. Yet worse was to come.

After a brief investigation, the Chongqing police discovered that several workers hired by SCFAI for a summer construction project had taken the poultry and eaten them. Their crew manager agreed to pay 7,000 yuan ($1,040) to compensate for the financial loss and the students’ emotional distress.

However, the theft drew widespread attention and sparked fresh criticism over raising animals on campus. Facing mounting pressure, the school’s leadership decided to ban the practice. The cooperative was over.

Hatching a plan

The Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative was a key part of the Healing Garden Project, which inhabits a patch of land on campus once piled high with construction waste. Seven years ago, Jin Lipeng, an associate professor in SCFAI’s School of Experimental Art, led students in repurposing the debris to pave paths and build planting beds. He envisioned an area that could restore nature and nurture people.

At the time, the campus cafeteria was sending hundreds of kilograms of food scraps — often mixed with unsorted plastic waste — to an incinerator dozens of kilometers away. Jin and his students began to use these leftovers as compost, converting roughly 40 tons of food waste into fertilizer over the years.

The idea for the cooperative stemmed from a graduate student’s thesis project in spring 2025 that looked at permaculture and the role of foraging chickens in loosening soil, eating pests, clearing weeds, and providing eggs. To test a theory, the student purchased five chickens of a local breed with red combs and black skin. They were allowed to roam freely through campus and returned at night to their hilltop coop.

Xu, an undergraduate majoring in sculpture, was already involved in the garden project and began informally caring for the chickens, buying them grain and taking them to the veterinarian.

In summer last year, as temperatures soared above 40 degrees Celsius, one bird died of heatstroke, and three others disappeared. Fearing that the sole survivor would get lonely, Xu bought a new one from the market. Then one of the escapees returned.

A few days later, Xu found six new adolescent chickens in the coop. A school janitor, who had bought them to raise for their meat, agreed to sell the birds to the students. These were soon joined by a common chicken brought from a roadside stall, a Plymouth Rock chicken, a new hatchling, and a wuhei black-boned chicken. (Two birds died before the theft — one from hypothermia, the other from a wild animal attack. The wuhei chicken was the only one left behind by the thieves; its dark plumage likely made it hard to spot at night.)

As the flock grew, the birds began producing more eggs than the students could eat. Jin, whose research area includes labor issues, proposed creating the cooperative as a student club and asked Xu to lead it. Soon, the students were dividing up their responsibilities: caring for the animals, sourcing and selling merchandise, writing articles, and managing social media channels. In June this year, several attended an international conference to introduce the cooperative’s work.

Those who joined the project felt that caring for the chickens brought them “healing energy.” Xu recalls one classmate who would often hold the birds and cry. “The theft this summer hit her especially hard, and she wasn’t the only one,” Xu says, adding that the cooperative not only fostered friendships but also helped some members find meaning.

While she doesn’t exactly share Jin’s grand ideals, Xu believes that through her work she came to understand seemingly distant but deeply personal issues such as permaculture and climate change.

“Most university students have no idea where eggs come from, what happens to food waste, or why rubbish gets incinerated,” she said in a speech at a climate change forum in May. “Dorm rooms are piled with takeout plastic. Delivery workers risk heatstroke in extreme temperatures. Yet few students have enough awareness to connect these to drought, heat, and carbon emissions.

“Our work lets people feel the pressure and causes of climate change firsthand,” she added, “and shows that through campus community-supported agriculture we can mount a small resistance.”

Making a mess

The cooperative began selling eggs for about 2 yuan each to residents on and around campus this March. The chickens laid two to eight eggs a day. Xu stored them in her apartment’s refrigerator, took orders through an online group chat, and delivered them to customers on her electric bike. She calculates that this brought in just over 500 yuan in total.

Fans of the project were kept up to date through the club’s channel on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, which has more than 6,300 followers. In addition, the cooperative sold themed merchandise including fridge magnets, tote bags, and silk scarves, which brought in about 2,000 yuan.

Not everyone was supportive, though. The most common complaint was that the free-roaming chickens often defecated on the pathways and at the entrance to the student dormitories. To prevent this, this summer the birds were fenced in on the hillside.

In 2022, Chongqing introduced regulations prohibiting the raising of livestock and poultry in urban areas. However, the restrictions apply only to commercial-scale farming, while exceptions can be made for educational purposes and scientific research.

While the number of chickens at SCFAI was far below commercial scale, the activity fell outside the definition of “backyard rearing,” putting it in a gray area. As such, the school took an open-minded approach, requiring only proper fencing and separation, despite repeated objections from others in the campus community.

The cooperative used old bamboo posts and tall netting to enclose the poultry on the hilltop. But the gate was never locked. “This is a public welfare project. Anyone was welcome to come in to spend time with the chickens,” Xu explains.

For security, the group installed an infrared camera to watch the flock at night and raised two goslings to guard the coop. “Geese bite hard. Once I went up the hill in a raincoat, and they didn’t recognize me, so they bit me,” Xu adds. “We’d thought the intruders would be stray cats or weasels — never thieves.”

Ruffling feathers

The theft sparked an outpouring of grief online. “Come home, little ones” and “My babies are gone” were typical comments posted by students in the aftermath.

In the coming weeks and months, Xu and her classmates had planned to step up marketing and sales, offer egg-based food delivery services, and write a handbook on community supported agriculture that could inspire other schools and universities.

That’s now all been scrapped. This fall, the school’s leadership announced a ban on keeping poultry on campus.

In a statement, it also said that officials had learned during mediation that the maintenance workers who took the birds had endured long hours of intense labor in hot weather, with limited food and lodging. Some students strongly objected to this version of events, arguing that chicken meat is cheap and widely available — and that the workers weren’t “desperate,” they just wanted to taste free-range birds.

“Pioneering ecological practice is inherently accompanied by trial and error and waiting,” the statement read. “We will review and consolidate, continue deepening our existing work, and wait for the right conditions to restart explorations.”

The cooperative maintained that its activities “filled a gap” in the school’s labor education by giving students hands-on experience as well as teaching responsibility and empathy. But there was no overturning the decision.

The sole survivor of the theft, the wuhei chicken, was moved to a student’s home for safekeeping and has quickly adapted to her new environment. Xu says the bird is even laying eggs again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Xu Lingni is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Kong Lingyu.

A version of this article originally appeared in FoodThink. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.title: China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.content:
DeepZang, China’s first Tibetan-language large language model, is being upgraded to better adapt to Tibetan dialects, enable real-time translation between Tibetan and Mandarin Chinese, and support offline use.

At a Monday seminar in Hohhot, capital of northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the model’s developer unveiled a series of upgrades scheduled between October and December. The seminar featured representatives from companies, research institutions, and universities.

DeepZang, developed by local technology company Choknor, was launched in March in Lhasa, capital of the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. Its app supports AI-powered conversations, translation, and speech transcription in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese, and English.

At the model’s launch, organizations including the Xizang branches of China Mobile and the People’s Insurance Company of China, as well as Sichuan Minzu Publishing House, signed agreements with Choknor to promote its adoption.

According to Choknor, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users across Xizang, the northwestern Qinghai and Gansu provinces, and southwestern Sichuan province, where most of China’s Tibetan speakers reside.

The company has said the model has cut the time needed for some Tibetan-Chinese translation tasks involving two or three people from 40 minutes to just over 10 minutes for one person. It also reported that the model has been used in such varied settings as helping non-Tibetan-speaking doctors communicate with local patients, generating Tibetan-language contracts for yak sales, and assisting grassroots officials in drafting Tibetan work reports.

The model has been trained on nearly 70 million pairs of standardized Tibetan and Chinese texts, along with more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan speech covering its three major dialect groups — Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo. The team collected the data from libraries, medical institutions, and monasteries, among other settings.

At Monday’s seminar, Choknor unveiled plans to develop offline language packages for Tibetan, Chinese, and English, allowing the app to function with limited or no internet access. The company also plans to pilot 50 simultaneous interpretation devices among at least 300 participants in Lhasa this December.

Tenzin Norbu, Choknor’s founder, said the company aims to bring DeepZang into “pastoral tents, tourist service counters, and grassroots hospitals,” enabling Tibetan speakers to “enjoy the benefits of artificial intelligence on an equal footing.”

Choknor said on Sunday that beyond fostering exchanges and integration among ethnic groups, DeepZang could help ensure the accuracy of Tibetan-language information and contribute to social stability and long-term security.

Founded in 2016, Choknor specializes in Tibetan-Chinese bilingual speech technology, scanning and translation tools, and optical character recognition. Its products include smart computer mice, scanning and translation pens, and an AI-powered Tibetan subtitling system.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.title: Is active listening to music a lost art, and is physical media bringing it back?
World.content:
When was the last time you actually paid close attention to the music you're playing?

Tech has made life easier, but it’s left us fatigued from endless doomscrolling and constant notifications. Despite having instant access to everything, none of what we buy or consume actually feels ours.

Even music and streaming have also reached a point wherein it’s also becoming wearisome. Were you one of those people who crashed out when The 1975 got rid of some of their songs on streaming platforms, or experienced firsthand when a song gets pulled out from your playlist and is no longer accessible? Because I have. And it’s funny because I am writing this while mourning the fact that one of my favorite songs from my favorite local bands—who have also recently stopped doing gigs—was removed from Spotify (These Kids Are Only Dreaming by Cheats, I still talk about you).

We are all finding new hobbies and activities that will help us lessen our screen time, hence the rising trend in analog activities such as journaling, reading books, and exercising. And music is a huge part of this conversation, too, as more people are revisiting opportunities to engage more deeply with music.

But where does music fit in this conversation? In an age where almost nothing feels tangible anymore, how do we create an engaging and tactile experience when we listen to music?

Active listening and the role of physical media

When we think about going analog, the same formula applies to music. The common denominator for all of these is intention.

We describe active listening as giving your full, undivided attention to something you are listening to. It encourages you to sit with the music, understand it on a deeper level, and reflect. Sure, you can also do this with songs on Spotify, but physical formats add a layer of action and intent.

Listening to music this way allows you to be purposeful by choosing what you want to listen to and commit to the entire listening journey. When you decide to purchase a record, making time to choose from a variety of genres and artists is itself an act of rejecting the modern impulse of playing and optimizing through algorithms.

So what makes it special?

In physical formats, you accept an album, or even a custom-burned CD, as a complete and cohesive work and an entirely different form of art. Even the extra bits inside, like the sleeve, notes, and lyrics, are visual assets you can appreciate as you play a track.

Even artists themselves are yearning for an option for their art to be presented in a way it was intended to be consumed. If we can honor Christopher Nolan’s intended way of watching his films – via an IMAX 70mm screen – then we also definitely can with music and physical media.

Just as Adele faced backlash back in 2021 for convincing Spotify to remove the shuffle button as the default for her album 30, she explained, “We don’t create albums with so much care and thought into our track listing for no reason. Our art tells a story, and our stories should be listened to as we intended.”

This was the only request I had in our ever changing industry! We don’t create albums with so much care and thought into our track listing for no reason. Our art tells a story and our stories should be listened to as we intended. Thank you Spotify for listening 🍷♥️ https://t.co/XWlykhqxAy — Adele (@Adele) November 21, 2021

Physical media honors this request in a way that makes skipping a track or optimizing your queue an active and conscious effort. Once you invest the effort into starting an album, you are more inclined to pay attention and justify that effort, rather than letting it fade into the background as noise.

This is also for those who want to physically own what they love because digitally saving it in your library will never hit the same. With physical media, you can rest easy at night knowing that even if your favorites disappear from digital streaming platforms, you will still have a copy of it.

Let’s get physical!

Interested but don’t know where to start? Here’s a short guide and a few starter recommendations:

The first step is to learn about the different types of physical formats (CDs, vinyl records, and cassette tapes) and where you want to start. They all have their own pros and cons, but here’s a short list of what they offer:

CDs if you want to prioritize portability and budget;

Vinyl records if you want the immersive experience and are willing to spend on records and a player hooked up to good speakers;

Cassettes if you are into its compact charm and the underground culture it offers

The next step: start with what you love! Make a list of some of your favorites and narrow it down according to your budget. Remember, your collection should feel personal–not curated for an audience. Your only audience is you!

Once you have your list of artists and/or albums, it’s time to hunt! There are still record stores up and running these days, such as Backspacer Records located in Kapitolyo, where you can find CDs and vinyl; Bear‘s Den Records in Legaspi Village, where you can also shop for CDs, vinyl, and even equipment. For cassette tapes, you can find most in thrift stores or in flea markets; United Cassettes PH is also a local webstore you can shop from. These are only a few suggestions, but of course, there are lots of other physical stores if you look around enough.

Of course, your physical media is useless if you don’t have the right equipment for it, so here are some of my curated recommendations:

A CD player is the way to go if you want to go down the CD road. There’s also the KC-918, a portable CD player that feeds into the Y2K nostalgia aesthetic if you prefer bringing it around with you on the go.

For your vinyl record needs, the Audio-Technica AT LP60X is a good entry-level turntable. And if you are fully committing to the vinyl lifestyle, lock it in with Big Fudge’s all-in-one cleaning kit for your maintenance needs.

For cassettes, this portable cassette player should do the trick.

Physical media is forever

The beauty of physical media is also intention through curation: keeping what truly matters to you rather than hoarding every new release. The analog lifestyle is never about overconsumption and feeding into consumerism; it’s about making choices.

This is not a sign for you to cancel your streaming subscriptions and replace them with physical media, and I am not saying that digital streaming should be condemned, not when it makes music and artists easily accessible. I am, however, telling you that there is no harm in taking some time off your screen and letting yourself consume intentionally. Allow yourself to slow down and give your senses a break every once in a while.

So put the phone down, clear your brain, and let the music speak for itself! – Rappler.com

This piece was written by BrandRap volunteer Beatrice Ira Levanza. Bea is a passionate creative whose works revolve around shared experiences and the mundanity of life. She enjoys consuming Philippine media and is eager to try new experiences in the name of art and culture. A fresh graduate with a Bachelor’s degree in Fine Arts, major in Advertising Arts, from the University of Santo Tomas, she hopes to continue creating meaningful work that resonates with people.

World.title: [Vantage Point] Landbank’s P182-million belated retreat
World.content:
This column and mounting legal pressure could have pushed Landbank to consign over P182 million in court after a nearly six-year freeze. But surrendering custody today cannot erase the unmitigated commercial injury caused yesterday—nor explain why a state lender sat on client funds for so long under the guise of neutrality.

Landbank has finally chosen to act. On August 10, nearly six years after it froze PPI-JKG Philippines Inc.’s corporate bank account and initiated an interpleader, Landbank asked the Manila Regional Trial Court to let it deposit the disputed funds with the court.

Only after Vantage Point (click here or click story below) exposed this ongoing paralysis did the state lender suddenly declare itself “ready, willing and able” to surrender physical custody of the balance. Landbank may attempt to frame the timing as purely coincidental. Readers, however, can decide for themselves whether that self-serving explanation deserves any credence.

The obvious question remains: Why only now? Landbank possessed the clear legal mechanism to deposit the funds the moment it filed its complaint for interpleader on October 2, 2020. Instead, it retained P182,760,217.77 inside its vaults for almost six years while insisting in open court that it harbored no beneficial interest in the money.

The institutional intervention began on September 23, 2020, when Christian Calalang wrote to Landbank claiming majority authority over PPI-JKG and requesting an immediate suspension of all corporate transactions pending an accounting.

That exact same day, PPI-JKG president Annabelle Arcilla submitted an official request for a P182-million manager’s check payable to Omniprime Marketing Inc. to meet pressing commercial obligations.

Landbank initially processed the application, formally debited the amount from the company’s account, but then withheld the physical release of the manager’s check immediately upon receiving Calalang’s letter.

The December 15, 2023 court testimony of Landbank Pearl Drive branch manager Nenita Camposano reveals the extraordinary nature of that stoppage.

Under cross-examination, Camposano confirmed that Arcilla’s transaction was already completed, that Arcilla had signed the received portion of the manager’s-check form, and that the only remaining operational step was handing over the check for deposit with Asia United Bank. Camposano then abruptly changed course after consulting Landbank Legal.

She identified Cesar Cabañez as the in-house lawyer she contacted. In her sworn testimony, she confirmed telling Cabañez that Arcilla was the fully documented, registered account signatory. Asked what Cabañez instructed, she answered: “He told me to not release the check”.

Under further questioning, she agreed that he issued that binding legal directive without ever seeing the corporate documents and board resolutions she held in her hands.

Landbank neither called nor emailed the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that day to verify whether Calalang was indeed PPI-JKG’s legitimate majority shareholder or president.

That courtroom testimony dismantles any suggestion that the branch arrived at a balanced, prudent judgment based on verifiable facts. Asked about the devastating commercial injury caused by the stoppage, Camposano answered: “It was not my decision”. She admitted on the stand that this was the very first time in her banking career that she refused to release a recognized depositor’s funds without a formal court order.

She also acknowledged under oath that losing an account holding P182 million would inevitably impair the branch’s current-account and savings-account (CASA) performance targets, though she denied wanting the money retained for that specific reason.

Who made the call?

I am certainly not inferring illicit motive from that admission. But it underscores the urgent need for Landbank’s senior leadership to explain who made the call, upon what verified records, and with what internal consideration of the bank’s own institutional targets.

Its recent four-page motion explains none of this. Landbank merely reiterates that Calalang and Arcilla asserted conflicting claims over corporate representation. While that might have justified a brief administrative pause to seek clarity, it cannot justify how an emergency precaution turned into a six-year commercial deprivation.

Landbank continues to maintain it has “no actual or personal interest” in the account. Precisely. Under Rule 62 of the Rules of Court, a special civil action for interpleader is provided so that an innocent stakeholder can consign disputed property with the court and step aside while rival claimants litigate.

If Landbank truly stood as a disinterested stakeholder, why did an internal bank lawyer urge Arcilla to “settle” with Calalang, when it was Arcilla who was the recognized, documented client of the branch?

Furthermore, if Landbank harbored no beneficial interest, why did it hold the money for nearly six years rather than consign it when the litigation commenced? While the funds sat idle in Landbank’s books, vendors remained unpaid, financing charges escalated, and binding contractual commitments accumulated.

The bank continually cites the legal doctrine of shielding itself from possible “double vexation or double liability”. Yet repeatedly invoking that legal doctrine does not mean the competing claims possessed equal evidentiary weight. Landbank possessed Arcilla’s formal account-opening records, verified signature cards, and established corporate mandate.

Calalang presented only a private letter accompanied by disputed corporate claims—wholly devoid of a temporary restraining order, an injunction, a final judicial decree, or an Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) freeze order.

Arcilla responded within twenty-four hours with a formal secretary’s certificate repudiating his authority, followed later by an amended General Information Sheet (GIS) establishing her status as president and 75% owner.

The contrasting behavior of other universal banks makes Landbank’s conduct impossible to justify. Records and representations supplied to Vantage Point reveal that Asia United Bank, Security Bank, and UnionBank all received comparable intervention letters from Calalang. Unlike Landbank, those institutions strictly adhered to established Know-Your-Customer (KYC) rules and honored the company’s verified signatories.

Philippine National Bank likewise protected roughly P8 million in company funds from Calalang’s extrajudicial demands. Those banks recognized that Calalang was not an authorized signatory on the corporate accounts and held no court order, and they properly released the funds to Arcilla.

This does not prove that every institution received identical documentation, but it demands an answer to a disturbing question: What did Landbank know that four other major banks did not—or what did those private banks diligently verify that Landbank chose to ignore?

Commercial injury

Landbank’s requested relief creates an additional irregularity. In its motion, the bank notes that the account contains P182,760,217.77, yet it petitions the court for permission to deposit an even P182 million.

What happens to the remaining P760,217.77? After immobilizing the company’s working capital for nearly six years, Landbank now seeks to consign the bulk of the balance to the court and secure a blanket judicial discharge from all further liability.

Arcilla has vigorously opposed this maneuver because consigning the funds at this late date would merely shift the freeze from Landbank’s vaults to the judiciary’s registry. Instead, she seeks the release of the funds under a court-approved counter-bond—a recognized procedural remedy that would allow PPI-JKG to fund its ongoing government license-plate production commitments while completely securing whatever lawful stake Calalang might establish in the future.

Vantage Point tried but failed to reach Arcilla, but a confidential source close to her confirmed that, beyond utilizing her own capital, she personally secured a US$4-million loan in May 2019 at an average of 7% annual interest to fund the license-plate project. Because confidential loan files were not disclosed, her accounting cannot be independently audited under Philippine bank secrecy statutes.

Nevertheless, releasing that P182-million check in September 2020 would have eliminated approximately 86% of the original loan balance. Applying her timeline, interest rate, and prevailing dollar-peso exchange metrics, compounding interest charges and currency depreciation have added an estimated P141 million in financing costs onto the company by September 2026.

That figure is an unadjudicated estimate, but it illustrates why prolonged financial paralysis is never a harmless administrative technicality.

Landbank’s latest court motion confirms that consignation was an available remedy all along. Moving the capital today cannot erase the years of commercial injury inflicted yesterday. – Rappler.com
