World.title: Passed from hand to hand, Paete’s taká tradition looks to its next generation
World.content:
PAETE'S PRIDE Painted taká horses, fish, dogs, and dinosaurs fill the shelves of the exhibit organized by Taká ng Paete.

While Paete, Laguna is renowned for its woodcarvers, its papier-mâché craft remains far less recognized

LAGUNA, Philippines – Horse-shaped forms sat on a table inside a cafe in Paete, surrounded by glue, brushes, oil, and strips of paper. Around them, participants in the Matutong Magtaká workshop were learning how taká is made, one layer at a time. Guiding them was Ka Ichu, a magtataká who has spent decades making taká by hand.

Taká is Paete’s traditional papier-mâché craft. The workshop was among the activities of the Taká ng Paete Festival and Exhibition on September 27. Taká ng Paete is an initiative that local artist Rizia Adao and her family launched in 2022 under the advocacy #KeepTheTakaAlive.

But the people who have kept the craft going are growing older. Ka Ichu said many magtataká her age already have great-grandchildren, and the younger members of their families no longer want to take it up.

“Yung mga apo nila, yung mga anak nila, ayaw na. Kasi hindi madali gawin,” she said.



(Their grandchildren, their children, no longer want to do it. Because it isn’t easy to make.)

Around the table that day, though, people had come to learn.

MATUTONG MAGTAKÁ. Participants learn how taká is made during the workshop in Paete, Laguna. Photo by Arabella Grace Sta. Ana/Rappler

A craft many have seen, few can name

Paete is widely known as a town of woodcarvers or mag-uukit. Taká rarely comes up in the same breath.

Pieces of taká are often seen as souvenirs, decorations, or goods sold in town. Less visible are the people who make them, and the long process behind each piece.

Rizia sees this whenever she faces a crowd during her workshops. She asks who knows ukit, and people raise their hands. When she asks about taká, hardly anyone does.

“Pero pag sinabi ko na yung name na ‘taká,’ wala nang nagtataas ng kamay. So that’s the recognition na need ng taká,” she said.

(But when I say the word ‘taká,’ no one raises a hand. So that’s the recognition taká needs.)

UNFINISHED. Unpainted taká animals, including a pig, a goat, and chicks, sit on a shelf in their plain brown finish. Photo by Arabella Grace Sta. Ana/Rappler

Rizia said there may be just as many magtataká in Paete as there are woodcarvers, if not more, despite the difference in recognition. Yet beyond the town and the people already familiar with it, the craft fades from view. The Ukit Taká Festival has started to help, she said, as more people now see taká through social media.

A life shaped by taká

Behind Taká ng Paete is a family that has lived with the craft for much of their lives. Rizia’s parents, Ka Jong and Ka Ichu, have been making papier-mâché for almost four decades, and Rizia grew up surrounded by it.

Ka Ichu was already making taká before her pieces reached buyers. By her recollection, it took shape as a business around the 1990s. She started with large ducks, mallards shaped in different poses with their wings spread, using molds she got from another maker in the area. She and her family even attached the wings themselves.

Soon after, they began displaying their pieces in town. Buyers who came to look included exporters from Manila, who asked her to bring samples. She delivered them, and orders followed, slowly at first. By around 1991, she recalled, the orders had grown enough that they needed their own gawaan, or production space.

KEEPING TRADITION. Ka Jong and Ka Ichu have been making papier-mâché in Paete for almost four decades. Photo from Rizia Adao

Local buyers came first. She supplied large decorative pieces to Rustan’s and SM, sourcing at the start from other taká producers in Paete since they did not yet have a production of their own. Taká was in its heyday then.

“Kasi talaga naman noon, parang boom na yung taká noon eh,” she said.

(Back them, taká was really booming.)

Prices were better, she recalled, and materials were cheaper. By 1992, she was supplying exporters. The orders were good from then until 2000 and stayed fairly strong until around 2005, before things began to slow down.

Shipped plain, painted elsewhere

Some unfinished pieces were exported to Europe, including the UK, shipped in a plain brown finish. Abroad, they were sold as do-it-yourself kits with paint and brushes, with students among the target buyers.

What she misses most from those years are the papier-mâché leaves and flowers, attached to sticks and painted into flower arrangements. She would like to bring them back. Buyers have since moved toward animals, she said.

When lockdowns began, Ka Ichu said, they still had export orders to finish. They went to the workshop one at a time and asked the barangay for passes, since the space was open-air. Their priority, she said, was their workers, who were paid through bank transfers.

It was after the pandemic that the difficulty of the work was felt the most.

When handmade meets a target price

Competition added to the pressure. Ka Ichu said buyers began moving toward items that were difficult to copy, while other importers imitated pieces and lowered prices. She relayed an exporter’s view that cheaper and faster production from China had pulled prices down, a comparison to fast fashion and slow craft.

For makers, that leaves little room to set a price.

“Kasi may mga target price, target na ito lang yung kaya ibayad,” she noted.

(Because there are target prices, buyers who can only pay this much.)

They want to raise the value of taká, she said, but there is a limit.

Rizia described what she sees as a disconnect between the value the makers produce and what actually reaches them. Based on her own experience, she said only about 10 percent of a piece’s selling price goes to the makers, while the rest goes to middlemen and business people.

This, she shared, is part of the reason the younger generation hesitates. There are young people who want to learn the craft. They just will not take it up as a livelihood if it does not pay enough.

The people behind every piece

Rizia herself paints on taká, but she points out that the creative process begins long before the painting. A magtataká prepares, shapes, layers, dries, and finishes the forms that she paints on.

Her exhibit at GITNA Art Studio, which she curated, puts those makers at the center. Pictures of the magtataká are displayed in the exhibit, so visitors meet the people behind the pieces as well as the finished work.

It is also tied to her Taká Registry Project, an ongoing effort to document Philippine papier-mâché as an art form, including its people, processes, and traditions.

ARTISTS. Photographs of the magtataká on display at the Taká ng Paete exhibit at GITNA Art Studio in Paete, Laguna. Photo by Arabella Grace Sta. Ana/Rappler

For some of the magtataká, being part of the exhibit changed how they saw their own work. Ka Ichu said many of them long had a low appreciation of their craft since they were paid minimally.

“Kasi nga, ang baba nung amount, ang baba nung binabayad sa amin,” she said.

(Since the amount is low, what we get paid is low.)

After Rizia invited them, Ka Ichu heard something new from her fellow magtataká: “Ah, artist pala rin kami (Ah, so we’re artists too).”

Rizia recalled that the exhibit opening left many of them in tears, seeing the craft and the people behind it side by side.

Keeping the taká alive

Rizia hopes taká will receive enough recognition and value, as other crafts in the Philippines have, so that the younger generation would want to take it up, and see it’s valuable enough to be paid enough.

Not everyone was sure of that at the start. According to Rizia, Ka Ichu hesitated when they began teaching workshops, wondering if anyone still wanted to learn taká. Ka Ichu herself said she was against the idea at first. Today, she shared, she is glad that their stock is finding its way to people and that schools have started to show interest.

How the craft is passed on and who will take it up next remain open questions.

But at the workshop, participants pressed paper onto the forms under Ka Ichu’s guidance, going through a process that generations of Paete artisans had learned through years of work and repetition.

For at least that afternoon, taká was passing into new hands. – Rappler.com

Arabella Grace Sta. Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

World.title: ‘Violation of privacy?’ Senate court takes down Sara Duterte trial livestream
World.content:
TAXES. Bureau of Internal Revenue Office of the Commissioner chief of staff Anne Lorraine Garcia-Marquez takes the witness stand on Day 36 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on October 8, 2026.

The BIR witness says the copy of the Letter of Authority displayed during the trial showed the names of some revenue officers

MANILA, Philippines – In the impeachment trial of Sara Duterte, it’s been the defense that has repeatedly objected to the presentation of the bank and tax records of the Vice President and her husband, Manases “Mans” Carpio, citing confidentiality issues.

But on Day 37 of the trial on Friday, October 9, there was a twist.

Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero ordered the Senate Clerk of Court to take down the livestream of the highly public proceedings over concerns on displaying the private information of some personnel of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR).

Escudero issued the directive after lawyer Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez, chief-of-staff of the Office of the BIR Commissioner, expressed worry following the defense’s flashing of the copies of the confidential letter of authority (LOA) the BIR issued to Duterte’s husband.

Carpio himself had consented to the presentation of the LOA but Garcia-Marquez said the documents showed the names of the revenue officers.

“I just want to raise that when the copy of the LOAs were flashed on the screen earlier… the names of some revenue officers were displayed. It should have been redacted,” Garcia-Marquez said.

Escudero said the court will redact the names on the documents to be submitted in court but the witness said her worry was due to the showing of the sensitive data of the BIR officers.

“We manifest, Your Honor, that there has been a violation of the privacy of the people involved. Their names were flashed for everyone to see,” private prosecutor Erwin Matib said.

The court vowed to address the issue.

After an hour-long break, Escudero asked the Clerk of Court to remove the original livestream and re-upload it with the redaction of the names of the BIR officers.

The livestream was taken down past 1 pm.

“We would like to remind not only [defense] Attorney Kristine [Ferrer] and the counsels for the respondent but also the counsel for the prosecution to be careful next time insofar as revealing names or addresses,” said Escudero.

“Given the public nature of these proceedings, as it might violate some provisions of the Data Privacy Act, as well as the security of certain officials of government engaged in various activities as part of their official functions and duties,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

Play Video

LATEST UPDATES

World.title: Bida ang saya: Is your fave Jollibee spot owned by Sara Duterte?
World.content:
At the trial, the prosecution presents Jollibee receipts issued by Gencorp, a company in which VP Sara Duterte is a stockholder

We know by now that Vice President Sara Duterte has some links to Jollibee because the company she declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) has franchises of the fast-food giant.

But just how many branches does Gencorp Industries Inc. (Gencorp) operate?

During the impeachment trial on Friday, October 9, the prosecution presented receipts from Jollibee branches in Davao City showing Gencorp as the owner.

RISIBO. A composite of five receipts of Jollibee branches in Davao City owned by Gencorp Industries where Vice President Sara Duterte is a stockholder. These receipts were presented by the prosecution in the impeachment trial on October 9, 2026.

There are at least five branches:

Jollibee Bolton is a known hangout spot of the Dutertes.

FAST FOOD. Former president Rodrigo Duterte (right) and Senator Bong Go (left) eat in Jollibee Bolton Street in Davao City on June 28, 2022, after Duterte’s son Baste took his oath as Davao City mayor. Photo by Bong Go/Facebook

Rappler first reported that Gencorp cornered millions of pesos in contracts with the Davao City government in 2022, coinciding with the time that Sara became the Vice President, and her brother Sebastian assumed the mayorship of their hometown. The arrangement raises questions on conflict of interest, and potential violation of the Constitution.

While Duterte herself declared that she is a stockholder of Gencorp in her SALN, the absence of her name in the company’s Securities and Exchange Commission documents has been a head-scratcher.

Play Video

“The reason why I think VP Sara included Gencorp in her SALN is because its value is huge,” prosecution witness, financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, theorized on Friday.

He explained that an investor would need between P35 million to P50 million for a Jollibee franchise with P35 million being a “very conservative [figure]…because you need working capital pambayad sa crew, pambayad sa manager, pambayad sa rent, initial inventory (to pay for the crew, the manager, rent, initial inventory).”

Cabrera, who reviewed voluminous financial records of Duterte, said upon comparison of Gencorp’s bank inflows and financial statements, it was concluded that the firm has P1.1 billion in undeclared wealth.

Cabrera said that overall, Duterte has P817 million in undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025, including P212.6 million from undeclared income from Gencorp.

How did the analyst compute that figure when Duterte’s stake at Gencorp hasn’t been disclosed in corporate filings?

“We applied a conservative 20% percentage,” Cabrera said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Financial analyst tells impeach court: Sara Duterte has P817M in undisclosed wealth
World.content:
The amount includes undeclared cash, properties, and income of the Vice President, her spouse Mans Carpio, and their companies

MANILA, Philippines – A financial forensic analyst called as a witness by the prosecution told the impeachment court on Friday, October 9, that Vice President Sara Duterte’s undeclared wealth tops P800 million.

Alexander Cabrera, a certified public accountant and a lawyer who is chairman emeritus of PwC Philippines, said that based on his review of voluminous financial records of the Vice President and her husband, Mans Carpio, the couple has around P817 million in undisclosed assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

The amount covers their undisclosed personal cash based on discrepancies between their audited financial statements and declarations in the Vice President’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), undeclared other personal and real properties, and undeclared income of their companies Cale88, Metro Chow, and Gencorp based on the mismatch between income tax returns and bank inflows.

Cabrera explained that Carpio’s financial records were included in the analysis because they have “absolute community of property” as a married couple.

“We used a conservative method. There’s no duplication in count,” Cabrera added.

The forensic report he produced also flags other behaviors in Duterte’s financial records, which he found suspicious, such as:

single, large credit card purchases, such as P205,007.29 for Ginza Inakaya and P111,109.24 for Don Quijote in Japan;

17 insurance policies not declared by the Vice President in her SALN;

and a variation of check kiting (Cabrera calls it “nagtitinikling ang pera“), where funds move in and out of an account through manager’s checks so the amounts won’t be included in year-end reports

Cabrera will be cross-examined by the defense on Monday, October 12.

He is already the last witness of the prosecution panel, which has decided to drop the bribery case against the Vice President. – Rappler.com

World.title: Cale88’s workforce, financial records draw scrutiny in impeachment trial
World.content:
Manases Carpio-owned Cale88 listed only two employees in its general info sheet despite reporting P150 million in sales in 2024

MANILA, Philippines – Senator-judges on Friday, October 9, scrutinized the financial records and workforce of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte‘s husband, Manases Carpio.

On Day 37 of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva raised concerns over Cale88’s 2024 general information sheet, which listed only two employees despite the company reporting P150.6 million in sales and P6.13 million in losses.

“This is alarming, Your Honor. You’re looking at a company with P150 million sales and P6.13 million in losses but only [has] two employees,” Villanueva said.

Citing the company’s financial records, Bureau of Internal Revenue chief of staff Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez said Cale88 reported P150,595,605 in sales classified as exempt from income tax and P169,564 in sales subject to regular income tax in 2024.

The company also reported a loss of around P6.13 million in the same year, Garcia-Marquez said.

Villanueva questioned how the company managed its operations with very few employees and who funded its continued operations.

Marquez said she had no personal knowledge of Cale88’s operations, adding that it would seem “impossible” for a banana chip manufacturer to operate with only two employees unless machinery handled much of the work.

Hontiveros flags Ukrainian remitter

Meanwhile, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros flagged Ukrainian company Arkmen LLC, one of the foreign-based entities that sent inward remittances to Cale88, citing alleged involvement in a fraud and money laundering investigation in Ukraine.

Hontiveros said her office checked the background of the foreign-based companies that remitted to Cale88 and found that Kyiv authorities investigated Arkmen LLC over alleged fraud and money laundering involving 1.225 million euros in May 2025.

Authorities reportedly ordered a search of its premises in March, while its assets were frozen in April.

“The last remittance of Arkmen LLC to Cale88 was in May 2025 after the start of the criminal proceedings,” Hontiveros said.

Hontiveros asked Marquez whether legitimate transactions involving international remittances from Arkmen LLC to Cale88 should have been reported as sales and subjected to tax.

“If these were sales, they should have been reported in the annual income tax return,” Marquez said.

Hontiveros had previously claimed that some Chinese companies that sent funds to Cale88 were Chinese state-owned enterprises that could be “advancing the interests of the Chinese Communist Party.” – Rappler.com

World.title: The Regime Is Laying a Trap for the US. Will Washington Fall for It?
World.content:
Myanmar has become increasingly salient in Washington’s economic and national security calculus.

However, the country is far from simple. Its military and political power is dispersed across multiple centers, demanding deft handling and nuanced thinking.

In the absence of a single like-minded counterpart, Washington may be tempted to look for a shortcut and treat the military regime as the easiest channel through which to advance U.S. interests. Doing so would risk falling into the trap laid by Naypyitaw: mistaking access to the military regime for access to Myanmar itself.

Will Washington take the bait? Or will Washington resist this temptation and build a strategy around navigating Myanmar’s intricate and decentralized landscape?

Washington’s calculus

For Washington, the central question will be how to address two particular interests that converge in Myanmar as cost-effectively and reliably as possible. Washington is seeking to reduce dependence on China-dominated rare earth supply chains while confronting a rapidly expanding form of transnational organized crime that directly harms Americans. The country borders India and China, links mainland Southeast Asia to the Indian Ocean and is the world’s fourth-largest producer of rare earths. Myanmar also serves as one of the primary hubs for scam compounds that directly defraud Americans of billions of dollars.

Under the Trump administration, Washington’s foreign policy has fundamentally changed. Longstanding traditions of promoting human rights and democracy have now been deprioritized in favor of an “America First” approach interpreted narrowly as protecting core national interests. The 2025 National Security Strategy (NSS) signed by Trump last November identifies “flexible realism” as one of its guiding principles. Under this approach, Washington seeks good relations and peaceful commercial ties with countries without requiring them to adopt democratic principles.

This change may have significant ramifications for Myanmar, where the U.S.’ concerns over democracy and human rights have historically been prioritized, constraining diplomatic engagement with the country’s military rulers and business deals that could benefit them.

Equally important, the NSS also recognized the Indo-Pacific as “among the next century’s key economic and geopolitical battlegrounds” and emphasized that successful competition in the region is essential to American prosperity. As Washington seeks to rebalance its economic relationship with China and reduce its dependence on China-dominated supply chains, Myanmar’s strategic importance could grow.

Washington’s calculus is also shaped by regional governments, including U.S. partners, and by its own private sector. Global volatility and geopolitical shocks have exposed vulnerabilities in regional supply chains and energy security. The added threat of economic coercion has placed greater pressure on governments, including the U.S., to seek stability and secure critical supply chains. To this end, regional governments have started high-level engagements with the regime to explore possibilities. These engagements may increase the appeal of normalizing relations with the military regime in Naypyitaw for Washington.

American businesses, whose voices carry weight, are watching these shifts as well. As regional governments signal openness to normalization with the regime, Myanmar may appear to become a viable market for foreign investment. These businesses may perceive that U.S. sanctions and other regulations could leave them at a competitive disadvantage to regional competitors. The first entrants into uncertain and unstable markets often absorb the greatest risks, but the willingness of American businesses to pursue investment despite uncertainty may make the prospect of securing an early foothold difficult to dismiss.

Washington’s blind spot

For Washington, this renewed attention on Myanmar has revived an older policy problem that it had tried to work around, as it struggled to develop a coherent approach to the country. For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Washington tended to work through a small number of central political actors, even though political authority and armed power were far more dispersed. Myanmar’s ethnic armed organizations, despite being political and military stakeholders, did not fit neatly into the U.S.’ engagement model. In practice, Washington’s political focus remained on Aung San Suu Kyi and the military regime, and its engagement with ethnic armed organizations was largely reduced to a national reconciliation framework, excluding powerful groups that did not participate in the ceasefire process.

Today, Myanmar’s political landscape has changed. For decades, Aung San Suu Kyi served as Washington’s principal democratic interlocutor in Myanmar, but she remains under detention today. The opposition is dispersed among the National Unity Government, ethnic armed organizations and other resistance actors. Intensified war since the 2021 coup has further shifted political and military power toward ethnic armed organizations. No single actor represents the opposition as a whole. Engaging Myanmar today therefore requires moving beyond an approach built around a select few central political actors, and Washington has yet to adapt to a decentralized political landscape, as Beijing has.

Understanding this blind spot, the military regime in Naypyitaw has positioned itself to exploit an intensifying geopolitical competition and unresolved gap in Washington’s approach to Myanmar. The military regime has paid millions of dollars to influential lobbying firms to help tailor its message to current U.S. priorities, pitching itself as a partner capable of advancing them. What remains uncertain this time, however, is whether Washington will take the bait.

A familiar bargain

Under sanctions and growing isolation, the regime has repeatedly staged political openings with pitches for engagement to the U.S. throughout its history. This history, however, offers a clear lesson: the military will act in bad faith and abandon its agreements whenever it sees fit.

In May 2002, the military released Aung San Suu Kyi from house arrest. One week later, it registered a firm in Washington to lobby for normalizing relations with the U.S. The regime pitched cooperation on issues prioritized by the Bush administration, including counternarcotics, terrorism, trade and public health. The opening did not last. In May 2003, regime-paid attackers assaulted Aung San Suu Kyi’s convoy near Depayin, and the military detained her again.

Another opening came under President Thein Sein in March 2011. That August, he met with Aung San Suu Kyi in Naypyitaw. Subsequently, his government released political prisoners, relaxed censorship, allowed the National League for Democracy to reenter electoral politics and pursued ceasefires with ethnic armed groups. Washington responded by sending Secretary of State Hillary Clinton to Burma in December 2011, restoring ambassador-level diplomatic relations and easing restrictions on investment and financial services. The political opening lasted nearly a decade before the military, under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, seized power in February 2021 and detained Aung San Suu Kyi again.

The 2011 opening, notably, was different. Thein Sein and other reform-minded officials made significant concessions and pursued genuine, if imperfect, political reforms. The changes allowed political freedoms and economic opportunities that had been unimaginable under previous military governments. Myanmar experts and analysts will continue to debate what could have been done differently to preserve that opening, but for Washington, dwelling on the past or trying to recreate it would only distract from addressing Myanmar’s present realities and building a better future.

The 2011 opening, and any hope of returning to it, was shattered by the 2021 coup and the military’s subsequent campaign of violence against its own people. The present reality is that the military leadership now ruling in Naypyitaw is not the one that pursued those reforms, but the one that overturned them.

The price of a shortcut

Normalizing relations with the regime is highly unlikely to secure access to rare earths or curb the scam compounds it supports. Instead, normalization would exacerbate these issues by giving a lifeline to the Min Aung Hlaing regime as it faces growing internal tensions, a new round of military defeats and economic pressures.

The military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party recently postponed its congress, reportedly due to leadership disputes. At the same time, the elevation of Min Aung Hlaing’s loyalists over more senior generals has raised questions about tensions within the armed forces. While exaggerating its success on the battlefield, the military now relies heavily on conscripts. Reportedly, more than 70 percent of its frontline troops are conscripts. While these developments do not necessarily indicate an imminent collapse, they contextualize the growing strains within the regime at a time when it is seeking international engagement.

The regime is also struggling militarily. In Kachin State, the military has failed to break the Kachin Independence Army’s resistance around Bhamo, while losing additional positions to resistance forces. In Rakhine State, a major offensive launched in September to retake territory from the Arakan Army has failed to achieve significant gains despite the deployment of thousands of troops backed by air and naval support. In Karen State, the Karen National Liberation Army and allied forces have continued to contest the military’s attempts to regain lost positions around Kawkareik.

Economic pressures are also adding to the regime’s mounting difficulties. Even Min Aung Hlaing, who has long presented an optimistic picture of Myanmar’s economy, recently acknowledged the regime’s failure to make meaningful progress. The regime’s pursuit of a loan arrangement with Belarus with high interest rates further suggests growing financial pressures and a need to secure alternative sources of financing. The regime’s efforts to circumvent international jet fuel sanctions also suggest that these measures are imposing constraints. With technical and material support from Chinese companies, the regime is developing its own aviation fuel production capacity at the Thanlyin refinery near Yangon to reduce its dependence on imported jet fuel. The project underscores the lengths to which the regime is going to secure a reliable fuel supply for its air force.

Will Washington take the bait?

The trap is laid. Washington’s recent actions indicate a trajectory towards normalization, but these three key drivers will shape what happens next in U.S. policy toward Myanmar.

Will Congress take a strong bipartisan stand? Although members of Congress have expressed concerns about engagement with the military regime, statements alone may do little to influence the administration’s calculations. The more consequential test will be whether Congress will press the Trump administration to implement the BURMA Act and pass the BRAVE Burma Act, which would “ turn the screws
