Anthony Albanese has waded back into alternative media after his fraught appearance on a satirical podcast earlier this year – though notably with a script this time. As the major parties struggle to engage voters online to the same degree as firebrands like Pauline Hanson, the prime minister has made his latest pitch to younger voters in a social media clip with a comedy sketch duo. In the clip posted on Friday, Swag on the Beat’s Jack Say and Isaac Gibbons pose as a couple meeting the parents for the first time. The unsuspecting boyfriend is confident he can charm his girlfriend’s father, until the door opens to reveal Albanese. The prime minister leans in and whispers: “I’m very protective of my daughter, and if you break her heart I can reinstate your HECS debt.”



The clip ends with a mock political endorsement, with Albanese saying: “Brought to you by the Australian government swag”. It had more than 90,000 likes on Instagram on Saturday morning. Related Article Social media The political fringes dominate social media. How is your MP doing? Albanese is ploughing ahead with his social media outreach despite the protracted backlash to comments he made on the Bush Deep podcast in July. After initially being forced to apologise for saying in a crude game he wanted to “shag” pop darling Kylie Minogue, the Liberal Party later hammered Albanese over a separate reference to the “couple of melons” he was gifted by the Japanese prime minister. Albanese denied he made a sexual innuendo about the leader but the media storm was such that the Japanese ambassador had to intervene and downplay the controversy. Albanese later said he would not have done the podcast if he had his time again.





“Plenty of Australians are on various forms of social media. It’s not only an opportunity for members of parliament to talk to Australians, it’s also an obligation to talk to Australians in a way which communicates who we are, what we believe,” the energy minister told reporters in Sydney. “There are very serious podcasts out there, which I do, and very serious social media posts. And sometimes there’s a lighter approach. I think that’s fair enough.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Smarmy management consultant’: Hanson attacks Taylor, Liberals in fiery CPAC speech
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘Smarmy management consultant’: Hanson attacks Taylor, Liberals in fiery CPAC speech Nick Newling October 10, 2026 — 1:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has offered to set aside her grievances with the Liberal Party to form government after the next election despite blaming the Coalition for her brief jail stint in the early 2000s. She has also promised to establish a royal commission into net zero. In a speech to the faithful at this weekend’s Conservative Political Action Conference in Brisbane, she repeatedly attacked Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, calling him a “smarmy management consultant” who was not fit to replace Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson attacked Angus Taylor at the Conservative Political Action Network on Saturday. AAPIMAGE “I know what it means to put personal history aside and turn the other cheek,” Hanson told the conference. “The Liberal Party threw me out. Then they threw me in jail. My convictions were overturned, but my family went through more than most people will ever, ever know.” “So yes. I do have reasons to hold a grudge, but I also have children and grandchildren. Their futures and your futures matter more. If I can put personal grievances aside for the sake of this country, others should be able to do the same. And before anyone gets the wrong idea, nobody has ever accused me of being a pushover, and I don’t expect that to start today.”



Hanson, Taylor and Nationals leader Matt Canavan were the main attractions at this year’s CPAC national conference, the first time a sitting Liberal leader addressed the room. While Taylor was billed as the keynote speaker, the ascendant Hanson attracted the warmest responses from the crowd. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership Jacqui Lambie is right about Pauline Hanson. There’s only one way to stop her ascension Peter Hartcher Political and international editor In a sprawling address that covered freedom of speech, housing affordability and the establishment of a nuclear energy industry in Australia, Hanson promised to come after Energy Minister Chris Bowen through the establishment of a royal commission into net zero should she win the next election. “Every secret meeting behind closed doors will be revealed, and every dollar taken away from taxpayers that left power bills higher will be accounted for,” Hanson told an uproarious crowd who almost universally cheered whenever any speaker mentioned their intentions to scrap net zero. “Every decision the uni-party has made to sell our country out will be exposed. And ministers like Chris Bowen, who signed off on these dodgy deals and kept them secret, will be held accountable.”



Speaking from Sydney, Bowen ridiculed the gathering and criticised Taylor for being the first Liberal leader to address a conference deemed too right-wing for his predecessors. “We’re going to see a whole bunch of crazy over the next few days as the Liberal Party and the One Nation Party try to outdo each other on the race to the right, and the race to the bottom,” Bowen said, claiming Hanson’s royal commission would hurt farmers seeking to “diversify their income”. Hanson congratulated Karl Stefanovic for his shift to the right of politics. AAPIMAGE Hanson also hammered the Liberal Party for a number of climate policies under their last term in government, including signing up to the Paris Agreement, espousing net zero and legislating the safeguard mechanism. Speaking before Hanson, Taylor pre-empted much of the criticism, acknowledging the mistakes of the former Coalition government, including “more-than-was-needed” spending during the COVID pandemic, signing up to next zero, and “allowing immigration numbers to creep up, especially student and bridging visas”.



“Under my leadership, we are a different and, I strongly believe, a better Liberal Party,” Taylor said. “Now, I acknowledge that some of you may have doubts, but if you believe our country can change for the better, then believe that the Liberal Party can too. Together with Matt Canavan’s leadership at the Nationals, the Coalition is once again conviction-led and unashamedly on the right.” The Liberal leader also framed the next election as a “spiritual fight” for the soul of the nation, as he and Canavan criticised the “socialist” Albanese government for failing Australian industry. Before entering politics, Taylor served as a management consultant and partner at McKinsey. During his address he said his business experience gave him an edge as a leader, after repeatedly criticising government ministers for holding lengthy careers in representative politics. Related Article Investigation

One Nation The ‘new Byron Bay’ favoured by Pauline Hanson and her most powerful aide Former Today Show host Karl Stefanovic – who had a lengthy career at Nine Entertainment, owner of this masthead – held interviews with the three leaders following their addresses. Hanson congratulated the morning-television-star turned podcast host for his move to the right in public discourse, saying: “It’s great to see that you’ve actually come on the right side of politics. You’ve become more conservative, and that’s great to see.”



While Taylor remained evasive under questioning over dealmaking with One Nation – to heckling from the audience – Hanson used her speech to signal her support for the Coalition making to defeat Labor. Canavan said parties fighting each other amounted to “getting distracted on side quests” which would do nothing to help remove Albanese from leadership. Hanson was disendorsed by the Liberal Party in 1996 by then-opposition leader John Howard, before that year’s election, for comments she made about Aboriginal Australians. She was subsequently sentenced to a three-year jail term after being found guilty of electoral fraud, though the conviction was later overturned, and Hanson was released less than three months into her term. World.title: Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Eric Jiang’s Rhomboid has its Melbourne premiere at fortyfivedownstairs

OPERA: The Spare Room by Helen Garner has its world premiere

JAZZ: Za Górami put on a five-star show at MPAC Sound Gallery

THEATRE: Eliza at Southbank Theatre is a psychological thriller

THEATRE: Koreaboo at Malthouse draws from lived experience

THEATRE

Rhomboid ★★★★

fortyfivedownstairs, until October 11 Heartfelt, funny and sexy. Eric Jiang’s Rhomboid beautifully captures the ambiguity of platonic and romantic love through the orbiting lives of Xavier (Ken Paolo) and Sebastian (Lawrence Hawkins). Chad Rosete, Lawrence Hawkins and Ken Paolo. George Jefford From high school through to the onset of their careers, Xavier and Sebastian have been trying to figure out what they mean to each other. As they get older, and other paramours enter their lives — the introduction of supporting actor Chad Rosete, who plays both Xavier’s casual hook-up Lachie and Sebastian’s serious partner Felix— their relationship becomes murky and untethered.



The chemistry between the cast is fantastic, and the dialogue is pithy and fast-paced, with pop culture references woven in. This doesn’t take away from the emotional depth of the story, as they delve into jealousy, queer identity and the unevenness that can exist in friendships and love. Sebastian candidly admits that he “loves being the only Asian in a white crew”, and that he feels threatened by other Asian queers who are “more successful, smarter or hotter” than him. Lawrence Hawkins and Ken Paolo as Sebastian and Xavier. George Jefford The set (by Amy Todd) is simple and flexible: a tower of blocks looms in the centre, assembled like Tetris. The actors move the blocks between scenes to transform into a club, a station, an art gallery, a mountain for hiking, or a wedding, with simple yet effective changes to lighting, blocking and sound. The shifting of time between scenes is seamless, as gentle instrumental piano plays and a moving scene is projected, as if peering out the windows of a car on a highway, onto the blocks.



Margot Morales’ direction shines through in these choices, setting up the story like it’s a New York City-set indie rom-com; even the lead photo for the show positions Sebastian and Xavier on a steel stairwell between two brick buildings. Related Article Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said The space is used well. When Sebastian is drunk, dancing erratically on his own in the club in the corner, and Xavier spots him from across the room out of the corner of his eye while dancing with Lachie, you can feel the tension and awkwardness. In scenes depicting text message exchanges, the characters are positioned apart across the blocks, facing away from each other and speaking out loud. The only critique is that it is a little long; tightening the script and scene choices would make the already strong material even punchier. A scene between three characters overexplains the significance of the rhomboid and feels clunky; the show is at its best when it leans into innuendo and subtext. Nonetheless, it was refreshing to witness theatre that centres queer young people unapologetically, without the usual trappings of a coming-out story. At the end, we’re left with this lingering thought: love isn’t clear-cut like a square — it’s angular and leaning like a rhomboid, changing and shifting with the passage of time.

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar



OPERA

The Spare Room ★★★★

Playhouse, until October 10 If you’re familiar with Helen Garner’s 2008 book, The Spare Room, you might think: how on earth could this be made into an opera? The Spare Room by Helen Garner has been adapted into an opera. Jeff Busby A semi-autobiographical meditation on what it is to care for someone who is dying, to put your own beliefs aside and support them indiscriminately, the book is visceral about the awfulness of cancer. The pain, the sweat, the pissing the bed. Levity is long gone. Composer Jane Hammond and her longtime collaborator, librettist Therèsa Borg, however, saw The Spare Room as ripe for the operatic picking.



With Garner’s blessing, a gestational process of almost five years ensued, finally resulting in Victorian Opera’s latest world premiere. It is a remarkable achievement, and it would be remiss not to mention: the author, composer, librettist, director, conductor, the two star performers and CEO of the company are all women. Natalie Jones and Antoinette Halloran star in The Spare Room. Jeff Busby In contemporary chamber style, Hammond has scored for 13 players, who here manage tiny moments of introspection and huge emotional outbursts. Bach is mentioned often in Garner’s text, and Hammond deftly weaves in some of the Three-Part Inventions, creating a gloriously layered amalgamation of styles and colours. Some of the magic is lost, however, in the amplification of voices and certain instruments, particularly percussion, which threw out the balance at times. Mic-ing opera singers means that, for the most part, there is no vocal light and shade, and we are left longing for some pianissimo.



As Helen, Natalie Jones is grounded and direct, with steely vocals that, suitably, border on shrill when the situation calls for it. Opposite Jones is Antoinette Halloran, perfectly cast as the woo-woo Nicola. Halloran still has such electric presence and the most magnificent stage face, and Nicola’s more expansive music suits Halloran’s lyric voice. Related Article Performing arts Helen Garner on the worst three weeks of her life The work itself gets better as the night progresses, and when the drama matches the book in its level of intensity. The confrontation between Helen and Nicola is extraordinary. Your enjoyment of this opera might depend on how wedded you are to Garner. There are moments of comedy, perhaps required for a two-hour stage adaptation, but do not align with the original text. There is a sense of belonging in seeing one’s own experience on stage. Cancer has touched almost everyone, and amid a very Melbourne staging, where there are comments about the weather, people riding bikes, this very masthead used as a prop – it’s validating to see women’s anxieties and naturalistic experiences presented in this heightened art form.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



JAZZ

Za Górami ★★★★★

MPAC Sound Gallery, October 8 Za górami is a Polish expression meaning “behind the mountains”, often used to begin fairytales (akin to “Once upon a time”). It’s also the name of a much-loved Polish folk song – one that served as the title track and thematic anchor for the 2024 debut album by Alice Zawadzki, Fred Thomas and Misha Mullov-Abbado. Misha Mullov-Abbado, Alice Zawadzki and Fred Thomas. Monika Jakubowska The UK trio have now adopted Za Górami as their collective moniker, and it couldn’t be more apt. Each tune in their repertoire is a short story in musical form, its narrative gently unfurling while carrying echoes of faraway places and centuries-old cultures. Monash University’s David Li Sound Gallery provided a wonderfully intimate setting for Za Górami’s concert in Melbourne, its pristine acoustics allowing every detail of the trio’s interactions to be heard with absolute clarity.



Alice Zawadzki arrived on stage barefoot, warmly greeting the audience before beckoning us into a hushed Argentinian tale of hidden love. As the trio’s music draws heavily from European, Latin and Sephardic Jewish folk sources, Zawadzki sang mostly in foreign languages and dialects: Spanish, French, Sardinian, Ladino. But the expressiveness of her voice and gestures – coupled with the subtle but exquisite musical arrangements – helped convey the poetry of the lyrics and the sentiments within them. Fred Thomas (on piano and drums) and Misha Mullov-Abbado (bass) are both masters of understatement, able to suggest emotional undercurrents with the flick of a brush, a lightly tapped cymbal or a shiver of bowed-bass harmonics. On Je Suis Trop Jeunette, Thomas rubbed a mallet across the piano strings to underline the delicacy of Zawadzki’s wistful lyrics; then the mood darkened, with emphatic chords and bass scampering beneath the singer’s soaring wordless explorations. Several tunes also featured Zawadzki’s violin – lightly plucked and effervescent, or gracefully harmonising with her elegant vocal lines. The final tune even included animal sound effects (courtesy of the audience, whinnying and neighing on command), adding an air of whimsy to this entrancing evening of musical storytelling.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas



THEATRE

Eliza ★★★★★

Southbank Theatre, The Sumner until October 31 Prognoses of AI’s impact upon humanity has reached fever pitch, but in Tom Holloway’s play, we are catapulted into the past to grapple with the very same questions we’re seeking answers to 60 years later. Dan Spielman (left) and Manali Datar in Eliza. Pia Johnson Dr Joseph Weizenbaum (Dan Spielman) is a mercurial visiting professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as intent on repressing the traumatic memories of his escape from Nazi Germany as he is on heralding the advent of digital computers. When his secretary, Becky (a bewitching Manali Datar) makes a seemingly inconsequential joke about the back-and-forth cadence of talk therapy, it opens the doors to the creation of the world’s first chatbot: Eliza.



The breathtaking scale of invention is mirrored in the expansiveness of Dale Ferguson’s vertiginous set. Rows upon rows of systematically aligned towers of working files and cascading sheets of glass lend an unexplainable depth and dimension to the stage, creating rabbit warrens for the characters to lose themselves in as their sense of reality and personhood begin to blur. The play traces the ethical quandaries inherent in AI back to its genesis. Weizenbaum is shown to be well-meaning, but his disavowal of personal disclosure, refusal to listen until it’s too late and his betrayal of Becky, in particular, is a recurring theme that can be extrapolated to AI’s routine, large-scale copyright thefts in the present day. Although set in the 1960s, Eliza raises philosophical and ethical concerns about the role of AI in society. Pia Johnson The famed sycophancy of AI that is leading to current crises of consciousness is shown to have had very much the same effect when it was conceived in the 1960s, as people yearned to unburden themselves to what they perceived to be a neutral entity. Under Paige Rattray’s direction, the rapid-fire play unfurls at the brisk pace of a psychological thriller as a collective psychosis and breakdown of legibility takes hold of the characters in different ways, as they talk around one another without truly understanding each other.



This strange incomprehension finds its expression in the motif of starlings, which is, incidentally, the namesake of a company spying on Weizenbaum’s exploits. Related Article Arts Culture wars and a swing to the right: A new take on Gone With the Wind is coming Through spectacular audiovisual mastery and a stunning Hitchcockian reckoning, the forward march of progress is disturbingly realised in increasingly absurd and surreal ways as Weizenbaum figuratively and literally chokes on the irreversible weight of what he has set in motion. Spielman excels as the fulcrum, superbly marrying the constant whirring of a beautiful mind with an inexplicable childlike naivete. Datar’s transition from unknowing to seemingly all-knowing in a role that Holloway resurrected from the annals of history is chilling, and there isn’t a role that Hamish Michael can’t play, as he dovetails seamlessly between aggrieved research assistant, enthused journalist and lofty powers that be. The philosophical and ethical concerns that Eliza raises are by no means new to anyone engaged in the broader debate around AI, but in this undidactic, morally nuanced play, the inextricability of latent humanity and technological advancement is laid bare once more.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



JAZZ

Julian Banks Quartet ★★★★

Cross St Music Hall, October 2 Almost a decade after releasing his previous album, saxophonist Julian Banks has brought his latest album to life in a rush of inspiration and energy. The Julian Banks Quartet performed at Cross Street Music Hall on Friday, October 2. Leila Maulen Just four months after recording the new material, here it was: available on CD and launched on Friday night with an exuberant live performance at the Cross Street Music Hall. The convivial Brunswick venue was the perfect place to hear this music. The tunes Banks writes – like the rooms at Cross Street – are warm, inviting and innately appealing without trying to impress.



The new album, OxyMoron, celebrates Banks’ renewed passion for playing and performing his own music after navigating various life challenges in recent years, and is imbued with a positive spirit that a live setting amplified. This gig clearly meant a lot to the saxophonist, and every phrase that emerged from his tenor was filled with feeling. His marvellously rich tone magnified the soulful allure of his melodies and added muscular vigour to his solos. Saxophonist Julian Banks has released his first album in a decade. Leila Maulen His bandmates (guitarist Louis King, bassist James Gilligan and drummer Joe Talia) gathered beside rather than behind him, reflecting their role as equal contributors in this enterprise. King’s electric guitar could float in a fuzzy haze or bite into a distortion-laden solo; Gilligan’s semi-acoustic bass guitar was by turns sinuous and insistent; and Talia conjured up languid shuffles and headily propulsive grooves with effortless ease.



Captain Happy skipped nimbly between shifting time signatures, while the album’s title track saw the band veering into crunchy rock territory without losing the sense of warmth or approachability that characterises Banks’ music. Perhaps the night’s most affecting piece was Little Dove – a ballad dedicated to Banks’ young daughter, whose burgeoning love of music helped reignite Banks’ passion for his own, and who sat proudly in the front row at the launch.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas THEATRE

Koreaboo ★★★

Malthouse, until October 10 Inspired by playwright Michelle Lim Davidson’s own experiences and directed by Jessica Arthur, Koreaboo is a two-hander that surveys contentious issues of race, diaspora and belonging, with a light touch. Heather Jeong (left) and Michelle Lim Davidson in a scene from Koreaboo. Gianna Rizzo



Davidson herself plays Hannah, a young Australian who travels to Seoul in an attempt to reconnect with her estranged birth mother, Umma (Heather Jeong). It’s only their second meeting. We learn that although she was born in South Korea, Hannah was adopted as a baby and grew up in Newcastle, NSW. At the start, the two women fail and flail in communication. Hannah was expecting a summer-long stay – a long enough period, perhaps, for meaningful reconnection; Umma (mother in Korean), however, believed it was just going to be a short vacation. The two women in Koreaboo fail and flail in communication. Gianna Rizzo Umma’s behaviour toward her daughter thrums with wariness, as though one were greeting a stranger. Maybe, she suggests, Hannah should be visiting Seoul’s touristy spots instead. The entire performance is staged in a small convenience store run by Umma, lovingly decked out in all manner of brightly coloured snacks, and with harsh fluorescent lighting thanks to designer Mel Page. The two women move within the space as they interrogate, parry and deflect.



Davidson explores a raft of issues, including the question of identity. Hannah’s hyphenated background (Korean-Australian) means she’s part of both cultures and wholly of neither, and at first, Umma’s brusque criticism of Hannah’s language skills feels like a wholesale rejection of her daughter’s “Koreanness”. Seeking both maternal and cultural acceptance, Hannah feels crushed to receive neither. Related Article Performing arts Star of ABC hit The Newsreader mines real-life family drama for new project Their common language – and one that helps them move toward connection and bridge distance, it turns out – is K-pop. The title actually refers to someone who’s not of Korean heritage but who is obsessed with Korean pop culture. Koreaboo swerves to the unexpected and surreal when both performers begin to sing and dance. There is a talent show in the offing to prepare for, and a chance for Hannah to become more Korean. It’s all surface-level cultural appropriation, though, much in the same way that Umma learnt English by watching TV, becoming so familiar with the lives of the characters in Sex and the City that she can quote from them. After a shaky start, Jeong and Davidson become good sparring partners and friends as they navigate the tricky mother-daughter relationship anew after years apart. Umma’s backstory is revealed: the reasons behind Hannah’s adoption and how her yearnings for a singing career were quashed because of filial obedience to her own mother. Korean culture is not just skincare and pop music, but, like a lot of Asian countries, there’s an expectation to conform to parental demands.



Koreaboo packs in a lot during its 90-minute stage time – maybe too much, as there is a lot of jumping about trying to cover a lot of ground. The beginning set-up takes a while to develop and can be tightened, and the ending feels rushed. And although the singing and dance sequences are overextended and as distracting as they are humorous, the play’s value is drawn from highlighting the possible consequences of adopting a child, removing them from their motherland, and raising them in an entirely foreign environment. Even if they embrace the riches of a new life in their host country, there are always losses to be reckoned with.

Reviewed by Thuy On OPERA

The Turn of the Screw ★★★

Palais Theatre, until October 1 Operatic takes on the supernatural span the centuries, but no modern work is more revered and feared than Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw. The 1954 opera follows a governess who takes up residence at an English country house, only to find the spirits of two dead servants are haunting the children now in her care. From left: Rachelle Durkin, Genevieve Gray and Oliver Thadoe Naing in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby



Finally, an opera where the muffled screams drifting in from Luna Park next door actually add to the drama, rather than detract! This is a piece that has potential to be The Shining-level unnerving. When staged up close and creepy, the eerie singing and sinister spectacle can captivate like a demonic spirit itself. Here, the huge set and vast stage dwarf the drama – in pivotal moments, the singers are far away from each other; we are far away from them. Detachment creates a disconnect that does not serve some excellent performances. Durkin, Michaela Cadwgan and Kanen Breen in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby It is, after all, a chamber opera. Britten scored it for just 13 instruments. Perhaps no Australian conductor knows more about the English composer than Paul Kildea, and the reduced Orchestra Victoria was guided superbly by him. Rachelle Durkin (Governess) was more maternal than hysterical, with a self-assured, impressive vocal performance to match. Kanen Breen’s voice is sharp and cold and uses his lithe physicality to intensify Peter Quint’s menace, despite donning the most unflattering wig anyone’s ever been cursed to wear (it’s a confusing choice, when it’s clearly mentioned how handsome Quint is).



One exceptional discovery to come from this production is soprano Genevieve Gray (currently a university student), who sings the older child, Flora. Gray possesses a vocal evenness and an array of colour that belies her youth. Neither a spook nor a snore, though with moments of satisfaction, this production feels like a missed opportunity to bewitch more people with the mystery and magic of operatic storytelling.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies MUSIC

Lady Blackbird ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 30 It’s been decades since Lady Blackbird – raised in an evangelical Christian household in New Mexico – abandoned her church-music roots, along with the religious doctrines that no longer defined her. Singer Lady Blackbird.



These days, the message underpinning her music is much more personal, but no less spiritually charged. The American singer (born Marley Munroe) has a voice to rival any gospel queen, but it’s now self-empowerment and self-acceptance she champions, rather than submission to an external force. In Melbourne on Wednesday, as part of her debut Australian tour, Lady Blackbird cut a striking figure as she arrived on stage: floor-sweeping black dress, elegant cane and signature platinum afro. Her three-piece band (guitarist Chris Seefried, bassist Jonathan Flaugher and Melbourne drummer Felix Bloxsom) stoked a gritty, distortion-flecked fire around the singer for Pink Floyd’s Mother, then retreated to the shadows for Blackbird, the haunting Nina Simone song that inspired the singer’s stage moniker. Related Article Melbourne live reviews This haunting play celebrates the solidarity and strangeness of found family On Collage, the amped-up fuzz of electric bass and guitar magnified the drama but almost submerged Blackbird’s glorious vocals. Then the mood softened – first with the addition of acoustic bass, then acoustic guitar. This was Blackbird in heartfelt confessional mode, her gorgeously grainy voice brimming with emotion on a clutch of originals: the soulfully swaying Lost and Looking, the jazz-tinted Five Feet Tall and the lilting, folky Man on a Boat. Seefried switched to piano for the wistful If I Told You before ushering in another cloud of psychedelia on a heady rendition of The Beatles’ Come Together. Blackbird’s musical world is unconstrained by genre, and her emotional commitment and authenticity allow her to make each song her own, whether it was written by her or others.



Imaginative arrangements and reharmonisations also allow the audience to hear old songs with fresh ears. In Blackbird’s hands, Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door became a hushed torch song, exquisitely understated. Her spellbinding encore – I Am What I Am – was equally unadorned, stripped of its Broadway sequins to become a quietly defiant affirmation of identity.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

Boom recruit Zak Butters says the Western Bulldogs are on the cusp of “something special”, and revealed he turned to Marcus Bontempelli for advice throughout the year before making his decision to head to the Whitten Oval. Butters, 26, is officially a Bulldog on a record nine-year contract worth between $17 million and $17.5 million after the AFL on Friday approved a convoluted side deal involving five clubs and a series of first, second and later draft picks exchanged. The Butters contract is the biggest in AFL history in total, though he will earn less than the $2 million per season St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has made. Ready to start: Zak Butters is looking forward to getting to work with the Western Bulldogs. AFL Photos “It’s good to make the decision and be here, and, yeah, I feel like it was a long time getting to this point,” Butters said.



Related Article Updated

Trading and drafting North board approved mammoth Blakey offer amid police investigation “And a few people told me along the journey that when you know, you know. And I felt like, yeah, once I knew, I just wanted to get it done, and get here and meet everyone and start my next journey.” Butters had already formed a friendship with Bontempelli, the Bulldogs’ skipper and legendary figure, which the club had felt was a factor in their favour in the intense competition for the midfield gun that also involved Richmond and Geelong. “He’s obviously one that I am looking forward to playing with, and he’s been an inspiration of mine since I was a kid, and probably more so the more I got to know him, not just this year, but along the journey and playing against him,” Butters told the Bulldogs’ website. “[I’m] trying to be the best, so you’re trying to learn off the best, and he’s he’s definitely one of them. So, over the last year as well, he’s just been a good sounding board and someone that you want to play footy with.



Related Article AFL 2026 How Nick Blakey can get to the Roos and what it will cost them “I feel like, as much as I can add to the footy club, that I’ll learn a lot from him, and some other guys at the footy club as well. So, yeah, I’m really looking forward to learning and becoming better off guys like Marcus and Bevo [coach Luke Beveridge] as well.” Butters grew up following the Dogs, his family residing in Darley on the western metropolitan fringe. He played for the Western Jets before being taken by the Power with the 12th pick of the 2018 national draft. He said one of the highlights of his life had been attending the 2016 finals, when the Bulldogs unexpectedly stormed to their second club premiership. “Yeah, I have loved the Bulldogs since I was a kid, had plenty of jumpers growing up, and loved a lot of different players. But, probably, 2016 is hard to top,” Butters said.



“I remember catching the train in from Bacchus Marsh, and watching the finals, and was lucky enough to sneak a few tickets through friends and family. And yeah, I remember catching the train home after the ’16 granny [grand final], and, obviously, catching the train back through the west to get to Bacchus Marsh, it was pretty chaotic and loud. “It’s still one of my favourite days that I’ve had in footy. So it’d be cool to try and run that back.” Butters said he wants to be role model for youth in the western suburbs, reinforcing that they, too, can reach the heights of elite football.

World.title: Delhi sealed off ahead of youth ‘Cockroach’ protest
World.content:
WorldAsiaIndia Delhi sealed off ahead of youth ‘Cockroach’ protest Saurabh Sharma , Aftab Ahmed and Sarita Chaganti Singh October 10, 2026 — 12:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

New Delhi: Central Delhi was sealed on Saturday, with thousands of police and paramilitaries on patrol, metro stations shut, mobile internet suspended and markets closed, to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit. The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party. A boy walks past security personnel guarding a march by Congress party workers and lawmakers demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India. AP Photo/Manish Swarup Touted by the organisers as a protest to “Save Democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after The Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process in which some 130 million voter names were removed. Opposition parties have long alleged that the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage and were quick to resurrect the allegations following the report. Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.



The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some key reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country as they are unable to win elections. People wave placards and shout slogans as they participate in a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities in Bengaluru, India. Getty Images Nonetheless, the near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks. It also comes months before a series of key state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled, most populous state of Uttar Pradesh. The protesters, led by the self-named “Cockroach Janta Party” (CJP), which began as an online satire, have said they will gather at Jantar Mantar – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi – at 10am (3.30pm AEDT).



Delhi Police said on Friday that they had not given permission for the protest as the request did not come on time, CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace. Related Article Protests India’s ‘cockroach’ protesters claim surprise victory as government accepts their demands Police also said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban. CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest as it was their fundamental right. In what is seen as a bid to thwart protesters arriving in Delhi and the central business district where Jantar Mantar is located, several long-distance trains to the city were cancelled on Friday and 57 metro stations shut from Friday night. Mobile internet services within a radius of four kilometres of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, the ANI News agency reported, citing a government order. You want braised duck, he wants the herbal brothiness of bak kut teh, and someone else is keen on nasi lemak. At this 21st-century vision of a hawker market, it’s no problem. Ten of Malaysia’s exemplars of street food have been tapped for a shiny eatery in QV. What it lacks in street-eating thrills, it makes up for with convenience and cleanliness. Then there’s the careful cooking.

Nasi lemak is spicy, comforting and refreshing. Dial up the good times by adding rendang powered by rempah, a coconutty, lemongrassy, gingery spice paste that’s slowly cooked to a dark rubble. Fat rendered from Hainanese chicken is used to cook the glossy, rich rice that accompanies it. Bak kut teh is anchored by a balanced broth gently humming with soy and garlic and marked by different cuts of pork – it’s one of the best Klang-style renditions in Melbourne.

It’s easy to see why families, older couples nostalgic for home, and solo diners are queuing out the door.

Good to know: QR-code ordering is via a menu that aggregates all 10 stalls’ dishes, making for a smoother experience.

World.title: Trump administration escalates war with International Criminal Court
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump administration escalates war with International Criminal Court Edward Wong and Jeanna Smialek October 10, 2026 — 12:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Trump administration announced on Friday it was imposing severe financial sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), its latest effort to cripple the global body that seeks to prosecute those accused of war crimes, genocide and other murderous criminal acts. The new sanctions, unveiled by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the US State Department, would prohibit transactions with the court after a grace period of six months. Any companies doing business with the court afterwards could be subject to punishment by the US government. The International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands. AP The threat of that could constrain the institution’s ability to carry out daily operations. Although the State Department had been preparing the sanctions for months, Rubio’s announcement came just hours after a committee in Norway said it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a South African lawyer who served for nine years as a judge on the ICC and worked as the top human rights official at the United Nations.



The sanctions are an intensification of the Trump administration’s push to undermine the court. In February 2025, just weeks after taking office, President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing agencies to come up with sanctions to impose on the court. At the time, he said the court was trying to violate American sovereignty and undermine “the critical national security and foreign policy work of the United States government and our allies, including Israel”. Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was recognised for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Martial Trezzini/Keystone via AP Rubio said in a statement on Friday that Trump would never allow the court to prosecute Americans. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” he said. Rubio announced in July that the United States planned to “systematically disable” the court, which Trump has long described as a threat to Americans.



The administration has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on court judges and prosecutors but the measures announced on Friday are broader. The ICC said in a statement that the American move was “an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order, which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law”. Many companies that have business ties with the court will be granted licences over the next 180 days to continue their work without financial punishments, the State Department said. During that period the Trump administration will assess whether its concerns regarding the ICC have been addressed, the department said in a statement. The administration can then adjust the licences based on that. The Treasury Department is helping to enact the sanctions and maintains a list of entities punished with financial restrictions.



Of nearly 200 nations in the world, 125 have signed the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court and are subject to its rulings. The United States never ratified the treaty establishing the institution, and both it and Israel are among those that are not bound by the statute. Judge Tomoko Akane, president of the court. Eva Plevier/Pool ANP via AP The court, officially established in 2002 and based at The Hague in the Netherlands, has a mission to investigate and prosecute genocide, war crimes and other serious offences. The Trump administration has in the past pushed back on the court’s ability to look into the conduct of US soldiers in Afghanistan and has also been highly critical of the court’s actions against Israel. In November 2024 the court issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel, and Yoav Gallant, the defence minister for much of Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip. Prosecutors had investigated the officials for war crimes and crimes against humanity in operations in Gaza, where thousands of Palestinian civilians have been killed and some have starved to death. Israel carried out airstrikes and ground operations after the deadly Hamas attacks in Israel in October 2023.



The Trump administration has already sanctioned 17 of the court’s officials, including judges and prosecutors. Rubio has suggested that even more sweeping punishments were necessary because of the possibility that the court could prosecute US citizens, and US service members in particular. Related Article Opinion

United Nations Yes, the UN is terrible – but right now, we need it desperately Nicholas Kristof Columnist Such actions would “mean the death of the US as a sovereign and independent nation”, Rubio wrote in an opinion essay published in The Wall Street Journal this past North American summer. Defenders of the court often point out that it has no police force of its own and would be able to arrest and try US citizens only if member states carry out arrests. The Trump administration is not the first to take on the ICC: under George W. Bush the United States also pushed back on the court’s ability to go after Americans. Yet the Trump administration’s effort to dismantle the institution – “brick by brick, if necessary”, according to Rubio – is an escalation, from scepticism and rhetoric to outright dismemberment.



“This is incredibly disturbing,” said James A. Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative legal organisation, calling the sanctions a “calculated attack” on international justice. Whether the American attack on the ICC will cripple the institution will depend in part on how its member nations respond, he said, and whether they stand by the institution. “We know that the court has been preparing for this much-rumoured eventuality,” he said. “We’ll have to see.” The European Union’s executive arm, whose 27 member countries are also members of the court, said in a statement that “the EU will work closely with the ICC to ensure it continues to operate effectively” and called the American move “deeply regrettable”. In a recent interview with The New York Times that was conducted before the latest sanctions were announced, Tomoko Akane, president of the court, said that the institution has been taking “measures to strengthen its resilience” in the face of the Trump administration’s threats. “A permanent body like the ICC must never be shut down,” she said. “The stakes extend far beyond the court itself.” The New York Times Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: 'Threatened to smash my face in': Mum of autistic teen struggles with awful noisy neighbours
World.content:
An Auckland mother says her autistic teenage daughter is being terrorised by noisy neighbours at their Kāinga Ora apartment complex.

"About six months ago new tenants moved in and have completely flipped our lives upside down," Jamie, who asked to keep her surname private to protect her daughter, said.

"They play extremely, extremely loud music that vibrates through my entire house. It's 24/7 constant banging, thumping, stomping, late night visitors, dogs barking. They are the most disruptive neighbours we've ever had."

Jamie said her daughter had severe noise sensitivity and was now wearing headphones all day to manage the noise.

"She can't eat properly, she's not sleeping, she stays up all night and sleeps during the day. She's isolated herself to her bedroom."

Jamie complained to Kāinga Ora, who visited and spoke to the neighbours, but said this didn't help.

"Basically I've just been stonewalled. Nothing seems to be changing."

"They either need to be issued some sort of warning that's going to stop this, or we need to be moved. They need to realise we can't live in an environment that's hostile to my daughter."

In a statement, Kāinga Ora regional director Taina Jones said staff had followed up on Jamie's complaints.

"We understand Jamie's daughter has autism and can be particularly sensitive to noise.

"We have taken Jamie's concerns seriously, however, as part of our enquiries we received differing accounts from those involved about when the music has been played, how loud it has been, and the broader circumstances surrounding the complaints."

Jones said the neighbours had been reminded of their obligations to be respectful to those around them, and that staff were still investigating Jamie's most recent complaint.

Jamie said she had attempted to resolve the issue herself by confronting the neighbours, but this went poorly.

"I had enough and I went to speak to them, just being very nice and calmly asked them, 'What is this banging? Is there something we can do to stop it?' and they were so hostile, threatened to smash my face in, and the police had to be called," she recounted.

"It's caused me to not want to leave my home, I'm isolated in my house. I go to step out my door and I've got to look left and right and then sometimes I decide I can't do it and go back inside and shut my door."

Jones said Kāinga Ora was aware of that altercation.

"Everyone has the right to feel safe and comfortable in their home. Our role as a landlord is to establish the facts and deal fairly with all parties involved.

World.title: New Zealand First pledges to increase minimum wage by at least inflation levels if in government
World.content:
New Zealand First has pledged to increase the minimum wage by at least inflation levels every year for the next three years, should it re-enter government.

It is also promising a permanent boost to the Working for Families in-work tax credit.

Over the last term of government, the minimum wage increased each year, with the most recent increase below the rate of inflation.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said workers needed to have the ability to afford the basics without falling behind the rate of inflation.

"As a government we cannot just view the economic recovery from a national level, it needs to start with our workers who are the backbone of our communities."

Peters has made the announcement at a public meeting in Invercargill.

Alongside the minimum wage announcement, Peters said New Zealand First would make permanent the temporary boost to the in-work tax credit introduced earlier this year to help families affected by the fuel crisis.

The $50 a week boost is set to expire in April, or if the price of 91 octane petrol drops below $3 a litre for four consecutive weeks.

Peters said New Zealand First would also increase it by an extra $70 a week, making the total $120 a week. The party estimated it would cost between $500 million to $600m a year.

ACT had campaigned on a minimum wage freeze, but New Zealand First had secured increases as part of the coalition agreement.

World.title: Will my savings be taken to pay for my husband's care? - Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

My husband and I have a freehold home. We both receive superannuation. He has, in his name, approximately $300,000 in terms deposits. He has sundowner dementia, and contributes nothing to our daily living costs, so I am still working full-time and contributing to KiwiSaver. I have several term deposits in my name, I received two small inheritances and an employment settlement.

My question is eventually my husband may need rest home care, once he has exhausted his savings, will they be able to take my money? It's a real concern as I have worked hard all my life and it does not seem fair I may not be able to have the benefit of using my savings to travel as planned.

Yes, if you're in a relationship, then both of your assets are assessed when it comes to deciding whether he will qualify for the rest home subsidy. The threshold amount is adjusted regularly but at the moment if someone is 65 or older with a partner who is not in long-term residential care, they can have combined assets of $164,731 or less not including the family home and car or $300,811 or less including the family home and car, and receive support to pay for rest home care.

So you'd be limited to that lower amount on top of the value of your house. In the past we've been asked about things like contracting out agreements, but they would not apply in this situation.

Are there any banking institutions still wholly NZ owned, without support from parent banks here or overseas?

The NZ-owned banks are TSB, SBS, Co-operative, Kiwibank and Heartland. There are other financial institutions like building societies, credit unions and finance companies.

I have medical insurance with Southern Cross Healthcare and their premiums keep going up and up each year as we age. I have just had their annual report sent through and the email says: "Our claims cost escalation reduced to 7.1 percent in FY26, down from 12.2 percent the previous year, considerably lower than the rest of the health insurance sector. This matters because lower claims cost growth helps reduce pressure on premiums and supports the long-term affordability of cover for members."

What I read from this is that we should be expecting lower premiums as this will reduce pressure and they are a not-for-profit society. Am I right in thinking this?

I think it's probably more accurate to think premiums won't rise as fast as they might otherwise have, rather than actually being lower.

I went to Southern Cross, who said: "The 7.1 percent figure shows the year-on-year increase in our claims costs, which comprises three things: the amount of procedures we fund, the number of procedures we fund, and the mix of procedures members claim for.

"The reduction … is positive for members. It doesn't mean premiums will fall however, but because claims costs are the biggest driver of premiums, lower claims cost escalation will contribute to a lower level of premium increases.

"Southern Cross is a Friendly Society, which means we don't have external shareholders to pay dividends to. However, we still need to make a surplus so we can pay future claims, maintain our financial strength and invest in services for members."

We have two uni students and another teenager, who won't go to uni. Eventually both sets of our parents will die. We have a $400,000 mortgage on a $1 million-ish 1970s home in Auckland. When the parents die, do we pay off the kids' student loans? We earn too much for them to get student allowance. Both will end up owing about $30,000 or $40,000 at the end of their degrees.

Liz Koh, founder of Enrich Retirement, said when student loans were interest -free then it was usually better to invest the money and earn a return, rather than paying off the loan.

"You could still give a lump sum to each child, including the one not going to university, for fairness, but advise them to invest it until such time as they wish to buy a house or go overseas - in which case there will be interest on the student loan."
