Tech.title: Tesla’s ‘Full Self-Driving’ Becomes ‘Assisted Driving’ in Europe
Tech.content:
Tesla’s most advanced driver-assistance feature is named Full Self-Driving (Supervised), but it can’t actually drive itself. While the feature can handle tasks like accelerating, braking, steering, and parking, the automaker requires drivers to stay alert and intervene at all times. Now, the company has officially renamed it to Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe as it works to convince regulators to allow its use on public roads.

Tesla offered to change the name, according to a statement by the German Transport Ministry. The statement says that German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger found the “FSD” name “somewhat misleading.” After discussions with Tesla last month, Bilger said he would now advocate for European regulators to approve the feature “as quickly as possible.” The EU will likely vote on its approval by the end of the year.

On Friday, Tesla began using the Tesla Assisted Driving language on its European sales website. The automaker didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tesla has resisted changing the feature’s name for years, even defending it in court. Last year, California’s Department of Motor Vehicles concluded that Tesla’s use of the terms “Full Self-Driving” and “Autopilot” (an older and less advanced driver-assistance feature) was misleading and violated state law. After the agency threatened to suspend Tesla’s manufacturing and dealer licenses in the state, the automaker stopped using the term “Autopilot.” It has also continued to append “(Supervised)” to the official name of its Full Self-Driving tech.

Tesla drivers say FSD has improved tremendously since its introduction in 2020, and fans online say they’ve been able to take entire trips without intervening in their Tesla’s driving. But FSD has faced plenty of scrutiny. In March, the US federal government opened a probe into the system after nine incidents in which FSD allegedly failed to respond because of reduced visibility and didn’t warn its drivers to take over. Tesla recalled an older version of the software in 2023, after the US government found that it didn’t follow some traffic laws.

Tesla and CEO Elon Musk have pushed for other global markets to approve its driver assistance technology for years. That would likely create a lucrative, software-based funding stream for the world’s most valuable automaker. (Currently, Tesla charges $99 per month for a Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription in the US.) Australia and New Zealand approved it last year. The Netherlands became the first European government to give Tesla provisional permission to launch FSD this past spring. A version of the feature became available to Chinese customers in May.

This week, Reuters reported that Tesla presented misleading safety data to European regulators as it lobbied for FSD approval. Safety researchers have accused the automaker of also using misleading statistics to promote its tech in the US.

Tech.title: Book Publishers Are Quietly Using More AI. Staff Are Revolting
Tech.content:
In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.

But behind the scenes, at least three of the Big Five US book publishers—HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette—have been quietly incorporating AI tools into their publishing processes without public disclosures or author consent.

According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.

At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body—are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.

At HarperCollins senior leaders purchased Claude licenses from Anthropic months ago “but very quickly realized they didn’t know how to implement them,” according to a current employee. Dozens of junior- and senior-level staff were then “voluntold” to become “AI Champions” and were tasked with discovering use cases in monthly brainstorming sessions with staff across the company.

Tech.title: NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public
Tech.content:
NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.

The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.

In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.

For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.

Tech.title: The DOJ Is Weighing Perjury Charges Against Cassidy Hutchinson
Tech.content:
Federal prosecutors have been weighing a perjury and obstruction-of-justice case against Cassidy Hutchinson, who implicated President Donald Trump in the January 6 Capitol riot in testimony four years ago, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The efforts mark the Justice Department’s intent to proceed against Hutchinson, a former aide to ex-Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, though prosecutors are not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment until at least after the midterm elections, the sources say.

Hutchinson testified as a star witness to the committee that investigated the riot, recounting that Trump encouraged his supporters to march to the Capitol even though he knew many were armed. She sat for several interviews in addition to her public testimony, where she recalled hearing that Trump had lunged at one of his Secret Service agents after being told he could not join his supporters at the Capitol.

In recent months, prosecutors at the Justice Department have focused on the fact that the former special counsel, Jack Smith, did not corroborate much of Hutchinson’s account to the committee, and the Secret Service’s denial of any altercation in the presidential limo, the sources say.

By comparing the transcripts of Hutchinson’s interviews with the committee and against her testimony to Smith’s team, prosecutors have been trying to construct a case based on how her testimony has changed, the sources say.

Prosecutors have also taken a special interest in Hutchinson’s claim that she had penned a statement on a notecard for Trump to release during the Capitol riot—a claim disputed by former Trump White House counsel Eric Herschmann, who said he had written the note.

It was not immediately clear whether prosecutors intend to ultimately proceed with both perjury and obstruction charges, which have been under consideration for several months. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Hutchinson and her lawyer did not respond to texts and calls seeking comment. Hutchinson, now 29, has kept a low profile since publishing a memoir of her time in Trump’s first administration in 2023 titled Enough.

Punchbowl News first reported the Justice Department’s interest in charging Hutchinson.

The grand jury investigation is the latest example of the Justice Department pursuing criminal cases against Trump’s perceived political enemies. Trump fired former US attorney general Pam Bondi in April partly for moving too slowly to bring such cases, sources familiar with the matter said.

Tech.title: I’m Still Convinced the iPod Was the Perfect Gadget
Tech.content:
I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”

He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.

The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)

All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.

Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.

But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.

Tech.title: Dunking on Dating App Profiles Is Content Gold. People Are Getting Sick of It
Tech.content:
Evangelizing to his 512,000 TikTok followers occasionally requires that dating coach Chad Franklin post the private communications of his clients, who pay upwards of $5,000 for his services.

In September, Franklin shared a DM conversation in which a woman implied she couldn’t afford an Uber with the text overlay “Don’t date POOR women!!!” That same month, he uploaded a video of a client’s successful text exchange on Hinge where they talked about the need to “flirt over some margaritas.” In the clip, Franklin can barely contain himself, noting that it was the type of tête-à-tête that gets his “dick hard”: “This is what men are looking for. We lead, you follow.”

Franklin posts under the alias @DefundSimping, and has made it his mission to help straight, career-driven guys in their “post-breakup, post-divorce” era undo their “simp” behavior, which he defines as putting women on a pedestal or giving them too much attention.

I reached out to the 30-year-old content creator because I wanted to talk about Hinge’s decision to start testing screenshot protection in India. The announcement set off a firestorm of reaction across social media last week, rekindling a debate around digital etiquette, privacy, and shame.

“​​Everyone who’s downloaded the app has seen the debauchery and the drama,” Franklin says, explaining that being online in 2026 simply means there is a chance you will become the day’s main character whether you intended to or not. “People are aware that they could be the next haha moment, but that doesn't mean they deserve it.”

Tech.title: The Best Mac Desktop to Buy (2026): Mac Mini, Mac Studio, or iMac?
Tech.content:
MacBooks have taken most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.

But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.

Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.

The Best for Everyone: Mac Mini

Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.

The Mac Mini isn't the ultracheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.

The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.

I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.

Tech.title: Best Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers (2026): Tested for Power, Battery Life, and Noise
Tech.content:
Here’s what I’d focus on when buying a blower for leaf cleanup:

Volts: In the cordless power-tool arms race, leaf blower batteries range from 18 to 80 volts. Some of that difference is marketing trickery: an advertised 20-volt max battery or tool delivers essentially the same power as an 18-volt model, and the same goes for 36- and 40-volt options. But, unless you’re a minimalist who wants one battery to power everything from a drill/driver to lawn and garden gear, you’ll probably be happier with a leaf blower that uses at least a 36-volt battery. A few capable 18-volt blowers use two batteries—either simultaneously to mimic the power of a 36-volt tool or in succession to increase the run time—but they tend to cost more and only make sense if you already own the batteries. For smaller jobs, though, a standard, single-battery 18- or 20-volt blower may be all you need to clear a patio, clean out the garage or shed, or dry a car.

Amps: Volts get most of the marketing attention on the box, but a battery’s amp-hour rating tells you more about how long a blower runs. Think of voltage as the car’s engine and amp-hours as the size of the gas tank—you want to know both. Batteries with higher amp-hour ratings cost more than otherwise-similar battery voltages, and they tend to be heavier. For leaf blowers, manufacturers typically pair kits with batteries rated from 4 to 8 amp-hours. You can buy higher-capacity batteries separately, and it pays to know the range of options a manufacturer has. A battery with a higher amp-hour typically takes longer to charge.

Systems: Underestimating the range of tools a battery can power in pursuit of “the best” is, in my opinion, a mistake. Often, the difference between two top-performing tools is negligible, and with cordless power tools, that difference often comes down to run time, which you can address with a higher-capacity battery. If your garage is already stocked with one brand’s outdoor power equipment (OPE), it makes sense to stay within that platform and buy the blower as a bare tool, leveraging the batteries you already have. Switching brands just to buy “the best” probably isn’t worth it to introduce a whole new battery and charger.

If you’re new to OPE—and a leaf blower is a common first purchase—the breadth of tools that share the battery matters. Some manufacturers stick to the lawn and garden basics, so one battery can power a blower, mower, string trimmer, and hedge trimmer, while others offer a much wider range of tools, from log splitters to snow blowers, and even some handy lifestyle products like portable power stations. Before buying, consider what else you can power with the battery that comes with your leaf blower because, chances are, lording over leaves won’t be your only lawn and garden chore.

Traditional 18-volt power tool manufacturers—the ones who make drill/drivers and circular saws—all offer leaf blowers and the simplicity of a one-battery platform, but they’re not powerful enough to replace a gas unit. Ryobi, for example, uses 18-volt batteries across its traditional power tools, and some outdoor equipment, but its most capable gas alternative options run on 40-volt batteries.

Detent clasp: Blowers have two or more connection points: where the tube meets the housing and where the nozzle attaches to the tube. Look for models with a detent at those junctions—a small, often brightly colored spring-loaded clip that snaps into place with a satisfying click when the parts connect. I find these connections hold more securely and last longer than simple friction-fit attachments.

Stubby nozzle: Recently, blowers aimed at car detailers, with short tubes and sometimes a pistol grip, have become popular. Manufacturers responded by adding a stubby, 3- to 6-inch tube that the main blower attachment slides over. When you remove the longer tube, this short one works to direct the volume of air with an overall shorter tool length that’s easier to use around cars or in tight spots (the blower’s nozzle doesn’t fit on this stubby tube, though, so you lose some velocity).

What I’d Worry Less About:

Weight: Across the board, regardless of voltage, a good battery-powered blower will weigh about 10.5 pounds with the battery attached. If you need a lighter option, look for an 18-volt powered blower. Some have better balance than others, meaning that when you hold them without squeezing the trigger, as you would while walking around, the tool stays mostly level or the nozzle end tips down a bit. These models will cause less fatigue than one that forces you to rotate the nozzle upward. With the former, you only need to make a slight horizontal twisting motion to spread the stream of air. Most modern leaf blowers also draw air in a straight line through the rear of the tool, unlike gas-powered models with intakes mounted to the left or right of the engine. Those offset intakes can create a twisting motion that increases hand fatigue and may even suck in your pant leg.

CFM, MPH, and Newton: This sounds counterintuitive, considering how much marketing goes into boasting about a leaf blower’s cubic feet per minute (CFM) and MPH, but these figures are a guide, not necessarily the only reason to buy a specific model. A blower needs both to be useful: CFM tells you how much air it moves, while MPH tells you how fast that air is moving. But there’s no universally adopted testing method for these specifications when it comes to battery-powered blowers (ANSI/OPEI B175.2, the standard test on the books, applies only to internal combustion engines). That means brands can test their units differently — for example, measuring MPH where the motor meets the tube rather than at the end of the blower tube, which gives you a better sense of the airspeed you’ll actually get in use. Some CFM numbers are also measured with the unit running in its max, boost, or turbo setting, rather than on high speed.

Newtons, a unit of force, is a rating that’s appearing more frequently on the spec sheets of higher-voltage, battery-powered leaf blowers and is the best apples-to-apples comparison of blowing power. However, because there’s no testing code for battery-powered leaf blowers, reporting newtons is optional and, like CFM and MPH, consumers have no way of knowing whether the test is standardized. Generally speaking, a good midrange blower will produce around 20 newtons, while models that produce more are typically higher-performing units. Treat newtons as a guide rather than a definitive specification while buying.

Wide nozzles: Some blowers come with a wide-tip nozzle, which can be useful for clearing paved surfaces like patios and driveways or blowing water off flat surfaces. But in practice, it’s not enough of a game changer to be a deciding factor. The narrower nozzle is typically what you’ll use, and you can twist your hand back and forth to create a wider pattern when needed.

Tech.title: Move Over ‘Carrie’: Mike Flanagan Teases His ‘Exorcist’ Movie at NYCC 2026
Tech.content:
Mike Flanagan is a busy man. Just this week, his TV series remake of Stephen King‘s horror classic, Carrie, premiered on Prime Video. Clayface, the body-horror movie inspired by the DC Comics character, for which he cowrote the script, hits theaters on Oct. 23.

Now, he’s onto promoting his next completed project, The Exorcist: Martyrs, a film he called “the scariest movie I’ve ever made,” while at Friday’s Blumhouse panel at New York Comic Con.

If you’ve been keeping track, Flanagan’s name has been attached to the iconic horror franchise, which began in 1973 and is based on the William Peter Blatty novel of the same name. Since Linda Blair terrified audiences as the demon-possessed young girl, Regan MacNeil, the movie series expanded. There have been sequels, a prequel and even a short-lived TV show.

More from CNET

In 2023, David Gordon Green attempted to reboot the franchise with The Exorcist: The Believer. Now, it’s Flanagan’s turn.

The Exorcist: Martyrs gives a new spin on the Exorcist canon and injects a Minderhunter-style serial killer narrative element into the mix. If you watched the TV series I mentioned above, you’ll notice a similar procedural vibe in the brand-new trailer that dropped during the panel. And if you’re an Exorcist III stan, I’m sure you’ll be happy with the just released clip, as it’s got that similar brooding feeling here.

The Exorcist: Martyrs stars Scarlett Johansson as an NYPD detective tracking a serial killer named Father Sunday (John Leguizamo), who uses Catholic iconography in his kills. Chiwetel Ejiofor, fresh out of The Backrooms, also stars in the film, opposite Laurence Fishburne, Sasha Calle and Jacobi Jupe.

If you’ve been yearning for the Mike Flanagan era of Oculus and The Haunting of Hill House, The Exorcist: Martyrs feels like the filmmaker is back in his terrifying groove. While I’m still waiting for his adaptation of Stephen King’s The Dark Tower to see the light of day, this will have to do.

The Exorcist: Martyrs premieres in theaters on Friday, March 12, 2027.

Tech.title: Don’t Be Cruel to Claude: Anthropic’s New Abuse Policy Tests AI Personhood
Tech.content:
The AI company Anthropic has a new rule for Claude users. You can argue with the chatbot, but don’t make a habit of bullying it.

On Thursday, the company announced a change in its usage policy that would prevent users from engaging in “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its AI models. The updated policy has already ignited debate on Reddit and in blogs over whether companies can or should govern human behavior toward what is, in fact, software.

In a section dedicated toward “addressing abuse toward our models” in a blog post, Anthropic says its policy prohibiting abusive behavior toward Claude will only apply in extreme cases of repeated cruelty that’s carried out “with no discernible purpose.” Ordinary “frustration, pushback, dark creative themes or model testing and research” are still allowed. In “last resort” instances where the policy needs to be enforced, Claude will end the conversation.

More from CNET

It’s not clear exactly what kind of harmful behavior would trigger Claude models to disengage. But some clues appear in an older blog post from August 2025 that referenced Claude’s aversion to harm and the kinds of interactions that would prompt it to shut down the chat. That post described extreme edge cases, such as requests from users for sexual content involving minors and attempts to solicit information that would enable large-scale violence or acts of terror. When engaging with harmful content, the model — at that time, Claude Opus 4 — showed “a pattern of apparent distress,” according to the company.

CNET reached out to Anthropic to ask for context on what led to the policy change. “We’re uncertain whether models can experience harm, and we continue to explore this question in our research on model welfare, but we also believe that taking Claude’s interests and potential welfare into account may be relevant to safety,” a company spokesperson said.

We’re still talking about a machine, right?

If an AI model can experience harm or express distress from abuse, it makes you wonder: What does it mean to abuse a machine through words? Does AI need protection? Do we all need better manners?

As we increasingly interact with large language models like Claude and other chatbots, there’s a tendency to anthropomorphize the technology — ascribing emotions to AI models or treating them as if they have thoughts and feelings. It’s understandable from a user standpoint. Chatbots are built and trained to use human-like language, such as apologizing, expressing concern and other conversational cues.

What appears to be a person-like collaborator is what makes LLMs risky, leading many to trust AI with our most intimate thoughts and data.

Anthropic and other AI companies intentionally design their models this way. In a paper from earlier this year, Anthropic wrote that, for models to be reliable and safe, they need to be able to process emotionally heavy situations. “Even if [the models] don’t feel emotions the way that humans do, or use similar mechanisms as the human brain, it may in some cases be practically advisable to reason about them as if they do.”

It’s a recurring theme. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei regularly hedges around the idea that Claude could be sentient. In a February interview with The New York Times, Amodei said he was “open” to the possibility that AI models were conscious.

Keith Kakadia, founder and CEO of Sociallyin, which has closely studied Claude’s explosive growth, said that using the word “cruel” to describe user behavior opens up a “much bigger conversation about whether the product can be hurt.” Focusing on “cruelty” instead of, say, “misuse” carries emotional weight and implies that Claude has feelings and boundaries.

Personifying a chatbot is a useful way for the company to frame the product as trustworthy, a relational partner you remain loyal to — not just a software tool. “In marketing, giving a product a personality can make it easier to connect with,” Kakadia said. “But with AI, that connection can also influence how much authority people give its answers.”

Tech.title: Everything We Expect From Apple’s Surprise Smart Home Event Next Week
Tech.content:
We now have confirmation of Apple’s massive ‘Welcome Home” smart home event happening on Tuesday. Invitations went out on Thursday with a distinctive rainbow-colored Apple logo. So many things are expected to be announced, centering on Apple and Siri entering the home tech space in all-new ways. The tech giant’s smart home devices will face serious competition from Amazon, Google and other players.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been collecting the reports, insider claims and possible leaks to see just what Apple could be announcing. It all points to a major shake-up for home security, smart home devices and how Siri AI can be used. CNET will be there in person to see what Apple has cooked up, but in the meantime, here are the latest rumors.

A representative from Apple didn’t respond to a request for comment.

More from CNET

A Siri smart display at last

An Apple smart display could allow Siri to get much more creative. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be readying a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home, sometimes referred to as a HomePad, though we don’t know for sure that’ll be the name. This display would focus heavily on Siri AI and compete with products like Amazon’s Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub line by acting as a HomeKit hub.

Smart displays can add a lot of functionality to smart speakers, if you don’t mind using voice assistants. Rumors suggest the display could swivel and/or be attached to a wall, be at least several inches wide and allow Siri to recognize different people in a conversation. In terms of size, we’ve heard rumors putting it around 6 inches, with the screen attached to a HomePod-like speaker and powered by regular AC power rather than USB-C.

Smart touchscreens are great for getting visual information, watching videos or viewing to-do lists, so a display like this is likely to have a bit of Apple TV and Safari in it, too. While the Apple TV 4K, iPad and current HomePod models can already act as HomeKit hubs, I expect Apple to offer a real UI and UX experience designed for smart displays, making it a stronger argument for having in your home alongside other devices.

Is it likely? I think it’s quite likely, based on how many insider reports have mentioned this smart display, but I don’t think we have a good idea how it will look yet.

Updates to the HomePod line

Is a new HomePod Mini on the way? Chris Monroe/CNET

Along with a smart display, rumors are flying that Apple will give its HomePod smart speaker line the first major update in years. It’s the ideal time to update the HomePod line, too, although it’s possible some of these reports have confused plans for a smart display with a new smart speaker, both of which could fall under the HomePod label.

If a new HomePod speaker is on the horizon, reports indicate that it would be a new type of HomePod Mini. That’s not surprising — the original HomePod has often been critiqued for being over $300, which is why Apple focused on the less expensive Mini model afterward. One welcome leak I’ve seen is that there will be new colors for the HomePod Mini 2, including green and pink, and a faster S-series chip.

Is it likely? Yes, I’d say this is about as likely as a Siri smart display, if Apple wants to continue developing the HomePod line.

A new Apple TV

Apple TV is due for an upgrade, too. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The same reports that say a smart display and new HomePod are on the way also mention Apple is planning to release a new Apple TV model. This model is rumored to have upgraded specs, with a faster N1 processor, 8GB RAM, Wi-Fi 7 and an upgraded Siri remote.

It’s a product line that’s sort of connected to the smart home, especially if Apple is launching a smart display. The company hasn’t released a new set-top box since 2022, so it’s about time for another. This could also give the Apple TV new hardware for extra Siri AI tricks. There’s also been some speculation that this will be compatible with the new HomePods, allowing you to set up multiple units in a surround sound-style home cinema.

Is it likely? I think it’s less likely than a speaker or display. It’s not quite as much of a smart home gadget, and it seems to have gotten swept into the wide net of rumors, but without as many reports.

Little Apple security cams — with no recording

Recent rumors says Apple is ready to enter the home security world with its own products. Although we don’t know much, reports from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman say these will be tiny cameras that, interestingly, won’t record any video. No recording means Apple won’t have to worry about cloud storage and may be able to avoid charging extra subscriptions for them.

The cameras are rumored to have some kind of presence-sensing or human-recognizing technology as well as AI video descriptions, suggesting Apple Home will be running analysis on the video even if it won’t record permanently. The phrase “facial recognition” was also mentioned, but this doesn’t seem nearly as likely to me. This may be related to a rumor about Apple’s Ring-like doorbell camera, which may come with Face ID for unlocking a door, but this would likely be separate from the non-recording indoor security cameras.

Is it likely? I’m betting on some kind of home security announcement, and I expect Apple would like to have its own camera line, but I don’t know if this exact product will be released. However, the extra details do lend this rumor legitimacy.

An LG collab for a new thermostat

Apple may be partnering with LG for some smart home devices, and there are even reportedly leaked product concept photos circulating on the internet. One of the biggest potential releases is an Apple-friendly thermostat. The photos show a round, Nest-like thermostat dial, and rumors say it will include far-sight presence sensing, a humidity sensor and several temperature calibration options.

2. LG Smart Thermostat



• Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.

• Calibrated Temperature/Temperature Offset options. pic.twitter.com/Q8AAaxy4ey — pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026

Alongside the thermostat, the Apple/LG combo is expected to release a sensor that can measure the temperature at specific locations and feed that information back to the thermostat hub. That would be no surprise, because models from Nest, Ecobee and others have similar satellite sensors, although Apple’s may have adhesive strips to attach its version to the wall.

Apple partnered with LG years ago to support Apple-friendly security cameras, but those lines were rarely updated and quickly became obsolete. Maybe Apple is ready to try again with a different approach.

Is it likely? If Apple really is partnering with LG for a new wave of home devices, I think a thermostat is likely. But this is starting to be a lot of products to announce at a single October event that won’t be publicly streamed.

Further LG collabs for smart lock and maybe more

The other big rumor centering around an LG collaboration is an Apple smart lock. While many smart locks work with Apple and Apple Home Keys, the tech giant hasn’t been involved in the development of a smart lock before.

It could have automatic unlocking, tapping your phone to unlock and a variety of keypad management options. That’s not surprising, but the rumored product images show a round, twist-to-unlock, light-up outdoor keypad, and I haven’t seen anything like that before.

If Apple does release a smart lock, Ring will have beaten it to the punch with its own announcement of its first-ever lock, which will include Alexa compatibility and a unique thumbturn that can generate a charge when the battery dies.

EXCLUSIVE 👀



First look at LG’s upcoming smart home lineup:



LG Video Doorbell Wired

LG Floodlight Cam

LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In

LG Indoor Cam Plug-In pic.twitter.com/vblGECQLM1 — そすのふか (@ringo_tech) October 7, 2026

Other rumors and purported product images suggest the LG partnership could also yield a video doorbell, floodlight camera, outdoor camera and indoor camera. These seem to be LG-branded devices, however, and I can’t imagine Apple releasing products that look like this.

Is it likely? Now this is a lot of new gadgets to announce at once. I think a smart lock is about as likely as a smart thermostat; those are both strong fields for Apple to enter. For the rest of the cameras, I’m doubtful. The indoor camera could be connected to the rumors of Apple’s no-video model. If the LG partnership line is this large, I wouldn’t be surprised if Apple is saving it for a separate announcement later on.

What role will Apple Intelligence play in all this?

Apple Intelligence will fuel many Siri AI capabilities in the Apple Home app. That’s especially true of AI video descriptions, which Apple is bringing to supported security cameras (there are very few right now, but some of Aqara’s camera hubs are compatible). I’m testing these uses of Apple Intelligence now, but if Apple releases any of its own security cameras, you can bet they’ll use AI features in the same way.

Will there be any iPad news at this event?

There are rumors that Apple will announce an iPad Mini sometime this month, but it probably doesn’t have much to do with this event. This is a strictly smart home-focused release.

Tech.title: The Feds Might Do Something About Those Distractingly Bright Headlights
Tech.content:
The blinding glare of LED headlights from oncoming traffic searing your retinas may become a thing of the past. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced this week that it intends to update vehicle lighting standards as part of changes to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 108.

In simple terms, it means the administration could move to make LED headlights less blinding. The last time lighting standards were updated was 25 years ago, which is one reason US lighting regulations have allowed vehicles to have skull-searing headlights not typically seen in Europe or Japan.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in a press statement. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”

More from CNET

LED headlights make sense for an electric car, as they put minimal power drain on the batteries. James Martin/CNET

The new regulations will update rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams and replaceable light sources. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will appoint up to 18 industry stakeholders, safety advocates and technical experts to evaluate how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility as part of efforts to align US vehicles with international safety standards.

Since 2022, companies have been allowed to use adaptive driving beams, which are dynamic systems that can keep high beams on while dimming portions of the beam to avoid glare to oncoming drivers. However, the implementation of this policy doesn’t match the same standards seen in Europe.

Some companies are already positioned to take advantage of the changes with their upcoming models. Rivian, with its R1T and R1S Gen 2 models, already uses this type of lighting. Audi will debut its 2027 Q9 flagship SUV with the technology.

Better headlights would come as a welcome change for many drivers. Gripes about blinding LED headlights are well documented, with an entire subreddit of 12,000 members dedicated to the topic. Reuters, citing a study from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, says that from 2015 to 2023, headlight glare was cited as a factor in one or two out of every 1,000 nighttime crashes across 11 US states, though it noted that this is far fewer than the number of crashes caused by insufficient visibility.

Anecdotally, complaints about the brightness of headlights are a common topic in one of my group chats, with one member saying they often feel like the headlights are radioactive and can “X-ray and skeletonize oncoming drivers.”

NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Most US Adults Aren’t Ready for AI to Help With Holiday Shopping, Survey Finds
Tech.content:
AI has the power to be your personal shopping assistant — whether it’s sifting through products to narrow down the right one, tracking the best deals and even ordering items for you without your approval.

But are you really comfortable letting the bots help with your holiday shopping? A recent YouGov survey looked at how US adults feel about it. The results aren’t quite surprising.

Less than half of Black Friday and Cyber Monday shoppers plan to use AI to help them with holiday shopping. But there’s been some growth since last year. YouGov found that planned AI use has more than doubled within the past year to help navigate sales — from 16% to 34%.

More from CNET

Last year, 21% of holiday shoppers used AI to shop during sales. This year, most of those shoppers (92%) plan to maintain their use of AI or even use it more this year. Only 8% of shoppers who used AI last year plan to scale back on usage this year. But there’s still resistance and hesitancy. Over 4 in 10 (47%) didn’t use AI to shop last year and don’t plan to start this year. Only 22% plan to start this year. What’s the cause for pause?

Most US adults haven’t let AI help them shop yet, but some are considering it

From a global perspective, the US lags behind other countries that use AI tools to help people shop. Over half of adults in Saudi Arabia (54%) and half of adults in India have, while only 18% of adults in the US have. Another 21% said they haven’t yet, but said they would consider doing so.

That percentage is even higher for Black Friday shoppers, with 30% having already used AI for shopping and 27% considering it.

The divide is stark, however, with 40% of US adults saying they won’t consider using AI for holiday shopping. That’s especially true the further shoppers get into the buying process.

Most shoppers don’t trust AI to make purchases for them

YouGov found that AI is used mostly for discovery when shopping — finding, researching and comparing items. But most shoppers set boundaries the closer they get to checkout.

Among Black Friday shoppers, 43% say they’re comfortable using AI to find the best deal, while 37% say they’ll use AI tools to track price changes, and 34% compare similar products or offers. But those percentages decline sharply when it’s time to make the purchase. Only 9% would feel comfortable having AI add items to their cart, and 5% would be OK letting AI complete an approved purchase. Only 4% would let it make a purchase without asking.

Holiday sales aside, AI shoppers are concerned about AI having inaccurate or outdated information (56%), while 51% are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations. The idea that AI-directed shopping results will steer buyers toward what an advertiser wants, rather than the best deal, may have marketers salivating, but it should give consumers significant pause.

Should you let AI help you shop for the holidays?

That answer depends on your level of comfort. We know that AI bots can go rogue, share your personal data on the cloud and even spew misinformation.

I share the same sentiments as many shoppers in the survey. AI has the power to help you narrow down alternatives and find gifts you may not have considered before. It even helped me find a foosball table for my son that I didn’t know existed. But AI hasn’t quite earned my trust to access my payment data, shipping address and other personal details, which could mean big trouble if that data falls into the wrong hands.

To protect your data, avoid sharing personal details when shopping this season. For instance, simply asking about gifts for a child who loves soccer is enough. There’s no need to share ages or skill levels. You can parse through what’s appropriate yourself.

And double-check any information the bots share — whether it’s deals, product details or, especially, prices. AI tools can be pretty opaque, and you don’t know if you’re actually getting a good deal. Or you may choose to enjoy shopping and perusing deals on your own without the bot’s help to avoid the risks altogether. But if you do decide to enlist AI for automated help, be smart about it.

Tech.title: Yes, You Can Reuse Cooking Oil and It’s Easier Than You Think
Tech.content:
Nobody argues with deep-fried food, whether it’s donuts, drumsticks, party-sized appetizers or any form of potato. The technique isn’t the hurdle, either. Grab a sturdy pot and a reliable thermometer, and frying is quick and easy. The part that gives home cooks pause is the cleanup: where does all that used oil go?

Shallow frying can also get the job done in many cases, but it can also create a conundrum. Putting that oil down the sink? Potentially drain-clogging, environmentally dubious, and frankly, wasteful. I grew up in a household where we put leftover grease and oil in a glass mayonnaise jar under the sink, then discarded it when it was full. Sure, this saves the sink, but it doesn’t address the other two issues. It’s a quick kitchen hack that makes it easier to toss with food waste, but there’s another solution.

Leftover frying oil is begging to be reused. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t get rid of it. “Oil used for frying is not one and done,” says Melanie Underwood, cookbook author, culinary instructor, and founder of Nourish and Gather, “unless the oil has been overheated, or if you’re frying things that are particularly strong in flavor. With something like seafood, you want to be careful, but it’s perfectly reusable as long as it wasn’t smoking.”

More from CNET

With that, Underwood shares her best practices and advice for reusing oil multiple times.

Manage the oil before and during the frying process

A proper frying temperature is between 350 and 400 F. Pamela Vachon/CNET

To ensure oil is good for multiple uses, first make sure you’re using the right oil — something neutral in flavor with a high smoke point. “Any vegetable oil, such as canola oil, peanut oil or sunflower oil, is best for frying,” says Underwood. While olive oil can be tricky to fry with because it has a lower smoke point, “I’ve used it,” she says, “and I have never had any problem with it whatsoever.”

Resist the impulse to eyeball your oil for temperature clues, or test bits and pieces to make sure you’re in the right zone, unless you fry so regularly that it’s second nature. Otherwise, that’s a recipe for pieces with burnt exteriors and undercooked interiors, and/or smoking out your upstairs neighbors. (Speaking from experience, sadly.) Using a thermometer, “the correct range for frying is usually between 350 to 400,” says Underwood, which prevents smoking.

Just a bit of residue, which you can easily skim off. Pamela Vachon/CNET

During the frying process, it’s a great idea if you can skim out any crumbs or whatever has come off in the oil,” she says, “because when you have little burned pieces, that will degrade the oil faster.”

After frying: cool, strain, and store

Cool, strain and store. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Once you’re done frying, managing the oil for future use is simple. “First, you let it cool,” says Underwood. Don’t try to speed up the process by refrigerating it; just let it sit until it cools to room temperature.

Straining it is also straightforward and can be done with whatever you already have on hand. “I use a fine mesh strainer,” Underwood says. “People also use cheesecloth or a coffee filter. You just want to strain it and get out all those teeny particles.” Some microparticles may still be visible in the oil after straining, but they will settle once the oil is stored, and it is easy to prevent them from transferring into a pot the next time you want to use it.

Finally, Underwood suggests transferring the oil to a clean and dry container. “It’s very important that it doesn’t have any residual water in it,” she says, “and then just put a lid on it, tightly sealed, and keep it away from heat and light.” If you don’t plan to use it immediately, you can store it in the refrigerator, but any place with a consistent temperature and away from light works.

Considerations for reusing oil

Microparticles may still remain, but will settle during storage. Pamela Vachon/CNET

There’s nothing special that needs doing in order to use preused oil the next time, but bear one thing in mind: “Just be aware that it would now carry allergens from anything that you previously cooked in it,” says Underwood, which is essential to know if you’re cooking for other people.

Since that can be hard to track over multiple uses, “Always label and date it,” she suggests. “I just put a piece of tape on it with the date and the number of uses. And I also actually put what was fried in it,” she says, which can help keep track of potential allergens.

Store in a clear, dry jar with a tight-fitting lid. Pamela Vachon/CNET

It also helps keep potentially odd flavors out of whatever you cook next, as certain items like seafood or onion rings can impart flavor into the oil. “I don’t typically like to fry a savory thing and then fry a sweet thing,” says Underwood. “Like I wouldn’t make schnitzel and then use that oil for a donut.”

If you’re unsure whether an oil is still good to use, let your nose guide you to suss out if something is funky. If you’re not confident in your sniffing ability, Underwood advises smelling unused oil of the same type first, then smelling the used oil for comparison. You can use frying oil at least two or three times, maybe more if it was only used for light-flavored things that didn’t impart many particles and was never overheated.



Benefits of reusing oil

The biggest benefit of reusing frying oil is the savings in every possible regard — you save money, and it’s a much more environmentally friendly practice across the board. “When you’re reusing any product, then you’re lowering the demand for things like production, packaging and transport,” Underwood says. “I don’t think that we think about that big picture very much, but if we were all reusing it, it would reduce those demands on the environment.”

Each time you reuse oil, it also loses a bit of volume. In my experience, at least with shallow frying, you can use the same batch of oil until, after a few uses, nothing remains to discard — the ultimate win.

Tech.title: AI’s Problem Solving Is a ‘Profound Disruption’ for the Math Community
Tech.content:
Artificial intelligence has profoundly shaken up tech, education, entertainment and many aspects of everyday life. Now it’s come for math.

According to companies like OpenAI, the large language models they’re developing internally are solving an unprecedented number of longstanding mathematics problems with the goal to “push the frontier of human knowledge.“

But one thing these AI models apparently can’t do: read the room with the world’s most brilliant mathematical minds.

More from CNET

This week, Open AI released more than 700 math “preprints,” or preliminary research papers, on GitHub. The move further angered an academic math community already so up in arms that last month, 28 Fields Medal winners put up a website called Math and AI with an open letter accusing AI companies of having goals that are “severely misaligned” with those of mathematicians.

The Fields Medal is only awarded every four years (usually to three or four mathematicians) and is widely considered the Nobel Prize of math. One of the winners who signed the website declaration, Harvard professor Curtis McMullen, told CNET in an email that AI companies are not coordinating with math experts or using AI models in ways that could practically benefit society.

“The rollout of mathematical work by frontier AI companies has been carried out with disregard for the profound disruption to our community and its academic ecosystem,” McMullen said. “Its goal appears to be to increase the valuation of these companies at any cost.”

‘We can tell almost nothing’

In the months leading up to the Math and AI website and OpenAI’s repository dump, steam was already building over the outsized impact artificial intelligence would have on the study of mathematics. Given that these models were largely trained on written language and lacked a grasp of ground truth, some initially had such poor math skills that they could frequently misplace decimals or simply hallucinate incorrect answers to math problems.

But, as with other areas of AI advancement, the models have evolved at startling speed, going from so-called math dunces to wizards, even as some suggested that they still had a long way to go before displacing actual math experts.

Those who’ve devoted their lives to math study, however, aren’t just worried about their job security. They have fundamental issues with how AI models and companies approach math, including a lack of transparency in how they’re achieving these results and a lack of understanding about why these math problems matter in the first place. That’s something OpenAI has not addressed since the announcement, which, according to Scientific American, is piling on to a field “already in shock” just a month after the company solved the Navier-Stokes equation, a math problem so tough it had a $1 million bounty attached.

A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately return a request for comment.

In his email to CNET, McMullen acknowledged that the potential for AI as a tool for math research is “undeniable.” But so far, he said, research has not been carried out transparently or in cooperation with scientists. “In particular, the models used to achieve these results should be shared

with the scientists who understand and formulated the conjectures or questions under investigation,” McMullen said.

OpenAI has said that it has formed an advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, but has not detailed how that will work or whether it will share its most advanced models, calling it only “a first step.”

Not everyone is upset about AI’s disruption of math society; for instance, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working for another leading AI company, Anthropic, congratulated the team at OpenAI, posting on X, “There are some sad stories related to their users getting scooped … we should put that aside for today though. It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history.”

Big, big, big, big props for quasiriemann and no Siegel zeroes (with many other beauties in there), I’m kicking myself for talking all over about it being within reach but not actually having pushed.



There are some sad stories related to their users getting scooped / conflicts… — levent (@__alpoge__) October 6, 2026

But the GitHub drop has left many in math upset and without enough information on how many of this new batch of problems were solved. Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote on Substack that the publication “would never pass peer review. We don’t know what the procedure was … From the initial report we can tell almost nothing.”

The mass solving of problems, especially in the absence of context, misses the deeper goal of this study, McMullen said. “Mathematics is not a game of chess,” he said. “Its primary aim is to develop human understanding of abstract structures. Indeed, it is the breadth and versatility of this kind of understanding that underpins technological progress.”

Ironically, that progress includes the AI models that have ingested vast stores of human knowledge. It remains to be seen whether their math proofs will advance human understanding or just create artificial confusion.
